Who sends and who collects the property tax bill in Jackson County, MO?

Two county departments split the work. The Assessment Department values every parcel, and the Department of Collection mails the bills and takes payment. If your question is about what the house is worth on paper, call Assessment at 816-881-1330. If it is about what you owe or how to pay, call Collection at 816-881-3232.

Assessment keeps real property customer service at 1300 Washington St. in Kansas City, and individual personal property at the Historic Truman Courthouse, 112 W. Lexington in Independence. Both counters open at 8 a.m. and close at 5 p.m. on weekdays, and holidays the county observes are closed. Collection also works from both courthouses and answers email at Collections@jacksongov.org.

A seller in Jackson County, Missouri should pull the parcel record from the county's public property access portal before listing. It shows the assessed figures that the bill is built from.

What does Jackson County cover, and who lives here?

Jackson County sits on the Kansas border in western Missouri and has two county seats, Independence and Kansas City. It was organized on December 15, 1826, and the Missouri River forms most of its northern edge. Neighbors include Clay, Cass and Lafayette counties in Missouri and Johnson and Wyandotte counties in Kansas.

The county counts 19 communities, among them Blue Springs, Grandview, Lee's Summit, Raytown, Oak Grove, Grain Valley and Sugar Creek. All of them share one assessment and collection system, with each taxing district adding its own levy line to the statement.

  • Land area: 604.52 square miles
  • Residents counted in the 2025 Census estimate: 732,994, up 2.2% from the 2020 base
  • Homes and apartments: 344,038 units
  • Share of households that own: 59.1%
  • Middle price tag on an owned home: $230,500

Median household income across the 2020 to 2024 survey years is $68,577, and typical gross rent is $1,197. Those who carry a mortgage report a median of $1,639 a month in owner costs, taxes included.

When is the Jackson County property tax bill due?

The bill is due on December 31. The county mails bills during November, and for 2025 the mailing was expected to finish by December 12. If nothing has arrived by about December 8, call the Collector, because an unreceived bill still carries the same deadline.

A mailed check counts only if the USPS stamps it by year end, and the county suggests mailing several days ahead because drop-box mail does not always get a same-day postmark. Checks go to the Jackson County Collector with the property account number written on them. Online payment through payments.jacksongov.org stops at 11:40 p.m. on December 31, and the two courthouse drop boxes lock at midnight that night. Cash should never go in a drop box.

Fees for paying online are a $2.00 transaction charge, plus $1.25 for an e-check or 2.75% for a debit or credit card. Paying in person or by check avoids those add-ons.

What are the key dates and steps for a Jackson County tax year?

Jackson County, MO tax calendar as posted by county offices
ItemWhat the county says
Bills availableEarly November, mailed through early December
Payment deadlineDecember 31, postmark or online cutoff 11:40 p.m.

Appeal bodyBoard of Equalization, 1300 Washington, Kansas City
Next level of appealState Tax Commission
Protest payments mailed toJackson County Collector, Attention: Protest, P.O. Box 219747, Kansas City, MO 64121-9747

Sources: Jackson County Department of Collection FAQ and Board of Equalization pages.

What is the process to contest a Jackson County assessment?

Start with the Board of Equalization, an independent panel of county taxpayers that now sits only at 1300 Washington in Kansas City. The 2026 application window ran until July 13, 2026, so that deadline has passed. Watch the board's page for the 2027 window.

Evidence that carries weight includes a certified appraiser's report, a sales contract with the settlement statement for a recent purchase, and written repair estimates. The board will not look at evidence shown on a phone or tablet at the hearing, and it does not make copies for you.

  • If you signed a stipulated value offered by Assessment, your board appeal is cancelled and you can no longer go to the State Tax Commission.
  • If you skip the stipulation, you keep the hearing, and a loss there can be taken to the State Tax Commission.
  • Commercial appeals to the Commission require a lawyer.
  • Withdrawing an appeal must be in writing from the homeowner and can be done any time.

Must the full bill be paid while a Jackson County appeal is open?

Yes. The county tells owners to pay the printed amount before year end, even when a hearing is still ahead. Recalculations for 2026 appeal decisions are suspended until January 2027, and when a lower value is set, the excess is refunded automatically.

Paying under protest is optional. Missouri statute 139.031 asks for full payment before the delinquency date plus a written statement of the grounds and the value you claim. The county notes that a protest can slow a refund, since protested money is released only on a set schedule, and that protesting does not protect or harm your right to appeal. Partial payments are taken for real property, but interest, penalties and fees accrue on whatever remains unpaid after December 31, and partial payments cannot be made online.

Is there a cap or credit on residential assessments in Jackson County?

The county announced a 15% assessment cap for qualifying residential homeowners, tied to a review of the 2023 single-family assessments. Per the county's FAQ sheet updated December 8, 2025, relief comes as a credit on the 2026, 2027 and 2028 bills, spread evenly across those three years. No application is needed, no refund checks go out, and the 2025 bill still had to be paid in full.

The county says the tax money had already been distributed to schools, fire districts, libraries and cities, which is why it is a credit and not a check. The relief covers residential real estate only, and vehicles and boats are not part of it. Call Assessment if your bill looks wrong rather than assuming a credit has posted.

Which senior programs exist for Jackson County homeowners?

Two county programs apply to residential property, and an eligible owner may use both. The Senior Property Tax Credit offsets future increases. The Senior Citizen Quad Payment Program lets the owner spread the county bill over four equal installments with no interest or penalties.

  • Both require age 62 or older by December 31 of the relevant year and the home as the only primary residence.
  • The Quad program also requires prior-year taxes to be current, a home assessed solely as residential, and ownership by the person, not a trust.
  • Taxes paid from a mortgage escrow are not eligible for the Quad program.
  • The credit covers ad valorem principal only. Special assessments and CID or TDD charges are due in full.

The state Circuit Breaker credit is a separate program run by the Missouri Department of Revenue at 573-751-3505.

Who owes the tax after a Jackson County house changes hands?

Unpaid real estate tax attaches to the parcel itself, so the incoming owner answers for any balance. The county explains that the year's tax is usually split between the two parties, with the buyer credited for the days the seller held title. Normally no money goes to the Collector at the sale itself, though a closing company may pay any amount that is currently due.

Tell the Assessment office the new owner and mailing address, because a bill can otherwise go to the seller's old address. When a lender pays from escrow, send the bill on to the lender. Ask the closing company which tax year it is prorating.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

When does Jackson County, MO stop accepting on-time property tax payments?

At the end of December 31. A mailed check must be postmarked by then, and the online system cuts off at 11:40 p.m. Interest, penalties and fees start accruing the next day.

Is it too late to contest my 2026 Jackson County value?

Yes. The 2026 filing window at the Board of Equalization ended July 13, 2026. Look for the 2027 window on the board's page, and pay the 2026 bill in full by December 31 meanwhile.

Does a refund after a value cut require a protest payment?

No. A lower value triggers an automatic refund, and a protest can slow it down. A protest payment must be on time, in full and accompanied by a written statement.

How is the tax split when a Jackson County home sells midyear?

The buyer owes the full bill by December 31, while the seller's share usually appears as a credit to the buyer at closing. Ask the closing company how your contract divides it.

What address do I use to mail a Jackson County tax payment?

Make it payable to the Jackson County Collector with the property account number on it. Protest payments go to Attention: Protest, P.O. Box 219747, Kansas City, MO 64121-9747. Call 816-881-3232 for the current regular mailing address.

Who answers a property tax question in St. Louis County?

Three county offices share 41 South Central Avenue in Clayton. The Assessor values real estate and personal property, the Board of Equalization hears disputes over that value, and the Collector of Revenue, which sits inside the Department of Revenue, sends the bills and takes the payments.

Who to call at St. Louis County, from county web pages
OfficePhoneEmailHours
Assessor, 3rd floor314-615-2555Assessor@stlouiscountymo.govCounter Mon to Thu 8:00 to 3:30; phone Mon to Fri 8:30 to 4:30
Board of Equalization314-615-7195boe@stlouiscountymo.govSame schedule as the Assessor
Collector of Revenue314-615-7100collector@stlouiscountymo.govCounter Mon to Thu 8:00 to 3:30

The Collector bills for more than 200 taxing districts, which is why two homes in the same city can receive very different totals. Read the district list on your bill line by line, because each line is a separate taxing body.

What sets St. Louis County apart from its neighbors?

Three waterways and one independent city frame the county: the Mississippi and the City of St. Louis to the east, the Missouri River to the north, the Meramec River to the south. About 508 of its 523 square miles are land. Clayton is the seat, Florissant is the biggest city, and the 1,004,125 residents counted in 2020 made it Missouri's most populous county.

The District of St. Louis was renamed St. Louis County on October 1, 1812. The city and county separated in 1877, when voters in the City of St. Louis chose to become an independent city, and in the 1960s suburban growth pushed the county's population past the city's for the first time. The county has since grown into dozens of incorporated municipalities, from Kirkwood, Webster Groves, Ladue and Clayton to Ferguson, Hazelwood, Chesterfield, Wildwood and University City. It also has 23 public school districts, among them Rockwood, Parkway, Lindbergh, Mehlville, Pattonville, Ritenour and Ferguson-Florissant, so the school line on a tax bill varies widely. Several of those districts keep a voluntary transfer agreement with St. Louis Public Schools for magnet programs, and the Special School District of St. Louis County runs schools for students with disabilities.

The QuickFacts profile estimates 990,911 people on July 1, 2025, down 1.4% from the 2020 base, in 448,637 housing units and 413,849 households. Roughly 69.2% of households own, a typical owned home is valued at $276,800, typical rent is $1,209 and typical household income is $82,936 (2020 to 2024). Commutes average 23.1 minutes. Residents 65 and older make up 21.4% of the population, the Census counts 957 building permits for 2025, and the 2020 density was about 1,977 people per square mile.

How often is a St. Louis County home reassessed?

Every odd-numbered year, state law requires the County Assessor to reassess all real estate in the county, according to the county reassessment page. The next reassessment is 2027.

The county site describes the office's aim as treating every owner fairly and giving clear, accurate and timely information. When a notice arrives, compare the value and the property class with what you know about the house, then decide whether to call the Assessor at 314-615-2555 before the appeal window closes. The Assessor answers value questions by phone on weekdays, while in-person visits run Monday through Thursday.

How does a St. Louis County owner dispute a value?

You appeal to the Board of Equalization, which is separate from the Assessor. The board hears value disputes for homeowners, businesses and manufacturers and also considers exemption requests from not-for-profit organizations. Contact it at 314-615-7195 or boe@stlouiscountymo.gov.

  • Deadline: state law, RSMo 137.275, requires the appeal to be lodged with the board on or before the second Monday in July. For 2026 that was July 13, now past. The next is July 12, 2027.
  • Method: the statute allows you to appeal in person, through an attorney or agent, or in writing.
  • Burden of proof: RSMo 138.060 says there is no presumption that the assessor's valuation is correct, and in a charter county with more than one million inhabitants the assessor must prove the value does not exceed true market value. The county counted 1,004,125 residents in 2020, so ask the board how that rule applies to your case.
  • Next step: the State Tax Commission hears appeals from the board's decision. Ask the board for its current filing instructions.

Bring a recent appraisal, a purchase contract, comparable sales or repair estimates to support a lower number.

What happens when St. Louis County tax is paid late?

Penalties begin after January 1. RSMo 139.100 directs the Collector to collect a penalty on unpaid tax after the first day of January, using the amount in RSMo 140.100, which is 18% of each year's delinquency for land in the back tax book. For land redeemed before a sale, the penalty cannot exceed 2% per month or fraction of a month.

Mailing counts. The same statute treats a payment delivered by United States mail as paid on the postmark date, and certified or registered mail uses the registration date. If the postmark falls within the allowed period, no added tax or penalty applies. The Collector's page links to a Pay Taxes page, a tax rates lookup and a customer service portal at csportal.stlouiscountymo.gov.

The Collector's page also carries a 2026 tax bill update. It says the department is aware of issues affecting the accuracy of some bills, including those of owners approved for the senior tax freeze, and that bills had not been mailed when the notice was posted. Check that page before relying on an amount, and call 314-615-7100 if your bill looks wrong.

How do St. Louis County taxes enter a closing?

The county's tax bill is part of every closing here. Title companies ask for a payoff or proration for the current year, and an unpaid prior year carries the 18% penalty described above. Ask the Collector for the balance on your parcel, then give the figure to the closing agent.

If a lender pays your tax from escrow, confirm that the last bill was paid before you list. If a senior tax freeze is on your account and your bill is among those the county says it is correcting, keep the corrected statement with your closing papers, and ask the Collector how the freeze is treated when the property changes hands.

The Collector also handles the county's tax sale for delinquent parcels, a step the Collector's page lists among its duties. The Collector's counter is closed on Fridays and weekends, so a seller who needs a same-week payoff letter should phone early in the week or pay by mail or online. Owners who are behind should ask the Collector for payoff figures and sale dates at 314-615-7100 instead of waiting for a notice.

Frequently asked questions

Where is the Assessor's counter?

Third floor of 41 South Central Avenue, Clayton, MO 63105. Phones are staffed 8:30 to 4:30 on weekdays, and the counter is open Monday through Thursday, 8:00 to 3:30.

Who hears a value appeal?

The Board of Equalization, reached at 314-615-7195 or boe@stlouiscountymo.gov. It operates apart from the Assessor and takes appeals from homeowners, businesses and manufacturers.

What is the filing cutoff for an appeal?

Missouri statute fixes it at the second Monday of July. July 13, 2026 is behind us, so the next one is July 12, 2027. Owners may appear personally, send an agent or attorney, or write.

Do all St. Louis County owners pay the same rate?

No. More than 200 taxing districts appear in the Collector's system, and the ones that cover your parcel set what you owe. A house in one school district can pay differently from a similar house in the next.

Does a postmark on the last day count?

Yes, if it travels by U.S. mail. RSMo 139.100 treats the postmark date as the payment date, and certified or registered mail uses the date of registration. Keep the stamped envelope or receipt.

What is Clay County, Missouri, like for a property owner?

Clay County is the northern suburban side of the Kansas City area. Liberty is the county seat, and Kansas City is the largest city, with a portion of it inside the county. It was organized on January 2, 1822 and named for Henry Clay. At 397 square miles of land it is the fourth-smallest county in Missouri by area, yet the 2020 census made it the fifth most populous with 253,335 residents. The Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 265,032.

The neighbors are Clinton County to the north, Ray to the east, Jackson to the south, Platte to the west and Wyandotte County, Kansas to the southwest. Interstates 29, 35 and 435 cross the county, along with U.S. 69, 71 and 169. Other communities include Gladstone, North Kansas City, Excelsior Springs, Kearney, Smithville and Missouri City.

Where do I pay Clay County property tax and who do I call?

The Collector's site is claycountymo.tax, where residents search a bill, pay and set up prepayments. Two offices take walk-in business, both open Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.

  • Main office: Administration Building, 1 Courthouse Square, Liberty, MO 64068.
  • Clay County Annex: 1901 NE 48th Street, Kansas City, MO 64118.
  • Collector phone: 816-407-3200. Assessor phone: 816-407-3500.
  • County Clerk, who takes Board of Equalization forms: 816-407-3570, with Stacey Tingle as the clerk.

The 2026 payment deadline is posted as Wednesday, December 31, 2026. The county follows the state holiday calendar, and its list shows offices closing at noon on December 24 and staying closed December 25 and 26.

How can I contest a Clay County value?

The county's Board of Equalization page lays out the sequence. Contact the Assessor before you send any form to the Clerk's office. The board can lower a value that sits above true value compared with other properties, and it can also raise one it finds too low, so weigh that before filing. The board page lists four members, with terms ending December 31, 2026, December 31, 2027, December 31, 2028 and January 31, 2027.

StepWhenHow
Informal hearing with an Assessor's appraiserAprilCall the Assessor's office for an appointment
Board of Equalization applicationPostmarked or delivered by 5 p.m. on the second Monday in JulyForms go through the County Clerk
Board of Equalization hearingAugustRequests go through the Clerk's office
State Tax Commission appealSeptember 30, or the 30th day following the board's final action if that falls laterFile after the board decides

The July date matches RSMo 137.275, and the commission step follows RSMo 138.430.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Clay County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What if a Clay County valuation jumped?

Missouri law shifts the burden in one situation. Under RSMo 138.060, when an assessed valuation rose at least 15 percent from the previous assessment, other than from new construction or improvement, the Assessor must prove the valuation does not exceed true market value. The statute also says no presumption exists that the Assessor's figure is correct.

  • Pull the prior and current notices and compare the percentage change.
  • Gather recent sales of similar houses near yours, plus repair estimates for defects the Assessor may not know about.
  • Book the April informal hearing, then decide whether to file with the board by the July deadline.

New residents should know that assessments follow where you lived and what you owned on January 1. The Assessor's office handles people arriving from another county or state, and the collector's site says to bring the previous county's personal property tax receipt to the DMV.

How does the Clay County tax sale work?

Unpaid real estate tax ends up in an online auction run through GovEase. The 2026 calendar shows how the process runs, and every date in it has now passed. Fees of $135 were added to bills still delinquent on May 4, 2026, and $115 more on June 1. The last day to pay by card, personal check or online was June 14, 2026, after which properties headed to sale needed cash, cashier's check or money order. The sale itself opened at 10:00 a.m. on August 24, 2026.

  • Owners of land sold in 2025 had an absolute right to redeem until 5:00 p.m. on August 25, 2026, with funds received in person at the Liberty office. Postmarks and drop box payments did not count.
  • After that, redemption continues until an investor claims a deed.
  • Land that failed to sell after the third offering became available over the counter beginning the week of September 14, 2026.
  • Overbid money is held for the person legally entitled to it. Homeowners and recorded lienholders have 90 days after the deed is claimed to apply, and after 91 days it passes to the county school fund.

The Collector's page also says the office does not partner with or endorse Title Bridge and will not accept due diligence performed by that firm. Only due diligence approved by the Collector's office counts toward a Collector's deed and a redemption.

The page for the next sale shows no 2027 dates yet. Ask the Collector at 816-407-3200 for the schedule.

How do Clay County schools affect a home sale?

School districts serving the county include Liberty, North Kansas City, Kearney, Smithville, Excelsior Springs and Missouri City. Liberty has two high schools, Liberty and Liberty North. North Kansas City runs a larger system with North Kansas City, Oak Park, Staley and Winnetonka high schools.

The Metropolitan Community College district covers the Liberty and North Kansas City portions of the county as its in-district taxing area. William Jewell College, a private four-year school, is in Liberty. Because each district sets its own levy, two houses with the same assessed value can carry different bills, so confirm the district on the statement before you quote a tax figure to a buyer.

What do Census figures say about Clay County housing?

The Census Bureau QuickFacts page for Clay County gives a picture of the market buyers are shopping in.

  • Housing units in 2025: 110,443, with 69.5 percent owner-occupied.
  • Middle value of owner-occupied homes, 2020 to 2024: $275,600.
  • Median gross rent: $1,243.
  • Median household income: $88,468.
  • Population density: 637.1 per square mile in 2020.
  • Building permits issued in 2025: 297.
  • Mean travel time to work: 22.8 minutes.

About 91.9 percent of residents lived in urban areas at the 2020 census, and 8.1 percent in rural areas.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Clay County, MO property tax due date for 2026?

Wednesday, December 31, 2026, according to the Collector's holiday and dates table. Offices are closed December 25 and 26 and open again after that. Pay at the Liberty courthouse, at the Annex on NE 48th Street in Kansas City, or through claycountymo.tax.

Who do I call to dispute my Clay County assessment?

Call the Assessor at 816-407-3500 and ask for an informal hearing, which is held in April with an appraiser. If that does not settle it, the County Clerk at 816-407-3570 handles Board of Equalization forms, and the board application is due by 5 p.m. on the second Monday in July.

Can the Clay County Board of Equalization raise my value?

Yes. The county's board page says the board can lower a value that exceeds true value compared with other properties, and it can raise a value it finds too low. Weigh that before filing, and bring comparable sales that support your number.

When is the Clay County tax sale?

The 2026 sale was held online through GovEase starting at 10:00 a.m. on August 24, 2026, so it has passed. The 2027 date is not posted on the Collector's tax sale page. Call 816-407-3200 for the schedule, and for redemption or overbid questions.

Do I owe Clay County tax if I just moved here?

Assessment depends on where you lived and what you owned on January 1. A person who moved in from another Missouri county or from out of state should call the Assessor at 816-407-3500. Use the personal property tax receipt from the earlier county when you register a vehicle.

Which Boone County offices handle a property tax bill?

The Assessor puts a value on each parcel, and the Collector turns that value into a bill and takes the money. The Collector's counter is in Room 118 of the Boone County Government Center, on the southwest corner of Ninth and Ash streets in Columbia. Office hours run 8:00 AM to 5:00 PM Monday through Friday, and the phone is (573) 886-4285.

Boone County stretches across 691 square miles of central Missouri, and the Missouri River marks its southern line. Columbia is the seat. Ashland, Centralia, Hallsville, Rocheport and Sturgeon are the other cities, while Harrisburg, Hartsburg, Huntsdale, McBaine and Pierpont are villages. Public schools come from several districts, among them Columbia 93, Southern Boone R-I, Centralia R-VI, Hallsville R-IV, Harrisburg R-VIII and Sturgeon R-V, and each district adds its own levy to the bill.

What do Census figures say about housing in Boone County?

84,371 housing units in Boone County for 2025 and estimates 191,746 residents. Only 57.7 percent of households own their home, which suits a county anchored by the University of Missouri, Columbia College and Stephens College. Sellers here often deal with tenants, investors and out-of-town heirs.

  • Typical home worth, 2020-2024 survey period: $272,800
  • Median household income: $72,758
  • Median gross rent: $1,088 a month
  • New building permits in 2025: 787
  • Residents 25 and older holding a four-year degree: 51.5 percent

Multiply that typical $272,800 value by the 19 percent residential assessment rate the Collector lists and you reach roughly $51,832 of assessed value, the figure the levy is applied against.

When must a Boone County tax bill be paid?

Payment is due once the bill is in hand, and the hard stop is the last day of the year. The Collector mails statements through November. If yours has not shown up by December 10, call the office, because a lost envelope does not erase the tax or the penalties.

A mailed check is on time when the postal postmark reads December 31 or earlier, a rule found in RSMo 139.100. The Collector's FAQ warns that mail drop boxes sometimes stamp the next day, so it recommends mailing several days early. In person, a drop box under the shelter at the Ninth Street entrance accepts payments until midnight on New Year's Eve.

After that, the Collector's FAQ says late charges grow every month starting in January until the account is cleared. Once a parcel is entered in the back tax book, RSMo 140.100 charges 18 percent of that year's delinquency, or at most 2 percent per month for an owner who redeems ahead of the sale.

Which dates matter on the Boone County tax calendar?

The county's Assessor and Collector pages supply the schedule below. The 2026 appeal window has closed, so anyone who missed it needs to watch for next year's notices.

Boone County tax calendar, from the Assessor and Collector pages
WhenEvent
January 1Value is fixed as the property stands on this day
Mid April to early MayReal estate assessment notices are mailed
Late April to mid JuneInformal hearings with Assessor staff
July 1Rolls are certified to the taxing jurisdictions
July 13, 2026Board of Equalization filing deadline for the 2026 year (passed)
September 30State Tax Commission filing limit, or 30 days after a board ruling
NovemberCollector mails the bills
December 31Final day to pay or postmark without charges
Fourth Monday of AugustTax certificate sale at 10:00 AM on the courthouse steps

What if my Boone County assessment looks too high?

The Assessor's page lays out three stages, and you move up one stage at a time.

  • Contact the Assessor as soon as your notice arrives. A short informal meeting shows how the value was built and settles many disputes.
  • Still unhappy? Complete the Board of Equalization appeal form and send it to the County Clerk. The county says the postmark must fall on or before July's second Monday unless the board extends the date.
  • Take the board's ruling to the Missouri State Tax Commission by September 30 or one month after the decision letter, whichever falls later.

The right to that last step comes from RSMo 138.430. The Tax Commission adds a practical tip: you may pay under protest. Send the whole bill by year's end with "paid under protest" on the check, then file a written statement with the Collector naming the market value you claim. Miss the appeal window and the only path left is to challenge next year's number.

Can Boone County taxes be paid in monthly installments?

They can. The Collector offers a plan covering real estate taxes and Neighborhood Improvement District assessments, and the current bill must be paid before you join. Each month's amount comes from last year's base tax divided by the months remaining, so a plan that begins in March spreads the base across ten payments.

The December installment is trued up to match the actual bill, and the balance must clear by December 31 or the plan can end and late fees apply. You can pay by coupon with cash, check or money order, by bank debit on the 5th or 20th, or by credit card on the 20th with 2.3 percent added.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Boone County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How are escrowed taxes handled in Boone County?

Where a lender collects tax money along with the mortgage payment, the lender requests the bill and pays it. If the request came before October 1, the owner gets an informational statement showing that the lien holder asked for it. A statement without that note should be forwarded to the mortgage company immediately.

Responsibility stays with the owner, though. The Collector's FAQ says unpaid real estate bills collect penalties after December 31 even when a servicer was meant to pay, so anyone with a new servicer or a loan that was just paid off should verify where the bill is going. Owners without escrow can pay directly from the informational statement.

Who owes the Boone County tax after a sale closes?

The buyer inherits it. The Collector's page states that tax is a lien riding with the real estate, so a new owner answers for any unpaid balance. That page also says buyers pay the full bill by December 31, that the parties usually prorate by months or days owned, and that no tax money is handed to the Collector on closing day.

Watch the calendar on closings from October 1 onward. The bill may still be printed under the seller's name and sent to the old address unless the buyer reports the new ownership to the Collector or Assessor. A seller who receives a bill for a house already sold should pass the buyer's name and mailing address to the Collector. For back taxes, RSMo 140.150 lets an owner pay the delinquent tax, penalty and costs to the Collector right up to the moment of sale.

Frequently asked questions

What is the last day to pay Boone County property tax?

December 31. A payment in hand or postmarked by then avoids charges. Bills go out during November, and charges build each month from January.

Where can I pay in person?

Visit Room 118 of the Boone County Government Center in Columbia between 8:00 AM and 5:00 PM on weekdays. A drop box at the Ninth Street entrance accepts payments until midnight on December 31.

Does the county auction tax certificates?

Yes. According to the Collector's page, the annual sale takes place on the fourth Monday of August at 10:00 AM on the courthouse steps and covers real estate with unpaid taxes.

What was the 2026 Board of Equalization deadline?

Monday, July 13, 2026, the second Monday of that month. It has passed, so the next chance comes with the following year's assessment notices.

Do I owe the tax if I never received a bill?

Yes. The Collector states that a missing bill does not release the owner from the tax or the late fees. Call (573) 886-4285 if nothing has arrived by December 10.

Where is Cape Girardeau County and how did it form?

Along the Mississippi in southeast Missouri sits Cape Girardeau County, where Jackson is the seat and Cape Girardeau is the biggest city. Land area is 579 square miles, with 7.8 more of water. The land varies widely: the areas around Delta and Dutchtown are flood plains once farmed as cotton plantations, while the western and northern parts are hilly and forested.

The county was organized on October 1, 1812, as one of five original counties of the Missouri Territory. It takes its name from Sieur Jean Baptiste de Girardot, a French officer who founded a trading post on the river in 1733. The present courthouse in Jackson was completed in 1908 after the first one, built in 1818, burned in 1870.

Neighbors are Perry, Scott, Stoddard and Bollinger Counties in Missouri, and Union and Alexander Counties across the river in Illinois.

Which towns and school districts are in Cape Girardeau County?

The cities are Cape Girardeau, Delta, Jackson and Scott City, though most of Scott City lies in Scott County. A buyer's school district often drives the price, and these districts serve the county:

  • Jackson R-II, with schools from Gordonville and Millersville to Jackson High School
  • Cape Girardeau Public Schools No. 63
  • Delta R-V, Oak Ridge R-VI and Nell Holcomb R-IV

The Assessor's page says new address requests are only for land outside the limits of Cape Girardeau and Jackson, so a house inside either city goes through that city's planning office instead.

What do the Census figures show for Cape Girardeau County?

Of the four Missouri counties in the Census comparison, this one has the lowest owner-occupancy rate and the highest health care receipts. The table lists Census QuickFacts figures.

MeasureCape Girardeau County
People living here, July 2025 estimate83,999
Homes with owner occupants66.8%
Typical owner-occupied home value, 2020-2024$220,700
Typical monthly gross rent$881
Adults 25 and up with a bachelor's degree or more33.1%
Health care and social assistance receipts, 2022$1.2 billion

Growth of 2.8 percent from the April 2020 base, and workers average a 19.5 minute trip to work, the shortest of the four counties. Builders took out 99 permits in 2025. Because a third of the housing is rented, many Cape Girardeau County sellers are landlords with tenants, and the same tax rules apply to them.

Which offices deal with property tax in Cape Girardeau County?

Most of them sit in the Jackson administration building at One Barton Square, and the Collector has a second office in the city.

  • Assessor Robert Adams: 1 Barton Square, Suite 201, Jackson, 573-243-2468. Real estate appraisal questions go to appraisal@capecounty.us.
  • Collector Barbara Gholson: Suite 303 in Jackson, 573-243-4476, and 2311 Bloomfield Road, Suite 102, Cape Girardeau, 573-335-2606. Hours are 8:00 to 4:30 on weekdays.
  • County Clerk Kara Clark Summers: 100 Court Street, Suite 301, Jackson, where appeal forms go.
  • Recorder of Deeds Andrew Blattner: Suite 203, 573-243-8123.

Treasurer Ronnie Maxwell sits at 100 Court Street, Suite 202, and tax payments go to the Collector instead.

How do I pay Cape Girardeau County property tax?

Tax bills fall due on receipt, and the county gives December 31 as the final day free of late charges. The Collector offers several ways to pay.

  • In person at either office, by cash, check, money order, cashier's check or card.
  • A drop box by the front door and in the south lot in Jackson, or the door slot at the Bloomfield Road office.
  • By mail to One Barton Square, Suite 303, Jackson, postmarked by the end of the month you are paying in.
  • Online or by telephone at 1-877-690-3729 with jurisdiction code 3516, each with a service fee.

If you need an immediate receipt, pay at the Collector's Office, since online and phone confirmations are not a paid receipt and the paid receipt takes several days. Credit cards are no longer taken by phone or mail. You can search or print tax bills and receipts through the county's online tax portal, using the owner name, parcel number or address for real estate.

How do I appeal a Cape Girardeau County assessment?

Start with the Assessor's office. The county reassesses real property as of January 1 of every odd-numbered year under RSMo 137.115, as the Assessor's page explains, and new improvements are added when they are finished. The appeal then runs in three steps:

  1. Informal hearing: call 573-243-3123 before the second Monday in July.
  2. Board of Equalization: hearings begin the third Monday in July, and signed forms must reach the County Clerk before the second Monday.
  3. State Tax Commission: file by September 30 or within 30 days of the Board's decision, whichever is later.

The county asks for evidence that the value as of January 1 is wrong. It lists a recent appraisal by a Missouri appraiser, a broker opinion of value from the last three years, an arm's-length sales contract from the past year, or repair and construction cost records. Foreclosure sales, tax sales and sales between relatives do not count as market evidence. Corporations, LLCs and partnerships file through an authorized agent, and at the State Tax Commission they need an attorney.

What tax credits did Cape Girardeau County voters approve in 2026?

On April 7, 2026, voters approved two real estate credits that limit increases on a primary residence. Proposition A is a senior credit for owners 62 and older under SB 190 and SB 756. Proposition B is a general homestead credit under SB 3 for any owner who lives in the home.

  • You must own the home, live there and owe the tax on it.
  • Rental property, commercial property and farmland do not qualify.
  • Delinquent taxes, interest or penalties block the credit.
  • The 2026 application period closed on June 30, 2026. The 2027 period runs February 1 to April 15, 2027.

The credit is applied to the November tax statement and is not a refund. It does not transfer to a new home or a new owner, and a transfer of title removes it, so a seller loses the benefit at closing and a buyer applies afresh. Questions go to homestead@capecounty.us or 573-987-5010. For the state statute, see RSMo 137.1050. The county also notes the Missouri Property Tax Credit claim, which uses Form 948 signed by the Assessor.

When is the Cape Girardeau County tax sale?

The 2026 Land Tax Sale took place on August 24, 2026, on the third floor of the Administration Building at 10:00 a.m., and the 2025 sale was held August 25, 2025. State law, RSMo 140.150, sets the sale on the fourth Monday in August each year, so the next one should fall in August 2027. Check the Collector's page for the parcel list, which changes as taxes are paid.

The statute requires a first-class mailed notice to the record owner and, for parcels assessed above $1,000, a second notice by certified mail. A missed notice does not cancel the debt. If your parcel went in the 2025 sale, call 573-243-4476 and the Collector will calculate redemption for your chosen date.

Taxes unpaid after the first of January carry a penalty, and land on the back tax book carries 18 percent per year of delinquency under RSMo 140.100. The statute lets an owner pay the Collector the back taxes with penalty, interest and costs at any time before the property is sold.

What should I do about taxes and the deed when I sell in Cape Girardeau County?

Pull the parcel record from the Collector's portal and the Assessor's real estate search, and confirm the owner name and any open balance. Let the title company pay a balance from proceeds, since unpaid tax stays attached to the land.

Recording is at the Recorder's office in Jackson. The office announced that marriage license and recording fees rise by $2 on August 28, 2026, and the Recorder reports document fees are split among county and state funds. Ask 573-243-8123 for the current deed fee before closing.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I pay property tax in Cape Girardeau County?

At the Collector's offices in Jackson (One Barton Square, Suite 303) or Cape Girardeau (2311 Bloomfield Road, Suite 102), in a drop box, by mail, online or by phone. Call 573-243-4476 or 573-335-2606 with questions.

What is the due date for real estate tax in Cape Girardeau County?

Due on receipt, with December 31 the last day before late charges. By mail, the envelope should carry a postmark no later than the end of the month you are paying in.

How late can I appeal a Cape Girardeau County assessment?

Get signed forms to the County Clerk ahead of the second Monday in July. Hearings begin the third Monday, and a State Tax Commission appeal is due September 30 or 30 days after the Board rules, whichever comes later.

Did Cape Girardeau County pass a homestead tax credit?

Yes. Voters approved a senior credit and a general homestead credit on April 7, 2026. Applications for 2027 open February 1 and close April 15, 2027, and delinquent taxes disqualify an applicant.

Does the Cape Girardeau County tax credit transfer when I sell?

No. The credit is tied to the primary residence and the owner who applied, so it does not move to a new home or a new owner. A buyer who qualifies must apply on their own.

Which Greene County offices deal with property tax?

Three county offices touch a Springfield-area tax bill. The Assessor values the property, the County Clerk runs the appeals board and builds the tax book, and the Collector of Revenue bills and takes payment. The Collector's page says the Assessor's values go to the Clerk, who applies the levies voters approved to produce the yearly tax book.

  • Collector of Revenue Allen Icet: (417) 868-4036, open weekdays from 8:00 with no lunch closure, and shut on November 26 and 27, 2026
  • Assessor Brent Johnson: 940 N Boonville Ave, Room 35, Springfield, (417) 868-4101 for real estate and (417) 868-4195 for personal property
  • County Clerk and Board of Equalization: 940 North Boonville, Springfield, MO 65802

The Assessor's door opens at 8:00 on most weekdays and at 8:30 on Wednesday, and both offices close at 4:30. The Collector's site lets owners look up statements and receipts, and card payments carry a processor charge of 1.5 percent for debit and 2.3 percent for credit (with a $2 minimum), or $1 for an e-check. That charge goes to the processor and not to the county.

After an online payment, the receipt posts to your account on the site within about three hours and is not emailed. Pay in the office when you need a receipt the same day, for example at a closing.

What does Greene County look like to someone selling a house?

Greene County lies in southwest Missouri, in the Ozark foothills, with Springfield as its seat and biggest city. The county was organized in 1833 and carries the name of Revolutionary War general Nathanael Greene. Wilson's Creek National Battlefield sits inside it. It borders Polk, Dallas, Webster, Christian, Lawrence and Dade counties.

Besides Springfield, the cities and towns are Ash Grove, Battlefield, Fair Grove, Republic, Rogersville, Strafford, Walnut Grove and Willard. Roughly 86 percent of residents were counted in urban areas in 2020.

From the Census QuickFacts table for Greene County:

  • 309,286 residents in the July 2025 estimate, and 442.6 people per square mile of land in 2020
  • 142,405 housing units, with 57.5 percent of homes owner-occupied
  • $221,300 median value of owner-occupied homes (2020 to 2024) beside a $989 median gross rent
  • $61,479 median household income
  • 966 building permits in 2025

How does the Greene County Assessor reach a value?

The Assessor is elected for four years, and Brent Johnson has held the office since 2021. The office's job is to list every taxable parcel and assess it each year as of January 1. It also maintains the tax map, changing parcel lines when the Recorder of Deeds sends warranty deeds, so a lot split or combined shows up there after the deed is recorded.

The state formula in RSMo 137.115 sets the residential ratio at 19 percent, with fresh values arriving in odd-numbered years such as 2027. A house increase above 15 percent has to be backed by an on-site inspection.

The Assessor runs a Public Access website, updated nightly, that shows address, owner, taxing district, school district, section, township and range, and map layers for lots, fire districts and city limits. Use it to confirm the taxing districts before comparing your bill with a neighbor's.

What are the steps to appeal a Greene County assessment?

Greene County's Clerk lays out three steps, shown in the table. The informal step is optional, and the County Clerk's page confirms that skipping it does not stop an owner from filing a formal appeal.

Greene County real estate appeal path, per the County Clerk
StepWhereDeadline
Informal talk with an appraiserAssessor, (417) 868-4101As soon as the notice arrives
Formal appealCounty Clerk, 940 North BoonvilleSecond Monday in July (July 13 in 2026)
State appealMissouri State Tax CommissionSeptember 30, or a month after the Board rules if that is later

The 2026 form deadline has passed. For the 2027 reassessment the same rule points to the second Monday in July, which is July 12, 2027.

The Board of Equalization has eight members, three named by the County Commission and five by the City of Springfield, and it meets at 9:00 a.m. on the second Tuesday of each month at 1126 N Boonville to certify tax book corrections. Each July it hears formal appeals, and in 2026 those hearings were in Room 212 of the Historic Greene County Courthouse. At the hearing the Assessor presents evidence for the value, and the owner answers with evidence of their own. The Board may raise, lower or leave the figure alone.

Does Greene County have a senior property tax freeze?

Yes. The Collector runs a Senior Tax Credit that lets qualifying seniors lock their real estate tax bill so it stays frozen in future years. Applications run January 1 through June 30 each year, so the window for 2026 has closed and the next opens January 1, 2027.

Collector Allen Icet announced that annual renewal is no longer required as of January 1, 2026. Credit holders must report a change in ownership or occupancy within 45 days and answer any audit request within 45 days. Remote applications need a copy of a government photo ID that shows the date of birth.

This matters when a house is sold. Report the sale within the 45 days, and ask the Collector's office what happens to the credit when ownership changes.

What happens to Greene County taxes that go unpaid?

A bill still open on January 1 picks up the statutory penalty (RSMo 140.100), set at 18 percent of the year's delinquency. Mailed payments are judged by postmark.

An owner contesting a value can pay in full before the delinquency date and file a written statement with the Collector naming the grounds and the claimed value. RSMo 139.031 then requires a suit against the Collector within 90 days. The State Tax Commission adds that an appeal can be filed before the bill is paid, but penalty and interest still apply if the bill is late.

Land with unpaid years can be offered at the August tax sale after the owner of record has been notified by mail. The owner can still pay off the balance before the sale. Ask the Collector at (417) 868-4036 for current figures.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Greene County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How should I deal with property tax when selling a Greene County house?

Look up the parcel on the Collector's statements and receipts page, print what is owed and give the figure to the title company. Check the Public Access map for the school and fire district, since buyers ask. If a senior credit is on the property, tell the Collector about the sale within the 45 day window.

Owners holding a vacant inherited home, a long tenant lease or a roof that needs work can ask for a written cash offer, with the tax balance settled out of the price at closing.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I pay Greene County property tax?

To the Greene County Collector of Revenue, online or in person, at (417) 868-4036. Weekday hours run until 4:30 p.m. Card and e-check payments carry a processor fee, and online receipts post within about three hours.

What was the 2026 Greene County appeal deadline?

July 13, 2026, the second Monday in July. The County Clerk had to receive the Board of Equalization form by then. That date has passed, and the 2027 deadline falls on the second Monday in July.

Do I have to see the Assessor before filing an appeal?

No. The County Clerk says an informal meeting with the Assessor is not required before a Board of Equalization appeal. Many owners still call the Assessor at (417) 868-4101 first because concerns are often settled there.

Can a Greene County senior freeze property tax?

Yes, through the Collector's Senior Tax Credit. Applications are taken January 1 to June 30. Annual renewal stopped being required on January 1, 2026, but ownership or occupancy changes must be reported within 45 days.

Who sits on the Greene County Board of Equalization?

Eight taxpayer citizens. The County Commission appoints three and the City of Springfield appoints five. The County Clerk serves as non-voting secretary, and the Board hears formal appeals each July.

Who values, bills and collects property tax in St. Charles County?

The job is split between two elected officials. One sets the market value of every parcel, and the other mails a single combined statement and hands the receipts to schools, fire districts and the rest. You will find both in the county Administration Building downtown, 201 N. Second Street, on a weekday schedule of 8 to 5.

  • Assessor Travis Welge: 636-949-7425 (real estate values), 636-949-7428 (informal hearings outside a reassessment year), 636-949-7420 (personal property).
  • Collector of Revenue Michelle D. McBride: Suite 134, 636-949-7470.
  • Payment website named in the county's tax guide: stcharlesmocollector.org.

Rates are not theirs to set. Each taxing body adopts its own levy, and the Collector's page says roughly 3% of what is collected remains with county government. Each parcel in the county falls under at least six jurisdictions: the state, the county, a school district, a fire district, an ambulance district and a library. Where you live inside the county therefore changes the total.

What makes St. Charles County distinctive for sellers?

Named for Charles Borromeo and organized October 1, 1812, the county takes in 593 square miles (560 of them land) of east central Missouri. St. Charles is the seat and O'Fallon is the biggest city. After the 2020 census only two Missouri counties were larger.

Growth followed the highways. Interstate 70 crosses the middle of the county, Interstate 64 serves the southwest, and Routes 364 and 370 connect the suburbs with St. Louis County. The wedge bounded by I-70, I-64 and Route 94 was once nicknamed the Golden Triangle and is now called the Westplex, home to St. Charles, St. Peters, O'Fallon, Lake St. Louis, Wentzville, Cottleville, Dardenne Prairie and Weldon Spring. High schools sort into five districts (Fort Zumwalt, Francis Howell, Orchard Farm, St. Charles and Wentzville), and each district puts its own line on the bill.

426,499 residents as of July 1, 2025, living among 174,278 housing units. Four of every five occupied homes are owned (80.5%), and the 2020 to 2024 survey puts the typical owned home at $320,800, with households earning a median $104,692 and renters paying a median $1,370. Workers travel 24.5 minutes on average.

How is a St. Charles County home valued?

The Assessor estimates what each property would sell for on the open market as of the tax date. Real estate is revalued every odd-numbered year, new construction is added to the rolls annually, and personal property such as vehicles is assessed every year (Assessor page).

The office says it looks at several kinds of information:

  • Property type: residential, commercial, industrial or agricultural.
  • Structure measurements, checked against building permits and aerial photography.
  • Location data such as zoning, road access and neighborhood.
  • Recent sales of similar properties, leaving out sales far above or below normal market value.

An assessment is a mass appraisal built on statistics for groups of similar homes. It is different from a sale price, which is the amount a buyer actually paid, and from an appraisal, which is one detailed opinion of a single property made for a private purpose. If your value moved although you changed nothing, the cause is usually the market for similar homes. Assessment notices go out each April under the county's guide, and the Assessor's website carries a property database for looking up your parcel.

What are the St. Charles County payment dates and methods?

Statements for real estate and personal property are issued by December 1. Tax is owed by December 31, and anything received once January begins picks up the penalty and interest printed on the statement. An undelivered bill does not excuse the debt.

  • In person at the first-floor payment windows or the drop boxes at 201 N. Second Street. Cash is accepted at the windows only; checks, money orders and cashier's checks can go in the drop boxes.
  • By mail to the Collector at Room 134. Mailed payments count as of the postmark, and cash should not be mailed.
  • By phone on the toll-free tax payment line, 1-855-227-7840, with the bill number ready.
  • Online at stcharlesmocollector.org. If you use your own bank's bill pay, start it at least five working days before December 31.

Owners who cannot pay the whole bill can make partial payments before December 31, which lowers the late interest and penalty that would otherwise apply. The Collector also takes advance payments during the year. Lenders and tax services receive an electronic bill file for escrow accounts, but the owner remains responsible for the full amount.

How does a St. Charles County owner contest a value?

There are three steps, and skipping the middle one closes the door on the last. Start with the informal hearing, go to the Board of Equalization if you disagree with the result, and only then reach the Missouri State Tax Commission (county appeal page).

  1. Informal hearing with an Assessor's staff member, held from the end of April through early June. The notice says to schedule within 10 days of its mailing date. Useful evidence includes a recent sales contract, a licensed appraiser's report, comparable sales and photographs of defects.
  2. Board of Equalization. The appeal form must reach the county Registrar by 5 p.m. on the second Monday in July. In 2026 that was July 13 and it has passed; the next one is July 12, 2027. The board hears cases in July and August.
  3. State Tax Commission. The filing deadline is September 30 or 30 days after the board's decision, whichever is later. For a property bought after the second Monday in June, the deadline is December 31.

The Assessor warns owners to be careful about companies that charge a fee to dispute a value, since the data they use is public and available free from the office. An agent who gives valuation opinions in Missouri must be certified or licensed.

Is there senior tax relief in St. Charles County?

Yes. The Collector runs a Senior Real Estate Property Tax Relief Program for the primary residence of residents who were at least 62 and living in the home on January 1 of the tax year. You must apply or renew every year to keep the credit.

The program began with tax year 2024 and works as a credit against future increases. A person who becomes eligible on January 1, 2026 sets the base year with the November 2026 bill and should not expect a reduction on that bill. The credit covers every taxing jurisdiction on the bill, including schools and fire districts, but it excludes bond debt levies and the State Blind Pension Fund. Only real estate qualifies, so a mobile home taxed as personal property does not. The 2026 application window ran March 1 to July 6, 2026 and has closed (program page). Ask the Collector at 636-949-7470 when the 2027 window opens.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy St. Charles County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Who owes the tax if a St. Charles County house sells?

Whoever holds title at the end of the tax year owes that year's bill. In practice the title company prorates the current year's tax between buyer and seller at closing, and the buyer pays the full bill in December (county tax guide).

Before you list, pull your parcel from the Assessor's database and compare the current value with recent sales on your street. If the value looks high and the second Monday in July is still ahead, the appeal steps above apply to you. If you owe back tax, the Collector holds the county tax sale each August, a process required by state law, so clear any delinquency well before then. Ask the Collector for a current payoff figure and hand it to the closing agent.

Which dates shape the St. Charles County tax year?

Yearly rhythm of assessment and tax in St. Charles County
DateWhat happens
January 1 of odd yearsAssessor revalues all real estate as of this date
March 1Personal property forms due to the Assessor
AprilNotices of Real Estate Assessment mailed
Late April to early JuneInformal hearings with the Assessor
Board filing cutoff (second Monday of July)Appeals due to the Board of Equalization by 5 p.m.
AugustCollector's annual tax sale of delinquent parcels
September 30State Tax Commission filing deadline, or 30 days after the board decision if later
By December 1Collector issues tax bills
December 31Final day for penalty-free payment

Sources: the county's Assessor, Collector and appeal process pages and the Assessor and Collector guide.

Frequently asked questions

Which office answers questions about a St. Charles County bill?

Call the Collector of Revenue at 636-949-7470 about bills and payments, and the Assessor at 636-949-7425 about value and classification. Both offices are at 201 N. Second Street in St. Charles and open weekdays from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Can a St. Charles County bill be paid in pieces?

You can pay part of it before December 31, which reduces the late interest and penalty that would otherwise build up. The Collector applies each partial payment to the base tax, interest and penalty and issues a receipt every time. Advance payments toward a future bill are also accepted.

When does St. Charles County reassess next?

Real estate is revalued every odd-numbered year under Missouri law, so 2027 is next. Notices arrive in April, and the informal hearing window runs from the end of April to early June. New construction is added to the rolls each year in between.

What if the Board of Equalization deadline is missed?

Missing it usually ends your appeal for that year. The county page warns that failing to file with the board blocks a further appeal to the State Tax Commission, except for newly purchased property. The deadline is 5 p.m. on the second Monday in July, which is July 12 in 2027.

Who covers the tax share at a St. Charles County closing?

Both, for their share of the year. The county guide says taxes are often prorated at closing and that the buyer then pays the whole bill at year end. Ask your title company for the proration worksheet before you sign.

How does Randolph County tax a house?

In Randolph County the Assessor values each parcel and the Collector sends the bill, and both offices work from the courthouse in Huntsville. Values are fixed on the first of January, statements follow in autumn, and the full amount must reach the Collector before the year closes.

The county sits in north-central Missouri and covers 488 square miles. It was organized on January 22, 1829, and Moberly, which grew up around a railroad repair yard, is the largest city. Huntsville is the seat. Clark, Clifton Hill and Higbee are the other cities, and Cairo, Jacksonville and Renick are villages. Macon, Monroe, Shelby, Audrain, Boone, Howard and Chariton counties surround it, and U.S. 24, U.S. 63 and Route 3 cross it. The Census Bureau counted 24,716 people in 2020 and estimates 24,513 for July 1, 2025.

The school district printed on your statement drives much of the bill. Houses fall in Moberly, Westran R-I at Huntsville, Higbee R-VIII, Northeast Randolph County R-IV at Cairo or Renick R-V, and each district has its own levy. Compare two Randolph County addresses only after checking that line. Moberly also hosts Moberly Area Community College and Central Christian College of the Bible, so rental demand near campus can differ from the rural townships.

Which Randolph County offices handle my tax questions?

Every county office is in the courthouse at 372 Hwy. JJ, Huntsville, MO 65259. Most keep weekday hours between eight in the morning and four in the afternoon. The main number is 844-277-6555, and each office has its own extension. The county home page links to the Collector's site and to the Assessor's property search.

  • Collector: Michelle Lee, Suite 1G, extension 310. Her office takes in current and back tax and passes it to the schools, cities, library, ambulance and fire districts.
  • Assessor: sets values and changes mailing addresses. Parcel records are searchable from the link on the county home page.
  • County Clerk: the place to ask for equalization board forms and dates.
  • County Commission: meets Tuesdays and Wednesdays at 9 a.m., with agendas on the county site.

Mortgage companies also call the Collector for tax figures or to pay from escrow. Bills are posted online now, so if yours is missing from the Collector's search, the page directs you to the Assessor.

What share of my home's value does Randolph County tax?

The Assessor starts from market value and taxes only a slice of it. RSMo 137.115 sets that slice at nineteen percent for houses, twelve percent for farmland and thirty-two percent for commercial parcels.

The Assessor revalues in odd years, using the January 1 date, and the figure rolls into the following even year unless a building is added. The next reset is January 1, 2027. When a house's value jumps more than fifteen percent for reasons other than new construction, the statute calls for an on-site inspection, and the owner can ask that the inside be viewed as well.

Census figures for the county show the kind of house those percentages are applied to.

What the Census Bureau reports for Randolph County housing, 2020 to 2024
MeasureRandolph County

Owner households71.4%
Households counted9,247

Figures from the Randolph County QuickFacts page, which also lists 89 building permits for 2025 and 10,977 housing units.

When does Randolph County want its tax money, and how can I pay?

The deadline is the last day of December. The Collector takes payment at the courthouse, by mail, through the drop box at the front of the building, at the drive-up window and online with Discover, MasterCard or Visa. The online convenience fee goes to the card processor, and the county shows the amount before you confirm.

A mailed check counts on its postmark. RSMo 139.100 treats mail as paid on the date stamped on the envelope, and a postal delay does not bring a penalty when the postmaster verifies it in writing. Once January arrives, the penalty in RSMo 140.100 applies: eighteen percent of the year's delinquency on land in the back tax book, capped at two percent a month on land redeemed before a sale.

  • Online, the oldest unpaid year has to be paid before the current one.
  • An unreceived statement does not excuse a late payment.
  • A receipt downloads after a search by name, account number or parcel number.

What can I do if I think my Randolph County value is too high?

Talk to the Assessor first, take the matter to the equalization board next and then, if needed, to the State Tax Commission. The commission advises calling the Assessor's office as soon as the notice arrives, asking how the value was reached and bringing proof of market value.

When the conversation does not settle it, ask the County Clerk for the equalization board's forms and filing dates. Under RSMo 138.060 the board decides appeals in a summary way, and no presumption favors the Assessor's number. A further appeal goes to the State Tax Commission under RSMo 138.430, due on September 30 or thirty days after the board's last action, whichever falls later.

Evidence outweighs frustration with the bill. The commission says that calling taxes too high is not relevant testimony, while a recent sale, photographs or an appraiser's opinion are. An owner who wants to protest the tax itself pays the whole bill before the delinquency date and files a written statement with the Collector, then has ninety days to file suit under RSMo 139.031.

Who covers the tax when a Randolph County house sells?

Ask the Collector for the balance before you sign a purchase contract, then expect the closing agent to divide the year's tax between seller and buyer. The January 1 assessment date means the bill stays with the parcel when ownership changes midyear.

A few habits keep a sale from stalling over tax:

  • Get a written statement of current and any delinquent amounts from Suite 1G.
  • Hand the title company the parcel number from the Assessor's record.
  • After closing, send both offices the buyer's mailing address so the next statement reaches the new owner.
  • Where a lender pays from escrow, confirm the payment posted before you list.

Owners with back taxes, an estate house or a vacant property in Moberly, Huntsville or a village sometimes pick a cash sale to close within weeks. That buyer needs the same payoff numbers, so the Collector's statement is the first paper to request whichever route you take.

Frequently asked questions

Where can I pay my Randolph County tax bill?

At the Collector's office, courthouse Suite 1G, 372 Hwy. JJ in Huntsville, or by mail, drop box, drive-up window or online. The office keeps weekday hours of 8 a.m. through 4 p.m., and the phone is 844-277-6555 extension 310.

When does Randolph County property tax become late?

After December 31. A mailed payment is on time if its postmark is that date or earlier. Penalties under RSMo 140.100 begin once January arrives.

What portion of my home's value is taxed in Randolph County?

Nineteen percent for residential property under RSMo 137.115, against twelve for farmland and thirty-two for commercial parcels. The levy rate for your school and taxing districts is then applied to that assessed figure.

How often are Randolph County homes revalued?

Every other year. The Assessor sets new values as of January 1 of odd-numbered years, so the next general valuation is January 1, 2027, and it generally stays in force through 2028 unless the house is improved.

Is it too late to dispute a value if the board date passed?

Maybe not. A State Tax Commission complaint is due September 30 or thirty days after the board finishes, whichever falls later, so a late board date can still leave room. Call the County Clerk right away for the board's dates.

Where is Camden County, Missouri, and how did it begin?

Camden County is the Lake of the Ozarks county in central Missouri, and its seat is Camdenton. It should not be confused with Camden County, Georgia, though the county's own site is camdencountymo.gov. The Census Bureau counts 709 square miles, with 53 of them water.

The state organized the county on January 29, 1841 as Kinderhook County and renamed it in 1843 for Charles Pratt, 1st Earl Camden. Its first seat, Oregon, became Erie in the rename. After a cholera epidemic in 1854 left only seven survivors in Erie, the seat moved to Linn Creek in 1855. Camdenton is the seat today, and Osage Beach is the largest city.

The 2020 census recorded 42,745 residents, and the 2025 estimate is 44,047. Adjacent counties are Morgan, Miller, Pulaski, Laclede, Dallas, Hickory and Benton.

Which cities and school districts serve Camden County homes?

The county's incorporated places are Camdenton, Lake Ozark, Linn Creek, Osage Beach and Richland, and Lake Ozark, Osage Beach and Richland each spill into a neighboring county. Climax Springs, Macks Creek and Montreal are census-designated places.

Public districts named on Wikipedia are Camdenton R-III, Climax Springs R-IV, Macks Creek R-V and Stoutland R-II. Camdenton R-III runs Dogwood, Hawthorn, Osage Beach, Hurricane Deck and Oak Ridge schools plus a middle and a high school. A house near the water in Osage Beach can sit in a different tax picture from one in Stoutland, because each district and fire or library district adds its own levy to the bill.

Ask the Collector for the parcel's levy breakdown, not just last year's total, if you want to know what a buyer will see.

What do Census numbers say about Camden County housing?

Camden County stands out for lake-area housing costs and an older population. The table pulls its figures.

MeasureCamden County

Housing units outnumber households by more than two to one, and Wikipedia reports that 52.8 percent of the county's housing units were vacant at the 2020 census. The Assessor reports over 70,000 real estate parcels. Median household income is $66,387, and retail sales per capita reached $26,572 in 2022, the highest of the four Missouri counties compared in the Census table.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Camden County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Who handles property tax in Camden County?

Three offices in Camdenton share the work, and the county phone line is 573-346-4440 with an extension for each.

  • Assessor Marty McGuire values real and personal property as of January 1. Real estate and GIS are at 50 Roofener Street, and personal property is at 1 Court Circle NW, Suite 6. The assessor's extension is 1260.
  • Collector Teresa Murray bills and collects at 1 Court Circle NW, Suite 4, extension 1200. A taxpayer portal lets you search records by name, statement number or parcel number.
  • County Clerk Rowland Todd, at 1 Court Circle NW, Suite 2, books Board of Equalization appointments and can be reached at extension 1220.

A real estate parcel number in the portal looks like 01-1.0-01.0-000.0-000-123.456, and the Collector says a statement number starting with R is a real estate bill. Search by the parcel number from last year's receipt for the cleanest result.

How do I appeal a Camden County property assessment?

You work through four steps, and the first costs nothing. State law reassesses every parcel in odd-numbered years, so the next full cycle falls in 2027, and owners whose value rose get a Change in Assessment Notice with the appeal rights printed on it.

  1. Informal appeal: call the Assessor at 573-317-3865 or 573-317-3896 (condominiums at 573-317-3838). Informal hearings usually run in April and May.
  2. Board of Equalization: a three-member panel of local taxpayers appointed by the County Commission meets in July. Book through the County Clerk, and file on or before the second Monday of July.
  3. State Tax Commission: file by September 30 or 30 days after the Board's decision, whichever is later. The commission's phone is 573-751-2414.
  4. Circuit court: at this level an attorney is expected.

The Board only decides fair market value, so bring comparable sales or an appraisal and leave out the argument that taxes are too high. For a rule check, RSMo 138.430 gives the appeal rights to the State Tax Commission and RSMo 137.275 sets the July cutoff.

What happens if Camden County property tax goes unpaid?

Statute treats January 1 as the line. Under RSMo 139.100 the Collector adds a penalty to taxes unpaid after the first of January, and a postmark by the due date counts as timely. Land that reaches the back tax book carries an 18 percent penalty on each year's delinquency, or up to two percent per month if it is redeemed before the sale, under RSMo 140.100.

A taxpayer who disputes a bill can pay it in full before the delinquency date with a written protest. The Collector impounds the disputed part, and the taxpayer must sue the Collector in circuit court within ninety days (RSMo 139.031).

The county's tax sale is announced for Monday, August 23, 2027 at 10:00 a.m. State law holds it on the fourth Monday in August (RSMo 140.150). Bidders must be Missouri residents, arrive at the courthouse by 8:30, and register at the Collector's Office first. A parcel offered at a "fourth sale" must be placed on hold in the Collector's Office for at least 150 days.

Is there a senior property tax freeze in Camden County?

Yes. The Assessor administers the SB 190 senior credit for people 62 and older. The 2026 sign-up window ran January 2 through June 30, 2026 and has closed. The 2027 window opens January 4, 2027 and ends June 30, 2027.

  • You must be at least 62 and live in the home as your primary residence.
  • You must hold the deed and owe the annual tax bill.
  • The property cannot be titled to an LLC or a corporation. Revocable or living trusts are accepted if you are named trustee.
  • Apply every year in person or by mail at 50 Roofener Street, with proof of identity, age and residency.

The freeze holds the assessed portion of the bill at the amount paid in the base year, and new construction can remove it. The state statute behind it is RSMo 137.1050. The credit follows the owner and the primary residence, so a sale ends it for the seller, and a buyer applies on their own.

What should I know about taxes and recording when I sell a Camden County house?

The title company pays the Collector from your proceeds when the parcel still has a balance, and the settlement statement splits the year's tax between buyer and seller. Check the collector portal before you list, because a lien on the parcel affects how fast a deal can close.

Deeds are recorded at the Recorder's office, 1 Court Circle NW in Camdenton, 573-346-4440 extension 1300. Fees posted effective August 28, 2026 are $26 for the first page of a deed and $3 for each added page, with an extra $25 if the document is not on 8.5 by 11 paper with a three-inch top margin. Land record searches use the Recorder's iCounty site at camdenmo.icounty.com.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I pay property tax in Camden County?

Pay the Collector at 1 Court Circle NW, Suite 4, Camdenton, or use the taxpayer portal at collector.camdencountymo.gov. Call 573-346-4440 extension 1200 with any question about a statement.

When is the Camden County Board of Equalization deadline?

Appeals must be filed on or before the second Monday in July, with the appointment set through the County Clerk at extension 1220. The Board meets during July.

Does Camden County have a senior tax freeze?

Yes, the SB 190 freeze for owners 62 and older. The 2027 application period runs January 4 through June 30, 2027 at the Assessor's real estate office, 50 Roofener Street, Camdenton.

When is the Camden County tax sale?

The next sale is Monday, August 23, 2027 at 10:00 a.m. Bidders must be Missouri residents and register at the Collector's Office before the sale.

How many parcels does the Camden County Assessor value?

More than 70,000 real estate parcels, according to the Assessor's page. Reassessment happens in odd-numbered years, with new construction added when it is finished.
