Which Jasper County, MO offices handle my property tax?

The Assessor sets the value and the Collector sends the bill and takes the money. Jasper County has Lisa Perry as Assessor and Steven E. McIntosh as Collector. Both have a presence at the Carthage courthouse, 302 S. Main, and the Collector also staffs the Joplin Courts Building at 633 S. Pearl.

  • Collector, Carthage: 417-358-0409 for personal property and 417-358-0411 for real property, Room 107
  • Collector, Joplin: 417-625-4324 for both kinds
  • Assessor, real estate: 417-358-0440, Room 201B in Carthage
  • Assessor, personal property: 417-358-0437

Counter hours at the Collector's offices are 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., Monday through Friday. The Assessor's office follows state holidays and keeps the same weekday hours.

What kind of county is Jasper County?

Jasper County lies in the southwest corner of Missouri along the Kansas line. Carthage is the county seat, and Joplin, the largest city, is partly in Newton County. The county was organized in 1841 and has 638.51 square miles of land. Webb City, Carl Junction, Oronogo, Sarcoxie and Purcell are among its other cities, and its neighbors are Barton, Dade, Lawrence and Newton counties in Missouri plus Cherokee and Crawford counties in Kansas.

Interstate 44, Interstate 49 and the old Route 66 alignment cross the county, and the Joplin area is also a metropolitan statistical area. In May 2011 an EF5 tornado struck Joplin. For a seller, the practical point is that city, school and fire district levies differ across these towns, and one county bill carries all of them.

The Census Bureau's quick facts for the period 2020 to 2024 give a picture of the housing stock:

  • Estimated population on July 1, 2025: 127,428
  • Housing units: 56,504
  • Owner-occupied share: 62.8%
  • Median owner-occupied home value: $166,900
  • Median household income: $60,694

Owners with a mortgage report median monthly costs of $1,219, and without one $491. Median gross rent is $973.

When are Jasper County property taxes due?

Statements are mailed in the first week of November, are due on receipt and turn delinquent after December 31. A mailed payment needs a USPS postmark on or before 12/31/26. The online payment page closes at 11:59 p.m. on 12/31/26, and money sent after that accrues interest and penalties once the site reopens in 2027. A payment postmarked late is returned unprocessed unless the late fees are included.

If no statement shows up by the end of November, the Collector asks you to call right away, and the office reminds owners that a missing statement does not remove the duty to pay. Technical trouble with a phone or online payment does not extend the statutory date, so plan for an in-person visit or the 24-hour drop box at either office if a website acts up.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Jasper County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How do I pay and what does it cost in Jasper County?

Ways to pay a Jasper County, MO tax statement, per the Collector's site
MethodDetail
In personCarthage or Joplin; cash, personal check, cashier's check, money order, credit or debit card
MailUSPS postmark of December 31 or earlier
OnlineCollector's website; closes 11:59 p.m. Dec. 31
E-check$2.00 fee
Credit card2.45% of the balance
Drop box24 hours at each office location
TelephoneToll-free number printed on the statement

The Collector explains that the service fee is not part of the tax and the county receives none of it. Under Missouri statute 139.055, only people who choose an electronic method pay that cost. Paying by check or in person avoids it.

How does the Jasper County Assessor decide what I owe on?

The Collector bills what the Assessor's records show, so errors in a mailing address, legal description or listed vehicle should go to the Assessor, not the Collector. For real estate, call 417-358-0440 and ask about your parcel's value and the notice you received.

Personal property works on a calendar of its own. Assessment lists are mailed in early January, due by March 1 without penalty, and may be filed online with the PIN from the mailed sheet. The Assessor does not accept emailed renditions. Tax is based on what you owned on January 1, even if you sold the vehicle later. Business owners assess equipment and furniture the same way, and landlords with rental or leasing space owe a tenant list by January 30.

A statement of non-assessment, which some call a tax waiver, can be used only to license a vehicle and requires bringing the title or registration to the office in person.

Can I appeal a Jasper County assessment?

Yes, through the county board of equalization. Missouri statute 138.060 directs that board to decide appeals from the assessor's valuation in a summary way, and it says there is no presumption that the assessor's number is right. The statute also puts the burden on the assessor in any other county when a value rose at least fifteen percent from the prior assessment without new construction or improvement.

Ask the Assessor's office, at 417-358-0440, for the filing deadline and hearing procedure for the current year, and bring comparable sales, a recent appraisal or a purchase contract. Pay by December 31 regardless of the appeal outcome, since interest and penalties start after that day.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Jasper County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What relief exists for older Jasper County homeowners?

The SB190 Senior Citizen Tax Credit is handled by the Collector. Applications for the most recent cycle ran from February 2 to May 31, 2026, at Room 107 in the Carthage courthouse, and could be filed online by QR code or PIN from a renewal notice. That window has closed, so ask the Collector when the next one opens.

  • The applicant must be 62 or older by midnight on December 31 of the initial credit year.
  • The home must be in Jasper County and be the applicant's primary residence.
  • The prior year's taxes must have been paid.

Renewal applications were accepted in the same period. The Missouri Department of Revenue runs its own Property Tax Credit for certain seniors and 100% disabled individuals, reachable at 573-751-3505, and that program is separate from the county credit.

What should a seller know about tax at closing in Jasper County?

Call the Collector for a current balance on the parcel before you set a closing date, since statements are due on receipt and become delinquent after December 31. Ask whether the escrow or title agent will pay the current year or prorate it, and put that in the contract. After the sale, the new owner should confirm the mailing address with the Assessor so that the November statement lands in the right mailbox.

Owners who inherited a house in Jasper County and are behind on earlier years should ask the Collector for the amount currently owed on each year before they quote a price to a buyer.

Frequently asked questions

What is the deadline to pay Jasper County property tax?

December 31. Mail needs a USPS postmark on or before 12/31/26, and the online payment page shuts at 11:59 p.m. that night. After that date, interest and penalties apply.

Where do I pay in Jasper County if I live near Joplin?

You can pay at the Joplin Courts Building, 633 S. Pearl, at 417-625-4324, instead of driving to Carthage. Both offices have a 24-hour drop box.

How much extra does it cost to pay online in Jasper County?

An e-check carries a $2.00 fee and a credit card costs 2.45% of the balance. The county keeps none of it. A check or an in-person payment has no such charge.

I did not get my statement. Do I still owe?

Yes. The Collector says failing to receive a statement does not cancel the tax, and any penalty and interest still apply. Call if nothing arrives by the end of November.

Who do I call to fix my address or vehicle on the statement?

Call the Jasper County Assessor: 417-358-0440 for real estate or 417-358-0437 for personal property. The Collector bills only what the Assessor's records show.

Cash Home Buyers in Missouri
Cash Offer in 24 Hours

Selling in Platte County? Get a Cash Offer

Selling in Platte County?

Which offices handle property tax in Platte County, Missouri?

Three county offices share the work. The Assessor, Marcus Farr, values property. The County Clerk builds the tax book and takes Board of Equalization appeals and tax credit applications. The Collector of Revenue, Sheila L. Palmer, mails and collects the bills.

The Collector is in the Administration Building at 415 3rd St., Room 212, Platte City, MO 64079, phone (816) 858-3356, with the counter staffed on weekdays from 8 to 5. The Assessor's real estate staff answer at (816) 858-3316 until 4:30 in the afternoon. The County Clerk's number for tax relief questions is (816) 858-3340. The collector's FAQ sends questions about value, names, addresses, vehicles and tax waivers to the assessor, and questions about missing statements to the collector.

What makes Platte County different for a home seller?

Platte County is part of the Kansas City metro area, and the Missouri River forms its southwestern border with Kansas. The county was organized on December 31, 1838, out of the Platte Purchase, and Platte City is the seat. Kansas City International Airport lies inside the county, and other towns include Parkville, Weston, Riverside, Dearborn and Smithville.

Four public school systems serve the county: Park Hill, Platte County School District Number 3 at Platte City, North Platte R-I at Dearborn and West Platte County R-II at Weston. The Census Bureau's latest figures show the highest home values of the three Missouri counties in this guide set.

  • 114,400 residents in the 2025 estimate, a gain of 7.2 percent over the 2020 base.
  • 47,969 housing units, about two thirds occupied by their owners (67.4 percent).
  • A typical owned home is valued at $345,100 for the 2020 to 2024 period.
  • Median household income reaches $96,227, and gross rent runs $1,334 a month.
  • The county issued 425 building permits in 2025.

Source: Census QuickFacts.

When are Platte County tax bills due?

Platte County statements are mailed in November and are due on receipt. Late charges start once December 31 passes, and the assessor's calendar also lists November 1 as the day bills go out through the Collector. To avoid penalty and interest, the envelope must be postmarked on or before December 31. Anything postmarked later comes back unprocessed unless the penalty and interest are added.

The Collector states that a statement that never arrives does not remove the obligation, and that trouble with the phone or web payment system does not extend the statutory deadline. Check the mailing address and legal description on each bill. If you did not get a statement by the end of November, call the office right away.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Platte County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How can I pay my Platte County bill?

The Collector accepts payment in person, by mail, online, by telephone using the 1-800 number printed on the bill, or through a 24-hour drop box outside the Platte County Government Complex. In the office, cash, personal check, cashier's check, money order and credit or debit card are accepted.

The drop box helps when the counter is closed. The Assessor's page lists county closures on November 26 and 27 and December 24 and 25 this year, so plan year-end payments around those days and ask the Collector for its own holiday schedule.

How does the 2027 reassessment affect Platte County owners?

Missouri law has the assessor reassess all real property on January 1 of each odd-numbered year, and Platte County's 2027 round is already underway. The assessor's FAQ says the aim is equalization, not extra revenue. Early estimates in that FAQ put about 8,000 parcels on track for a decrease, about 900 for an increase under 1 percent, and just under 13,000 for an increase over 15 percent.

A parcel projected to rise more than 15 percent, excluding new construction, gets a written notice and an exterior inspection. An interior look happens only if the owner asks for it. Estimated 2027 values appear on the assessor's Beacon property search beside the current 2026 value, and the assessor says they may change before final values are set in early 2027.

Assessment rates are 19 percent of market value for residential, 32 percent for commercial and 12 percent for agricultural property. A $50,000 home, as the assessor's own example shows, would carry an assessed value of $9,500. Source: Platte County Assessor, Real Property.

What steps does a Platte County owner follow to contest a value?

The assessor describes a three-stage path with a separate date at each stage. Start with the informal review, then use the county board, then the state.

Platte County real property appeal steps listed by the assessor
StepWhereTiming
Informal hearingAssessor's appraisers, (816) 858-3316Before June 30
Board of EqualizationForm from the County ClerkReturned before the second Monday in July; hearings in July
State Tax CommissionComplaint for Review of AssessmentSeptember 30, or thirty days after the board rules if that is later

Bring pictures, a recent sale of your property or an appraisal to the informal meeting. An increase notice must be mailed on or before June 15. If you plan to pay under protest, the State Tax Commission guide says to pay in full by December 31, mark the check "paid under protest" and file a written statement with the collector.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Platte County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What relief programs apply in Platte County?

The assessor's newsletter describes two county-run credits, both run through the County Clerk, and neither one a freeze on value. SB-190 is the senior tax credit, which protects a qualifying participant's base-year tax liability. SB-3, the Homestead Tax Credit enacted in April 2026, targets owner-occupied primary residences not already covered by SB-190 and limits yearly tax growth to 5 percent or the Consumer Price Index, whichever is greater. The newsletter says its full effect will show in the 2027 cycle.

Homes in either program are still reassessed, and a Greater Than 15% notice does not remove a participant from the credit. Call the County Clerk at (816) 858-3340 to ask about eligibility. The state Property Tax Credit claim is separate and pays up to $1,100 to qualifying owner-occupants who are seniors or 100 percent disabled (Missouri Department of Revenue).

What should a Platte County seller do about the tax bill?

Collect the latest bill or look up the parcel on the assessor's Beacon search before you list. Notices go to the owner of record at the last address the assessor has, so a seller who moved should file the assessor's change of address form to keep notices from being lost.

Confirm payoff figures with the Collector in Platte City, and have the title company explain how the year is split at closing. The collector's statement is due on receipt, so a sale in November or December leaves little time between the bill arriving and the postmark deadline.

Frequently asked questions

When do Platte County property taxes become delinquent?

Late charges begin after December 31. The envelope must be postmarked by that date, and later payments are returned unless penalty and interest are included.

Where do I pay Platte County property tax in person?

Go to the Collector's counter in the Administration Building at 415 3rd St., Room 212, Platte City, any weekday between 8 and 5. A 24-hour drop box sits outside the entrance to the government complex.

Did my Platte County value go up more than 15 percent?

Check the Assessor's Beacon search, which shows 2027 estimates beside the 2026 value. A projected increase over 15 percent, excluding new construction, triggers a mailed notice and an exterior inspection.

What is the deadline for a Platte County Board of Equalization appeal?

The County Clerk must receive the completed form ahead of the second Monday in July. The assessor also asks owners to meet an appraiser informally before June 30.

Does the SB-3 Homestead Tax Credit freeze my Platte County home value?

No. SB-3 limits tax growth on an eligible primary residence to 5 percent or the CPI, whichever is greater, and homes in the program are still reassessed. Ask the County Clerk at (816) 858-3340 about eligibility.

Jefferson County, MO Property Tax Guide: Offices, Appeals and Selling With Tax Due

Cash Home Buyers in Missouri

  • Jefferson County, MO Property Tax Guide: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Jefferson County, MO Property Tax Guide sale
  • Turn the Jefferson County, MO Property Tax Guide offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling in Jefferson County? Get a Cash Offer

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Jefferson County?
We buy Jefferson County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

Which Jefferson County offices send, value and collect the tax?

Three offices share the job. The Assessor values the property, the County Clerk runs the first appeal board, and the Collector sends the bill and takes the payment. All three work from the Administration Center at 729 Maple Street in Hillsboro, the county seat.

  • Assessor, real estate questions: 636-797-5343. Personal property: 636-797-5466. Hours are Monday through Friday, 8 am to 5 pm.
  • County Clerk, Board of Equalization appointments: 636-797-5478.
  • Collector, bills and payments: 636-797-5406, mailing address P.O. Box 100, Hillsboro, MO 63050.

Rates come from the school, fire, ambulance and other districts that cover your parcel, not from the Assessor or Collector. A house in Fox C-6 and a house in Hillsboro R-3 can carry quite different totals for that reason.

What does the Jefferson County housing picture look like for sellers?

Jefferson County sits on the Mississippi River south of St. Louis and covers about 657 square miles of land. Arnold is the largest city, Hillsboro is the seat, and Festus, De Soto, Crystal City, Herculaneum and Pevely fill out the list of incorporated places. The county is part of the St. Louis metropolitan area, and in 1980 it held the mean center of U.S. population.

The Census Bureau's QuickFacts page counts 233,132 residents as of July 2025 and 96,228 housing units. For 2020 to 2024 the survey shows a typical owned home worth $237,200, an ownership rate of 82.2% and a median household income of $82,851. Workers spend 30.6 minutes getting to their jobs on average.

With more than four in five households owning, a large share of tax bills here are paid by lenders from escrow, which makes the lender request rule in the due-date section below worth knowing.

How does the Jefferson County Assessor value a home?

The Assessor uses mass appraisal. Replacement cost of the buildings is reduced for depreciation, then land value is added to reach fair market value (Assessor FAQ). Missouri requires every parcel to be reassessed in odd-numbered years, and 2027 is the next one.

Market value is then multiplied by the assessment level for the property class. A $100,000 house is carried at $19,000 of assessed value.

Assessment levels used in Jefferson County (Assessor FAQ)
Property classShare of market value taxed
Residential19%
Commercial32%
Agricultural12%

Your bill can change without a reassessment. A new garage, an adjoining acre or a finished house that had been prorated during construction all move assessed value, and a voter-approved levy change moves the total even when value stays flat.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Jefferson County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

When is Jefferson County property tax due, and what happens if it is late?

Real estate tax is due December 31 and becomes delinquent on January 1. Bills go on the county website in November and are mailed late that month. If nothing arrives by December 1, call the Collector, because a missing bill does not excuse the deadline.

  • Pay at 729 Maple Street, online, or by the phone line at 1-877-289-0099 (the Collector's FAQ lists a convenience fee of 2.5% with a $1.95 minimum for debit and cards, and $4.95 for e-check).
  • Mailed payments need a postmark of December 31 or earlier, so check the last pickup time at your post office.
  • Mortgage companies must send the Collector a written request for each bill they plan to pay. If you received a paper bill, your lender did not ask for it.

The Collector has no power to waive penalty or interest, citing section 139.100 and an Attorney General opinion. Under RSMo 140.100, land in the back tax book carries an 18 percent penalty on each year's delinquency, and the penalty on land redeemed before sale cannot exceed 2 percent per month.

What are the steps to contest a Jefferson County value?

Start with a phone call to the Assessor. An appraiser reviews the value with you and looks at any evidence you bring. If that does not settle it, you file with the Board of Equalization through the County Clerk. The county's assessor page and the State Tax Commission both give the second Monday in July as the filing cutoff. The 2026 date was July 13 and has passed, and the next one is July 12, 2027.

  1. Call the Assessor at 636-797-5343 and ask for an informal review.
  2. Call the County Clerk at 636-797-5478 for the forms and a hearing date.
  3. Bring five copies of any written evidence: one for each board member, one for the board secretary and one for the Assessor.
  4. Expect a certified letter with the decision, usually within 5 business days.
  5. If you still disagree, file a Complaint for Review of Assessment with the State Tax Commission, attaching the board's decision letter.

The county's collector page gives the State Tax Commission cutoff as September 30 or 30 days after the board decision, whichever is later. The Commission's own guide says the 30 days run from the date of the letter, and that a property owned by an LLC, trust, corporation or estate needs an attorney to file.

Taxes still have to be paid by December 31 while an appeal is open. Paying under protest follows a specific procedure: full payment before the delinquency date plus a written statement of your grounds and your claimed fair market value. Writing "protest" on the check does nothing on its own.

Which tax relief programs apply to Jefferson County homeowners?

The county lists two. One is a Real Property Tax Credit for Seniors, enacted February 15, 2024, with details on the county's Assessor FAQ page. The other is the state's Property Tax Credit Claim, which returns part of the real estate tax or rent paid during the year.

  • The state credit is capped at $1,100 for owners who live in their home and $750 for renters.
  • You may qualify if you are 65 by December 31 of the prior year, or you or your spouse are 100% disabled, or you are 60 or older and receive surviving spouse benefits.
  • Household income, counting Social Security, cannot exceed $30,000 for a single person or $34,000 for married homeowners.
  • File with form MO-1040 and schedule MO-PTS, or form MO-PTC if you do not file an income tax return.

An owner whose house is destroyed by a tornado, flood, fire or earthquake can ask the Assessor to remove the residential value on a pro-rata basis under section 137.082, using the Destroyed Residential Property form.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Jefferson County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How are taxes handled when a Jefferson County house sells?

The Collector's FAQ says that in most closings the seller's share of the year's tax is credited on the settlement statement and the buyer is responsible for the full year. Your settlement statement or title company shows the exact split.

Once the new deed is recorded at the Recorder of Deeds office, the Assessor's file shows the new owner. The name on a real estate bill changes only through a recorded deed, so the bill address and the owner name will not update from a phone call alone.

If a house you are selling has a delinquent year, ask the Collector for the amount due including penalty and interest before you accept an offer, and have the title company pay it from the proceeds.

Frequently asked questions

By what date must a Jefferson County real estate bill be paid?

December 31 of the tax year. Payments postmarked after that date are charged penalty and interest, and the Collector cannot waive either one.

Can I still appeal my 2026 Jefferson County value?

No for the county board. The second Monday in July was July 13, 2026, and has passed. Missouri reassesses in odd-numbered years, so 2027 brings new notices and a July 12, 2027 filing date.

Who do I call if my Jefferson County tax bill never arrived?

Call the Collector at 636-797-5406. The county asks owners to call if nothing has arrived by December 1, and the deadline stays December 31 either way.

Does my mortgage lender pay the Jefferson County bill?

Only if it sent the Collector a written request for your bill. If the paper bill came to you, the lender did not request it, so call the lender to learn where it wants the bill sent.

Who pays the year's tax when I sell my Jefferson County house?

By the Collector's account, the seller's portion is usually credited at closing and the buyer owes the whole year's bill. Your settlement statement lays out the split.

Who sends and collects property tax bills in Franklin County, Missouri?

The county collector of revenue bills and collects, and the assessor values the land. Doug Trentmann is the Franklin County Collector, in Room 103 at 400 E Locust in Union, phone 636-583-6353. His office handles current and delinquent taxes for the county and 64 other taxing entities, and also levee, railroad and utility taxes, plus merchant and manufacturer licenses.

The county website lists four ways to pay:

  • Online through the Property Tax Bill Pay page on the county website
  • By phone at 877-690-3729 with jurisdiction code 3570
  • In the Collector's office with a check or cash
  • By mailing a check using the address on the bill

The county notes that a nominal convenience fee is charged for these services.

The assessor does not figure taxes, set rates or print bills. Franklin County's own assessor page says each taxing jurisdiction sets its own levy, so questions about the rate go to those bodies and their annual budget meetings.

What kind of county is Franklin County for a home seller?

Franklin County is a large exurban county on the south side of the Missouri River, part of the St. Louis metro area, with Union as the county seat. It was organized in 1818 and named for Benjamin Franklin. German families arrived in numbers starting in 1833, steamboats once carried freight on the river, and the railroads later made the county a transport center. Wineries around New Haven and Berger sit inside the Hermann American Viticultural Area.

The county covers 923 square miles of land, which makes it the fourth-largest in Missouri by land area. Incorporated places are Berger, Gerald, New Haven, Pacific, St. Clair, Sullivan, Union and Washington. Gray Summit, Lake St. Clair, Stanton and Villa Ridge are census-designated places. A seller in a city pays a city bill too, so a Washington or Pacific address means two sets of statements.

The Census QuickFacts table shows what the housing stock looks like:

  • 108,090 people in the July 2025 estimate, 3.3 percent more than the 2020 base
  • 48,091 housing units, and 76.5 percent of occupied homes lived in by owners
  • $227,600 typical value for a home lived in by its owner (2020 to 2024 median)
  • $73,165 median household income and a mean commute of 28.3 minutes
  • 794 building permits in 2025

How big is the Franklin County assessment roll?

The Franklin County assessor tracks more than 73,000 parcels with over $1.511 billion in assessed value, the thirteenth highest among Missouri's 114 counties and St. Louis City. Roughly 50,000 parcels are classed residential, 24,000 agricultural and 3,400 commercial. The office says it reassesses all real estate every two years and mails more than 20,000 value-increase notices a year.

Statute fixes the percentages. The residential ratio in RSMo 137.115 is 19 percent of true value, and farm and commercial parcels use their own percentages. Raising a house more than 15 percent without new building requires an on-site inspection first.

The assessor also fields requests from title companies and mortgage lenders, and the county's property search site lets an owner pull up the parcel record before calling. Check the acreage, square footage and bedroom count on the record, since errors there change the value.

What are the key dates on the Franklin County property tax calendar?

The county assessor publishes a yearly calendar that a seller can use to see where a house stands in the cycle. The table lists those dates as the county gives them.

Franklin County assessment and billing calendar, per the assessor
DateWhat happens
January 1Valuation date for all real and personal property
March 1Personal property list due, with penalties if late
June 30Real estate and personal property rolls go to the County Clerk
Second Monday in JulyLast day to file a Board of Equalization appeal
September 30State Tax Commission deadline, or later if the Board's letter came within the last month
October 1Tax rates set and certified to the County Clerk
November and DecemberCollector prepares and sends bills
December 31Current taxes must be paid before they become delinquent

Source: Franklin County Assessor page. Utilities and railroads report to the assessor by April 1, and the clerk certifies those values by April 20.

How do I challenge a Franklin County valuation?

Begin with the assessor's staff. They hold many informal hearings, mostly in reassessment years, and the office says it tries to settle concerns before they turn into Board filings. Ask which sales the value leans on, then line them up against houses on your own street.

The formal step is the Board of Equalization, with the July deadline shown in the calendar above. Franklin County's assessor page says its own staff presents the facts to the Board. A value that jumped 15 percent or more for reasons other than new building puts the burden on the assessor under RSMo 138.060.

After the Board, the State Tax Commission is the next level, and the county's attorney represents the assessor in that case. A claim that a property should be exempt altogether goes to circuit court instead. Owners that are LLCs, trusts, estates or corporations need a lawyer to file.

Can seniors or disabled owners in Franklin County get property tax relief?

Missouri does not exempt the property of seniors or disabled owners, according to the Franklin County assessor. It points instead to the Missouri Property Tax Credit, which gives income-limited seniors and disabled residents a refund or income tax credit based on property tax or rent paid. Details are at the state Department of Revenue site, and Aging Ahead answers questions at 636-629-3143.

The assessor adds that the Homestead Preservation Act credit needs a legislative appropriation and is not funded at this time.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Franklin County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What happens if Franklin County taxes go unpaid past December 31?

Per the assessor's calendar, a bill left open after December 31 becomes delinquent and draws penalties. The statutory penalty is 18 percent of that year's delinquency (RSMo 140.100), and postmarks decide whether a mailed check was on time.

Owners who dispute a value can still pay in full and file a protest statement with the collector, then sue the collector inside 90 days, as RSMo 139.031 requires. That same section allows a credit or refund for tax paid by mistake when the application comes within three years.

Land with old unpaid years goes into the county's annual August tax sale. Owners can redeem at any point before it by paying the tax, penalty and costs. The Collector can give the figure for a specific parcel at 636-583-6353.

How do I handle property tax when I sell a Franklin County house?

Pull the parcel from the pay site and print the current bill, then ask the Collector at 636-583-6353 whether any earlier year is open. The title company will need the parcel ID and the figure, and who owes which part of the current year is decided by the sales contract.

If the house is inherited, behind on taxes or has tenants or repairs outstanding, a cash purchase can pay the tax balance at the closing table, out of the price. Franklin County deeds are filed at the Recorder of Deeds, and the county website has a Record My Deeds link on its home page.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I pay Franklin County property tax?

At the Collector's office, Room 103, 400 E Locust in Union, or online, by phone at 877-690-3729 with code 3570, or by mail. The county says a nominal convenience fee applies to these services.

When is the Franklin County tax deadline?

December 31. The assessor's calendar says current taxes must be paid by that date, and after it they are delinquent and penalties are applied.

What is the route for contesting a Franklin County assessment?

Call the assessor, then file with the Board of Equalization by its July deadline. If the Board does not change the value, the State Tax Commission is the next stop.

How often does Franklin County reassess homes?

Every two years, according to the assessor's page. New construction gets assessed every year, and the county mails more than 20,000 notices of increased value annually.

Is there property tax relief for Franklin County seniors?

There is a state refund and credit. The Missouri Property Tax Credit helps seniors and disabled residents with limited income. The county assessor notes the Homestead Preservation Act credit is not funded now.

Which two offices in Bloomfield deal with my tax bill?

The Assessor lists and values property. The Collector of Revenue mails the bills and takes the money. Both keep an address on South Prairie Street in the county's government building.

  • Collector of Revenue: 401 S. Prairie St, P.O. Box 80, Bloomfield, MO 63825; (573) 568-3327; staffed weekdays from half past eight until half past four, and shut on state and federal holidays.
  • Assessor: 401 South Prairie, P.O. Box 307, Bloomfield, MO 63825; (573) 568-3163. The office site offers real estate and personal property lookups by account number, name or address.

Stoddard County fills the southeast corner of Missouri, with 823 square miles of land. Bloomfield is the seat and Dexter the largest city; Advance, Bell City, Bernie, Dudley, Essex and Puxico are the other incorporated cities, per the county's Wikipedia article. A slice of Mingo National Wildlife Refuge falls inside the line.

When does the Collector expect payment?

Payment opens November 1 and the deadline is December 31. Bills are printed once the County Clerk hands over the tax books in the fall, and they reach mailboxes in November.

After the deadline, extra charges land on the first day of each month, with the amounts shown on your statement. The Collector's FAQ says a check in the mail must bear a U.S. Postal Service postmark dated inside the month, because a payment that falls short of the added penalties is returned. A bill that never arrived does not erase the penalty.

The Collector's website looks up a bill by owner name, parcel number, property address or account number, and shows payment history. You can pay with cash at the counter, a personal check, a money order or a cashier's check, or by card on the website or by phone, where a convenience fee applies. The drop box by the entrance to the government building is open around the clock, yet a late check left there without the penalty comes back to you. The resources page adds that tax paid out of a mortgage escrow account will not appear in the online database.

Is a monthly plan available for the real estate bill?

Yes. The county has run an installment plan since the 2010 tax year. It starts from last year's real estate payment, divides it by eleven, and collects ten equal pieces, then the actual balance as the eleventh. The program page says money leaves a checking or savings account automatically, on the 5th or the 20th.

  • You cannot join while any real estate tax is past due.
  • A parcel whose tax runs through a mortgage escrow is not eligible.
  • A missed withdrawal can end the plan, and any amount left unpaid at year end draws the usual penalties.

Can an older homeowner freeze the bill?

A homestead credit exists. As of 2024, a county resident who is 62 or older on January 1, owns the home and lives in it can lock in the real estate tax on that home. The credit's page stresses that it does not exempt you from tax. You still pay a bill, just a frozen one.

First-time filers have from January 1 to June 30. Renewal paperwork is mailed beginning February 1 and is also due June 30. A notary must witness the first application, and the license or state ID has to show the home address. The homestead covers a primary residence on up to five acres, which leaves out barns, commercial ground and farmland.

The page also addresses new construction and additions. Ask the Collector at (573) 568-3327 how a sale or a remodel would affect your frozen base year before you list.

Where do I turn if the assessed value looks too high?

Call the Assessor at (573) 568-3163 and ask for this year's Board of Equalization filing date. At the board, RSMo 138.060 removes any presumption that the assessor is right. In a county of this type the assessor must carry the burden of proof when a parcel's assessed value climbed 15% or more from the prior assessment, unless new construction or improvement explains the jump.

Paying while you contest follows RSMo 139.031. The whole bill is due before delinquency, along with a written statement of your grounds delivered to the Collector. Circuit court suit for recovery has to begin within 90 days of that protest.

What about tax certificates and closing day?

Land with unpaid tax may be offered for sale on the fourth Monday in August, according to RSMo 140.150. The collector first mails a letter to the record owner. When the assessed value is above $1,000, a second letter goes out by certified mail. Notices of delinquent tax certificate sales appear on the Collector's site.

At closing, the Collector's FAQ gives the working rule: taxes ride with the land, not the owner. The statement is passed to the buyer, and buyer and seller agree who pays what when the bill comes due. Buyers are expected to learn the tax status before they buy, so a title company will probably ask for a payoff or a proration. Missouri's Form MO-PTC is a separate state refund claim for some seniors, disabled owners and renters, and the Department of Revenue decides who qualifies.

How strong is the local economy and housing market?

The job base is modest. 644 employer establishments in 2023, with total employment of 8,455 and a yearly payroll of about $389 million. Retail sales in 2022 were $572,476,000, or $20,165 per resident.

About 56.7% of residents aged 16 and up are in the labor force, and the typical commute is 23.1 minutes. Among adults 25 and older, 83.7% finished high school and 16.7% hold a bachelor's degree or more. Owners with a mortgage report monthly costs of $1,110 in the middle, and those without one report $443. For the current levy on a specific parcel, read the rate lines on the tax statement or ask the Collector, since the online levy page is an archive that stops at 2022.

The county holds 11,585 households of about 2.42 people each, and 21.5% of residents are 65 or older. Broadband subscriptions reach 86.9% of households. Prices run far below the $276,800 figure for St. Louis County. The Census table puts the middle owner-reported home value at $143,300 for 2020 to 2024, with owners living in 71.8% of homes.

Seven public districts reach into the county: Advance R-IV, Bell City R-II, Bernie R-XIII, Bloomfield R-XIV, Dexter R-XI, Puxico R-VIII and Richland R-I. Density is 34.8 per square mile, and 66.4% of residents lived in rural areas at the 2020 census.

Frequently asked questions

Where is Stoddard County property tax paid?

At the Collector of Revenue, 401 S. Prairie St in Bloomfield, by mail to P.O. Box 80, Bloomfield, MO 63825, or online through the Collector's website.

What is the last day to pay without penalty?

December 31. Collection begins November 1, and extra charges start accruing on the first of each month once the deadline has passed.

Is there a way to spread the bill over the year?

Yes, for real estate tax only. Ten equal monthly withdrawals are followed by a final payment of the balance. Past-due accounts and escrowed parcels cannot join.

Which party pays the tax at a sale?

Buyer and seller decide that at closing. The Collector says the statement should go to the buyer and that taxes stay with the property.

What age qualifies for the homestead freeze?

Sixty-two on January 1, plus ownership and primary residence of the home. New applications are accepted from January 1 through June 30.

Who runs property tax in Howell County, and where do I find them?

Both offices work out of the county building on the West Plains square, 35 Court Square. The collector's site names Janet Crow as County Collector and puts the office in Room 201, phone (417) 256-4001, fax (417) 257-0090. Hours are 8:30 am to 4:30 pm Monday through Friday, including the noon hour, and the office closes on state holidays.

The assessor, Daniel Franks, has Suite 202 at (417) 256-8284 and opens at 8:00 am. His site offers GIS mapping and a subscription parcel search at howell.missouriassessors.com. The collector's duties go beyond houses: it prepares separate statements for personal property such as cars, trucks and boats, for real estate, and for utilities such as railroads and gas lines, and it issues merchant licenses.

How do I pay my Howell County tax bill?

Statements are mailed each November and count as due on receipt. After December 31 they turn delinquent. A mailed check that is postmarked January 1 or later comes back unless it includes late fees. If November ends with no statement in your mailbox, call at once, since the missing paper does not erase the tax.

The collector distributes what it collects each month to the taxing entities that levy against your parcel.

Who owes the tax if I sell or move partway through the year?

The assessor's information page quotes RSMo 137.075 and says liability attaches to whoever holds property on January 1, even a buyer who closes that same day. It gives the example of someone leaving Missouri in June 2026: that person is still taxed for 2026 and the law offers no proration.

That page is written around vehicles and other personal property, which taxpayers list with the assessor before March 1. A house is different in practice, since the sale contract and the settlement statement set how the year's real estate bill is divided. Read the proration clause before you sign.

What share of a Howell County home's value is taxed?

Missouri taxes 19 percent of a home's true value, 12 percent of farmland and 32 percent of commercial property, a rule found in RSMo 137.115. Real estate is revalued every odd year.

  • Raises above 15 percent for a home, new building excluded, require an on-site inspection.
  • You may ask for the inspector to come inside, and the notice must give you thirty days to do so.
  • Under RSMo 138.060, the assessor must prove a raise of that size is justified when you appeal.

Pull up your parcel record on the assessor's site before you call, so you can quote the parcel number.

What are my options if the number looks wrong?

The Board of Equalization comes first, with a cutoff on the second Monday in July. The State Tax Commission is next, and it gives you 30 days from the Board's letter. Signing a stipulation with the assessor settles the case for good.

Paying under protest is a separate tool. RSMo 139.031 calls for payment of the whole bill ahead of delinquency, a written explanation filed with the collector, and a lawsuit against the collector within ninety days. The collector holds the contested share in its own fund while the case runs. A tax paid by mistake can be credited or refunded when the taxpayer applies within three years.

When does Howell County auction delinquent property?

The collector's page sets the sale for the fourth Monday in August, and RSMo 140.150 agrees. Until the gavel falls, an owner can settle by paying the tax, penalty, interest and costs. The collector mails notice to the record owner, though a letter that goes astray does not wipe out the debt.

A seller with a balance should ask (417) 256-4001 for a payoff and have the title company wire it from proceeds at closing.

What is the story behind Howell County?

Josiah Howell bought the first settlement in Howell Valley, and the county took his name when it was organized on March 2, 1857. The first circuit court met in a log cabin about a mile east of West Plains, according to an 1876 account. A small wooden courthouse went up on the West Plains square in 1859 and burned in 1862. The county reorganized in 1865, lost its records to a fire in 1866, and built a three-room frame courthouse measuring about 24 by 30 feet in 1869.

Today the county covers 927 square miles of land on the Arkansas line, which makes it the third largest in Missouri by land area. Part of the Mark Twain National Forest lies inside it. West Plains is the seat and largest city, joined by Brandsville, Mountain View and Willow Springs, and the census-designated places of Pomona and South Fork.

Which colleges, libraries and neighboring counties frame a Howell County sale?

Howell County borders Texas, Shannon, Oregon, Ozark and Douglas counties in Missouri and Fulton County in Arkansas. Missouri State University-West Plains, a satellite of Missouri State University, is in the county seat, and the South Central Career Center in West Plains offers vocational and technical programs for grades 9 through 12. Public libraries operate in Mountain View, West Plains and Willow Springs.

Private schools listed for the county include Faith Assembly Christian School and Ozarks Christian Academy in West Plains and Trinity Christian Academy in Mountain View. Population peaked at 40,400 in 2010 and was 39,750 at the 2020 census, with the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate back above 40,000.

What do housing numbers look like in Howell County?

Census Bureau figures for 2020 to 2024 give a picture of a county where most households own:

  • Estimated population on July 1, 2025: 40,798
  • Housing units: 18,288 across 15,965 households
  • Homes occupied by owners: 70.3%
  • Median owner-occupied value: $173,000
  • Median rent: $733
  • Monthly owner costs: $1,109 with a mortgage and $394 without
  • Persons per household: 2.48, with per capita income of $27,570
  • Median household income: $50,993, with 18.6% of residents in poverty
  • New building permits in 2025: 67

At the 2020 census the median age was 41.5 and 21.0 percent of residents were 65 or older. Roughly 70 percent lived in rural areas. Public schools include West Plains R-7, Willow Springs R-IV and Mountain View-Birch Tree R-III, plus smaller districts such as Fairview, Glenwood, Howell Valley, Junction Hill and Richards. Workers spend about 23 minutes getting to their jobs, and 17.8 percent of adults 25 and older hold a bachelor's degree or higher.

What phone number pays a Howell County tax bill?

Dial 1-800-652-0405 for current taxes. Enter county number 18, then the PIN printed on your statement. Back taxes cannot be paid by that line.

Who is the Howell County assessor?

Daniel Franks, in Suite 202 at 35 Court Square, West Plains. His office is open weekdays from 8:00 am to 4:30 pm and answers at (417) 256-8284.

When must personal property be listed in Howell County?

Before March 1 each year, according to the assessor's page. Property is assessed as it stood on January 1.

Is Howell County tax prorated if I leave Missouri?

The assessor says no. The tax rests on what you held on January 1, and the law has no proration. A home sale contract can still split that year's real estate bill between buyer and seller.

Where can I check my Howell County parcel before an appeal?

Use the assessor's site, howell.missouriassessors.com, or call (417) 256-8284. Have your parcel number ready, and file any Board of Equalization appeal by the second Monday in July.

Who handles property tax in Phelps County?

Two offices in the courthouse at 200 N Main Street, Rolla, MO 65401 share the work. One values the property and the other bills it and takes the money. Neither sets a rate; each taxing district's voters do that.

  • Assessor Tim Kean, Suite 126, (573) 458-6135, fax (573) 458-6149, hours 8:00 to 4:30 on weekdays
  • Collector Faith Barnes, Suite 129, (573) 458-6155, collectorgroup@phelpscounty.org, open weekdays through lunch until 4:30
  • County Clerk, (573) 458-6115, for questions about levies and tax rates
  • Recorder of Deeds Robin Kordes, (573) 458-6095, for the deed itself

The assessor's office tells callers it cannot discuss the dollar amount of a bill. It answers questions about assessed and market value only, and the collector answers the rest.

How is a Phelps County tax bill calculated?

The collector gives two formulas. Divide the assessed value by the adjustment factor to estimate the assessor's market value, and divide the assessed value by 100 and multiply by the levy to find the tax. The rates are 19 percent of market value for residential land, 12 for farmland and 32 for commercial use, as RSMo 137.115 provides.

Take a Phelps County house at the Census median of $206,500. At 19 percent, its assessed value is about $39,235. That number, in hundreds, is multiplied by the combined levy of the school, fire, city and other districts that cover the parcel. The collector notes you pay only the districts that apply to your address, not every levy in the county.

The assessor values real estate on a two year cycle, but the 2025 reassessment was bigger than usual. The assessor's site says the state tax commission found local values slipped out of the 90 to 110 percent compliance band after several years of rising sales prices. The average residential assessed value rose by about 10 percent that year, while agricultural and commercial values stayed flat except for new construction or changes in condition.

What if the Phelps County assessor visits my property?

Field staff are canvassing the whole county to refresh photos of homes and outbuildings and to note condition, with a focus on parcels not visited in more than five years. The assessor's site says the work is required by RSMo 137.130. Staff drive white Ford Bronco Sports with the assessor's logo on the doors and wear vests marked Phelps County Assessor, and each carries a county photo ID. Owners who asked to be called first are called when possible.

State law also limits large jumps. Under RSMo 137.115, a residential parcel cannot be raised by more than 15 percent without a physical inspection, unless new construction explains the increase, and the owner has at least thirty days after the written notice to ask for an interior inspection.

How do I appeal a Phelps County valuation?

Start by calling or stopping in at the assessor, (573) 458-6135, and ask which comparable sales and condition notes support your number. Missouri law backs the owner who disagrees. An increase must be reported to the record owner, and the owner gets a hearing if the county's equalization board reviews it (RSMo 137.180).

Ask the county clerk at (573) 458-6115 for the board's forms and filing deadline. The board starts with no assumption that the assessor is right, and an increase of 15 percent or more outside new construction leaves the proof with the assessor (RSMo 138.060). Next in line is the State Tax Commission, open to the owner by the statutory date or thirty days after the board finishes, whichever falls later (RSMo 138.430).

When and how do I pay Phelps County real estate tax?

Statements are mailed in early November. The collector sets December 31 as the last day, and a postmark after it brings late fees. Mail should carry the stub, called the statement topper, because it holds the account number. The collector advises against bank bill pay services, which often send errors and no topper.

Ways to pay at the Phelps County Collector
MethodFee noted by the collector
Online e-check at tax.phelpscountycollector.com$1.50 to the processor, Forte
Online credit or debit card2.4 percent
By phone at (573) 458-61502.4 percent per transaction

In person by cardBank fees apply

The collector says it keeps none of the online fees. One check can cover any mix of real estate and personal property statements, but the amount must be exact because the office cannot process a payment written for the wrong sum. Installment plans exist for real estate and personal property, so ask at the counter for the form. If you have not received a bill by Thanksgiving, call right away.

Is there a senior tax freeze in Phelps County?

Yes. Phelps County seniors may qualify for a freeze on real estate taxes under Senate Bill 190 as expanded by Senate Bill 756. The applicant must be at least 62 by December 31 of the application year, own and live in the home as a primary residence, and be responsible for its taxes. Only one owner needs to be 62.

The application period for base year 2026 ran from March 1 through May 31, 2026, and it has closed. The freeze starts with the 2027 tax year, and the collector asks for at least 90 days to process. After that, participants send an affidavit every year during the same March through May window.

  • The freeze covers one primary residence only and is not retroactive to age 62.
  • It does not carry over to a new home; a move means a new application and a new base year.
  • A transfer of title removes the home from the program, as does a missed annual affidavit.
  • Debt levies and newly voted tax increases still show on the bill.

Questions go to the collector at (573) 458-6155 or seniortaxrelief@phelpscounty.org.

What happens when Phelps County property taxes go unpaid?

Delinquent parcels are auctioned once a year on the fourth Monday in August, starting at 10:00 am in the Community Room of the Phelps County Courthouse. The collector cites RSMo 140.150 for the date. The 2026 sale has passed, and the next one falls in August 2027. Notice runs in the Rolla Daily News on three consecutive Wednesdays beforehand, and the list appears on the collector's website.

A buyer does not own the house right away. The owner, a lienholder or an occupant can redeem during the year after the sale by paying the collector the purchase amount and costs, and the buyer earns simple interest of 10 percent a year on the tax and cost portion. Phelps County has advertised many more parcels than it sells, since most owners pay before the day arrives. An owner who is behind can ask the collector what it takes to come off the list before the sale.

What is Phelps County like for a seller?

Phelps County lies in the central part of Missouri, was organized on November 13, 1857 and named for John S. Phelps. Rolla is both the seat and the largest city, home to Missouri University of Science and Technology. The county also includes St. James, Newburg, Doolittle and Edgar Springs, and it is crossed by I-44, US 63 and Routes 8, 68 and 72. Part of the Mark Twain National Forest lies inside its borders. School districts include Rolla 31, St. James R-I, Newburg R-II and Phelps County R-III.

Where is Christian County, Missouri, and who bills its property tax?

Christian County sits in the Ozarks of southwest Missouri, between Springfield and Branson. Ozark holds the courthouse, while Nixa has the most people. The county covers 564 square miles, and neighbors include Greene County to the north, Webster and Douglas to the east, Taney to the south and Stone and Lawrence to the west. Part of the Mark Twain National Forest lies inside its borders, and the James River and branches of the White River drain it.

Growth has been steady. The county's own site notes that the 1980 population of 22,402 rose by nearly 150 percent to 54,285 by 2000. The 2020 census counted 88,842 people, and the Census Bureau's mid-2025 estimate is 96,725. The Collector of Revenue mails the bills and the Assessor sets the values, with both offices in the historic courthouse on the square in Ozark.

How do I reach the Christian County Collector and Assessor?

  • Collector of Revenue: Ted Nichols, 100 W. Church, Room 101, Ozark, MO 65721, (417) 582-4330, open weekdays from 8:00 in the morning to 4:30 in the afternoon, lunch hour included.
  • Assessor: real estate questions go to 417-582-4310 and personal property to 417-582-4320.
  • Payments: in person, by mail, online at christiancountycollector.com, by the toll-free number printed on the bill, or in the around-the-clock drop box at the courthouse's west side.

The Collector's page says the office collects what the Assessor's records show and cannot change a statement on its own. Errors in a mailing address, vehicle list or legal description go to the Assessor before payment. Partial payments and wrong amounts are not accepted.

When are 2026 Christian County property taxes due?

Statements for 2026 were scheduled to be mailed on November 2, 2026. They are due on receipt and go delinquent once December 31 passes. A mailed payment must carry a USPS postmark of 12/31/26, and the online payment page closes at 11:59 p.m. that night. The Collector warns that technical trouble with phone or web payment does not extend the deadline.

Residents of four smaller towns get an in-person option. For one day each, from 9 a.m. to noon, the Collector's staff will take payments at city halls: Billings on November 16, Clever on November 17, Sparta on November 18 and Highlandville on November 19, 2026. Bring the whole statement. Those stops accept cash, check or money order only, and checks must be in blue or black ink.

If no statement arrives by the end of November, call the office. A statement that never arrives does not excuse the tax.

Which fees apply to electronic tax payments in Christian County?

Electronic payment fees are not part of the tax. The Collector's page says the county receives none of the service fee and points to RSMo 139.055, which lets the cost fall only on those who choose to pay electronically.

Way to payFee

Cash, personal check, cashier's check or money order at the office or drop boxNo service fee listed

The Collector adds that a paid receipt can be shown from a phone screen at the DMV or Department of Revenue.

How does the Christian County Assessor value property?

The Assessor's office values everything taxable in the county on the January 1 assessment date. Its page lists more than 42,951 real estate parcels and over 38,457 personal property accounts, with a total assessed value above $2 billion for 2025. Assessed value is a share of market value that depends on class: 19 percent for residential, 32 percent for commercial and 12 percent for agricultural land.

Value is one half of the bill. The other half is the levy set by each taxing district. The Assessor counts thirteen school districts, eight road districts, ten cities, nine fire districts and nine other levy districts, such as ambulance, senior services and the junior college. Totals therefore differ from one part of the county to another, and the district names on a bill explain why. Value Change Notices, exemption applications and address change forms are on the Assessor's page.

What are the steps to contest a Christian County assessment?

Missouri gives every owner a path from the Assessor to a county board and and finally to the State Tax Commission. Under RSMo 137.275, a Board of Equalization appeal must be lodged by the deadline that falls on the second Monday of July. A later appeal to the commission under RSMo 138.430 must be made within the chapter 138 deadline, or 30 days from the board's last action if that date is later.

  • Look at the Value Change Notice and the market data on the Assessor's page.
  • Call the real estate line at 417-582-4310 to ask for an informal review.
  • Ask the County Clerk for the board's form and hearing dates.
  • If a property's assessed value rose 15 percent or more, RSMo 138.060 puts the burden of proof on the Assessor, apart from increases caused by new construction.

Who qualifies for the Christian County senior tax credit?

The Senate Bill 190 senior citizen real estate tax credit has strict rules, posted on both the county home page and the Assessor's page. Renewal for people already approved is automatic if they still qualify and made no new improvements, though a spouse who has newly reached the age needs an application.

  • First-time applications are available March 1, 2027 and accepted until June 15, 2027 at the Collector's office, Room 101.
  • The applicant must be at least 62 by midnight December 31, 2026.
  • The home must be in Christian County and the applicant's primary residence since at least June 29, 2026.
  • 2026 taxes must be paid, the personal property assessment must be completed and every applicant signature must be notarized.

What should a Christian County seller do about the tax bill?

The Collector's page states that the current owner is responsible for all taxes due on the property, and that tax obligation is fixed as of January 1. Have the title company explain how the closing statement divides the year, and ask the Collector for the exact balance before the closing date.

Census Bureau QuickFacts for the county put the middle owner-occupied home value at $274,900 for 2020 to 2024, household income at the midpoint of $83,437 and 75.9 percent owner occupancy. The county had 38,594 housing units in 2025 and issued 495 building permits that year. The average commute is 25.5 minutes, and 89.6 percent of residents had not moved in the prior year.

Frequently asked questions

By what date must 2026 Christian County, MO taxes be paid?

December 31, 2026. A mailed payment needs a USPS postmark of 12/31/26, and the online system closes at 11:59 p.m. that night. Unpaid balances go delinquent after that, and the Collector says phone or web trouble does not extend the deadline.

Where do I pay Christian County property taxes in person?

At the Collector's office, 100 W. Church, Room 101, in Ozark, any weekday between 8:00 and 4:30. A 24-hour drop box also sits at the courthouse's west side. Courtesy payment days are set for Billings, Clever, Sparta and Highlandville on November 16 through 19, 2026.

What are the card fees on a Christian County tax payment?

Credit cards add 2.45 percent of the balance, debit cards add $4.00 and e-checks add $2.00. The county does not receive that service fee. Payments made in person with cash, check or money order carry no listed fee.

Who sets the value of my Christian County home?

The Christian County Assessor, Jeremy Burns, values property on that January 1 date and applies the state rates of 19 percent for residential, 32 percent for commercial and 12 percent for agricultural land. Call 417-582-4310 about real estate. Tax districts then apply their own levies to that assessed value.

Can seniors reduce their Christian County tax bill?

Possibly, through the SB 190 senior citizen real estate tax credit. First-time applications open March 1, 2027 and close June 15, 2027, and the applicant must have turned 62 by December 31, 2026. Approved owners renew automatically. Applications go to the Collector's office in Ozark.

Where is Cass County, Missouri, and what is its past?

Western Missouri holds Cass County, right against the Kansas line and inside the Kansas City metro area. Harrisonville serves as the seat, and a slice of Kansas City itself falls within the county. It covers 697 square miles of land. Cass is one of the few counties in the country that borders two counties of the same name in different states, Johnson County in Missouri and Johnson County in Kansas.

Organized in 1835 as Van Buren County, it took the name Cass in 1849 for U.S. Senator Lewis Cass of Michigan. James Lackey was the first settler on the site of Harrisonville in 1830. The town was platted in 1837 and named for Representative Albert G. Harrison. During the Civil War it was emptied in 1863 when federal forces pushed residents out, and most of the buildings were burned.

The 2020 census counted 107,824 people, of whom 70.3 percent lived in urban areas.

Which cities and school districts are in Cass County?

The county's Helpful Numbers page lists fourteen municipalities with phone lines: Archie, Belton, Cleveland, Creighton, Drexel, East Lynne, Freeman, Garden City, Greenwood, Harrisonville, Lake Winnebago, Peculiar, Pleasant Hill and Raymore. Wikipedia adds Lake Annette and Strasburg to its list of cities. Small slices of Kansas City and Lee's Summit also lie inside the county line.

Twelve full K-12 districts reach into Cass, according to Wikipedia:

  • Harrisonville R-IX, Belton, Raymore-Peculiar R-II and Pleasant Hill R-III
  • Archie R-V, Drexel R-IV, Holden R-III and Kingsville R-I
  • Lee's Summit R-VII, Lone Jack C-VI, Sherwood Cass R-VIII and Midway R-I

Two homes with equal assessed values can still produce different bills, since each school, fire and library district adds its own levy. Read the district names on the bill itself.

How does Cass County compare on housing and income?

Among the four Missouri counties in this comparison, Cass grew fastest and earns the most per household. Census QuickFacts supplies the figures below.

MeasureCass County
Residents (July 2025 estimate)115,859
Change since the 2020 census base7.5%

Owners occupy 75.6 percent of homes, 7.0 percent of residents live in poverty, and the average trip to work takes 28.0 minutes, the longest of the four counties. Retailers took in $2.0 billion in 2022. The steady permit count means newly built subdivisions in Belton, Raymore and Peculiar sit beside resale houses, which gives an older home in Harrisonville or Pleasant Hill real competition.

Who collects and assesses property tax in Cass County?

The Collector and the Assessor are neighbors on Cantrell Road in Harrisonville.

  • Collector Chris Molendorp, 2725 Cantrell Road, 816-380-8377, collector@casscounty.com, with weekday counter service from eight until half past four
  • Assessor, 2733 Cantrell Road, 816-380-8400.
  • County Clerk Kathy Lambertz, Historic Courthouse, 102 E. Wall Street, who handles the secretarial work for the Board of Equalization.

The Collector's drop box is at Annex 1, 201 W. Wall Street, and a payment placed in it before midnight on December 31 is timely. The county's FAQ stresses that the Treasurer's office, held by Steve Cheslik, does not take property tax. Recorder of Deeds Mike Medsker handles deeds. The portal at casscountycollector.org lets you search tax records and print receipts.

What is the Cass County due date, and what do late payments cost?

Under the Collector's General Information page, a Cass County real estate bill is payable once you get it, with December 31 as the outer limit. Statements go out during November. The postmark from the U.S. Postal Service counts, and the county refuses its own metered stamps. Call 816-380-8377 if November ends without a bill.

After December 31 the Collector adds penalties and fees that may climb to 25 percent in year one of delinquency. Not getting the bill is no defense. The debt stays with the land, so whoever owns the parcel next is responsible for what is owed.

The bill is printed with the owner and address on file at that moment. A house that changes hands from October 1 on can therefore generate a bill addressed to the previous owner. That seller should pass the buyer's name and mailing address to the Collector, and a buyer still waiting on December 10 should phone the office.

How is a Cass County tax bill calculated?

Two inputs produce the bill: the assessor's value and the rates adopted by each taxing body over the parcel. The Collector's worked example takes $9,500 of assessed value, divides it by 100 and multiplies by 5.66 percent, which gives $537.70.

  • Houses and other residential property: 19 percent of market value
  • Commercial property: 32 percent
  • Farm ground: 12 percent

Under the county's FAQ, a $50,000 house therefore carries $9,500 in assessed value. Odd-numbered years bring a countywide update, and new construction is added once it is complete. A higher value can still leave the bill unchanged when levies drop, and the county says levies are normally set in September. Ask the Assessor at 816-380-8400 whether Cass has adopted a homestead credit under RSMo 137.1050 before you count on one for the home you are selling.

What are the steps to appeal in Cass County?

The county's FAQ frames the dispute around one question, market value, and warns that complaints about the size of the bill carry no weight. Photographs, the price of a recent sale of the property or testimony from a recent appraiser all help.

  1. Talk it through with the Assessor's staff.
  2. Return the Board of Equalization appeal form to the Assessor. The 2026 deadline was a July 13 postmark.
  3. Go to the State Tax Commission. For 2026 the date was September 30, or 30 days from the Board's last action if that came later.

Both of those 2026 dates are behind us, and the next round follows the 2027 reassessment. The County Commission appoints the Board, and the County Clerk's office does its paperwork. The underlying statutes are RSMo 138.430 and RSMo 137.275.

When is the Cass County tax certificate sale?

The auction of tax certificates happens each year at 10 a.m. on the fourth Monday of August inside the Harrisonville courthouse, 102 E. Wall Street. This year's sale, on August 24, is over, and August 2027 holds the next. The Collector's page says a parcel can be offered once its real estate tax remains open past March 1 of the next year. RSMo 140.150 fixes the sale day and has the Collector send notice to the record owner before the list is published.

The owner can still pay the back tax plus penalty, interest and costs ahead of the auction, and the Collector's website has a bidders area for buyers. For someone selling, that listing works as a clock: if the closing pays the balance, the parcel comes off.

What happens to Cass County property tax at closing?

The Collector's buyer and seller notes describe a split: the tax is usually prorated, and the buyer is credited for each month or day the seller held the house during the year. Nothing is handed to the Collector on closing day. The buyer then pays the whole annual bill by December 31. A lender that escrows the tax should be told about a payoff and normally refunds the cushion or applies it to the loan.

The Cass Recorder's FAQ promises same-day to 24-hour turnaround on real estate recordings, skipping weekends and holidays. Deeds on record do not state the price. That office will not phone with closing news or search for liens, so lean on the title company, because liens can sit with the courts or the Collector as well.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I pay Cass County property tax?

Pay the Collector at 2725 Cantrell Road, Harrisonville, on weekdays. A drop box at 201 W. Wall Street is timely until midnight December 31, and the Collector's portal at casscountycollector.org shows bills.

How big is the Cass County late penalty?

Penalties and fees can reach 25 percent in the first year of delinquency, and they begin after December 31. A mailed payment is on time only if the U.S. postmark is December 31 or earlier.

Does the buyer or seller pay Cass County property tax at closing?

Taxes are generally prorated, with the buyer credited for the part of the year the seller owned the house. No tax is paid to the Collector at closing, and the buyer pays the full bill by December 31.

When is the Cass County tax certificate sale?

Each August, on the fourth Monday at 10 a.m., in the courthouse at 102 E. Wall Street, Harrisonville. A parcel can be offered when its real estate tax is still open after March 1 of the next year.

How do I contest my Cass County assessed value?

Call the Assessor at 816-380-8400 first, then send the Board of Equalization form to that office by the July postmark date. Disagreeing with the Board's result takes you to the State Tax Commission.

What is Lincoln County, Missouri, and why has it grown so fast?

Lincoln County is an eastern Missouri county on the Mississippi River, across from Illinois, with Troy as its seat, and it belongs to the St. Louis metro area. It measures 640 square miles in total, 627 of them land. Pike, Calhoun (Illinois), St. Charles, Warren and Montgomery counties touch its edges.

The county dates from December 14, 1818 and honors Major General Benjamin Lincoln of the Revolutionary War. Its population went from 52,566 in 2010 to 59,574 in 2020, and the Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 66,676, up 11.9% on the 2020 base.

The housing count tells the same story: 24,289 units in July 2025, and 252 building permits issued in 2025.

Which school districts and communities serve Lincoln County?

Five districts based in or serving the county, and the levy of the one covering your address shows up on your bill. Lincoln County R-III in Troy is the biggest, running Troy Buchanan High School and New Horizons High School.

  • Lincoln County R-III (Troy), with Boone, Cuivre Park, Hawk Point and Main Street elementaries among others
  • Elsberry R-II
  • Silex R-I
  • Winfield R-IV
  • Wright City R-II, which covers the southern parts of the county

Moscow Mills, Old Monroe and Winfield sit in the southeast corner of the county, and Foley, Truxton and Whiteside are other named communities.

What do the Census figures say about Lincoln County households?

Homes here are valued at about $244,300 for owners in the 2020 to 2024 data, and 79.0% of households own. Income per household is $89,278 in 2024 dollars, and 7.9% of residents live in poverty.

Who sets and who bills Lincoln County property tax?

Kevin Bishop is the County Assessor, at 3 Front Street in Troy, and Jessica Zumwalt is the Collector of Revenue, at 1 Front Street. The Collector's taxpayer portal lists 636-528-0316 for the office and searches records by name, statement number or parcel number.

The Assessor's page breaks a bill into three parts. The assessor sets value, the taxing authority (a school, city or fire district) picks a rate from its budget, and the collector gathers the money. The Assessor has no hand in the rate.

The Collector's list of recipients is long: the state, county, ambulance, hospital, SB-40 board, county health center, schools, cities and fire districts. The same office takes drainage and neighborhood improvement district charges and merchant license fees, and it handles escrow payments from mortgage holders.

How are Lincoln County homes assessed?

A residential parcel is assessed at 19% of market value, farmland at 12% and commercial property at 32%. The Assessor revalues real estate in odd-numbered years such as 2021, 2023 and 2025, using a January 1 date, and checks for new or lost improvements in the even years between.

Field appraisers walk every parcel each year in marked county vehicles with ID badges. If someone without identification is on your land, the office asks you to call it. In a revaluation year the office compares recent sale prices with its own appraisals to decide whether land and buildings go up.

A change in value must come with a Notice of Change in Value. You may ask for an informal hearing, then go to the Board of Equalization, whose filing deadline is the second Monday in July. The board convenes on the third Monday in July, and the State Tax Commission follows it.

Which dates define the Lincoln County tax year?

Value is fixed on January 1 and payment is due on December 31, with several local dates in between. Transfers are posted to the new owner up to August 31, so a statement for a house sold after that date still goes out in the previous owner's name.

  • January 1: valuation date for real estate
  • Second Monday in July: appeal filing deadline for the board
  • Third Monday in July: the board convenes
  • Second week of July: the tax sale list starts running in the Lincoln County Journal and Elsberry Democrat
  • Fourth Monday in August, 10 a.m.: tax sale on the courthouse east steps
  • December 31: tax due

When a statement for a house you sold after August 31 reaches you, the Assessor's page says to ask the County Collector about forwarding it to the new owner. Compare the title company's closing statement to see how each side's share was credited.

What happens at the Lincoln County tax sale?

Real estate with three years of delinquent tax must be offered at the sale, which takes place on the fourth Monday in August at 10 a.m. on the courthouse's east steps. Owners may pay in full beforehand, and the collector says a high share do once the advertisement appears.

Bidders register from 8 a.m. in Room 103 of the courthouse, sign an affidavit saying they owe no delinquent tax, and must be present. A bidder who lives outside Missouri has to name a Lincoln County citizen as an agent. The opening bid covers the taxes, interest and charges.

The winner receives a certificate of purchase and pays the later taxes, but has no right to possession during the one-year redemption period. Any bid above the opening amount goes to the county treasurer for the owner of record, and money unclaimed after three years goes to the schools. The collector advises buyers to see an attorney first.

How do I pay or protest a Lincoln County bill?

Look up your bill on the Collector's taxpayer portal, call the office, or visit 1 Front Street in Troy. Searches accept a statement number such as R plus digits for real estate, a parcel number or an owner name, and the portal returns up to 100 records.

To protest a value, pay the full bill to the collector by December 31, mark the payment as a protest, and attach your reasons and the value you claim. A mailed payment needs a postmark of December 31 or earlier.

An attorney must file for an LLC, trust, estate or corporation. A taxpayer who never got notice of an increase, or who bought within 30 days of the statement mailing, may appeal straight to the State Tax Commission.

What should a Lincoln County seller check when taxes are owed?

Open your parcel record, request a written payoff from the Collector, and confirm that the Assessor shows the right owner and acreage. Ask which drainage, neighborhood improvement or other district charges appear on your bill.

  • Compare the statement with the title company's closing statement.
  • Ask whether any year is on the August tax sale list.
  • Ask the Collector about senior relief programs if the owner is an older homeowner.
  • If the sale closes after August 31, ask the Collector who will receive the statement.

The payoff comes out of the sale price at closing, so get the number in writing first.
