Frequently asked questions

Is Lincoln County property tax due December 31?

Yes. A mailed payment needs a postmark on or before that date to avoid penalty and interest.

On what date is the Lincoln County tax sale?

The fourth Monday in August, at 10 a.m. on the courthouse east steps in Troy. Bidder registration starts at 8 a.m. in Room 103.

How often is Lincoln County real estate revalued?

Every two years, in odd-numbered years such as 2025 and 2027, as of January 1. The even years pick up new construction and lost improvements.

When must I file with the Lincoln County Board of Equalization?

By the second Monday in July. The board convenes on the third Monday in July.

Which Lincoln County office do I call about a balance?

Call the Collector of Revenue at 636-528-0316. For a question about value, contact the Assessor at 3 Front Street in Troy.

Which Warren County offices handle a property tax bill?

Property tax in Warren County runs through two suites of the Administration Building on Mockingbird Lane in Warrenton. Kathryn Smith is the Assessor, in Suite 202, reachable at 636-456-8885 extension 1227. Her staff puts a value on every parcel. Julie Schaumberg is the Collector, in Suite 200, at 636-456-3330, and her staff mails the bills and receives payment.

The Collector keeps weekday hours from eight until four-thirty, and email goes to collector@warrencountymo.gov. It states that it cannot add to or change a tax statement unless the Assessor makes the change first. Questions about value belong with the Assessor, and questions about paying belong with the Collector.

The Collector's site posts a 2026 rate PDF, a side by side of 2025 and 2026 rates, a tax sale list and a holiday calendar. The Assessor's site offers parcel and personal property searches, and it says emailed assessment forms are not accepted. Use the e-file option or the mail.

When are Warren County property taxes due?

The Collector mails statements in the first week of November, and December 31 is the last safe day. No bill by Thanksgiving? Phone the Collector. An unreceived statement still leaves the tax, and any late charge, owed.

Warren County property tax dates drawn from the Assessor and Collector pages
DateWhat happens
January 1Ownership on this day fixes who is taxed for the year
March 1Personal property lists go to the Assessor
First week of NovemberStatements are mailed
ThanksgivingCall the Collector if no bill has arrived
November 26 and 27, 2026Collector's office closed
December 24 and 25, 2026Collector's office closed
December 31Last postmark date to avoid penalty and interest

With the Thanksgiving and Christmas closures, the number of open days before the deadline is smaller than it looks. A 24 hour drop box stands to the right of the entrance.

How does the Assessor value a house in Warren County?

Real estate here is revalued every second year, in the odd-numbered ones, on January 1 values. That puts the most recent cycle in 2025 and the coming one in 2027. In even years the only changes come from new construction or demolition.

Field appraisers visit every parcel, measure any added square footage and adjust depreciation on buildings. State law fixes the taxed share of value: 19 percent for residences, 12 percent for farm ground and 32 percent for commercial property. A jump of more than 15 percent on a home, apart from new building, requires a physical inspection first.

Rates come from elsewhere. Schools, the county, fire districts and other taxing bodies vote on theirs, and your total depends on which of them cover your address.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Warren County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How do you appeal a Warren County assessment?

The Notice of Change in value arrives when reassessment or new construction raises a figure. Weigh it against what a buyer would pay.

  • Request an informal hearing with the Assessor's staff and carry proof of value, for instance the price from your own purchase or an appraisal.
  • Still no change? Book a Board of Equalization hearing through the Assessor before the legal cutoff.
  • The Board's ruling can go to the State Tax Commission, which hears appeals filed within 30 days of that ruling or by the chapter's own date if later.

The Assessor's page says a complaint that taxes are high is not relevant testimony. Only the market value of the house counts. An owner who pays the whole current bill before it goes delinquent can lodge a written protest with the Collector, then has 90 days to file suit in circuit court. With a timely Commission appeal pending, the disputed slice is held in a separate fund.

What happens if tax is still owed when a Warren County house sells?

The Assessor's site says whoever owns property on January 1 is liable for that calendar year's tax. A March closing therefore leaves the seller as the named owner for the year, so the settlement sheet needs to say who covers the bill.

Get the parcel's balance from the Collector ahead of closing day. The counter refuses short or wrong amounts, and any delinquent year has to be settled before the current one. Confirm the oldest year first, because anything delinquent comes ahead of the current bill.

  • Accepted: cash, personal check, money order, cashier's check, plus cards at the office or online.
  • By phone, call the outside vendor at 1-877-690-3729 and give jurisdiction code 3563.
  • A single check may pay more than one bill.
  • Send the bottom stub of the statement along with the check.

Does a move out of Warren County change the vehicle tax bill?

No. Vehicles are taxed on what the owner held on January 1, according to the Assessor's site, even if the car was sold the next day or the owner left Missouri in June. The law has no proration.

A seller moving soon after closing still gets that year's personal property statement, with the same December 31 postmark date. The Assessor adds that a taxpayer arriving in Missouri on March 1, 2026 is first assessed on January 1, 2027, and pays that bill in December 2027.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Warren County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What do Census figures show for Warren County?

By the Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate, 39,016 people live in Warren County, 9.8 percent more than in the 2020 base. The county has 17,361 housing units, and 80.2 percent of homes are lived in by their owners. Owned homes had a median value of $260,400 in the 2020 to 2024 survey, the top figure among Stone, Warren and Webster, while median rent was $995.

Owners with a mortgage paid a median $1,485 a month and those without paid $499. Builders took out 360 permits in 2025, against 212 in Stone and 226 in Webster. Work is common: 62.8 percent of adults are in the civilian labor force, and the county's transportation and warehousing receipts came to $113.4 million in 2022.

Where is Warren County and which schools serve it?

Warren County lies on the north side of the Missouri River and is part of the St. Louis metropolitan area. It covers 438 square miles and was established on January 5, 1833. Interstate 70, U.S. Route 40, Route 47 and Route 94 cross it, and Route 94 is known as the Missouri Weinstrasse for its vineyards.

Warrenton is the county seat. The other cities are Foristell, Marthasville, Truesdale and Wright City, and the villages are Innsbrook, Pendleton and Three Creeks. Public school districts are Warren County R-III in Warrenton and Wright City R-II. The statement shows which district a house sits in, and that choice moves the rate.

Neighbors are Lincoln County to the north, St. Charles County to the east, Franklin County to the south, Gasconade County to the southwest and Montgomery County to the west. The county belongs to the Missouri Rhineland, with award-winning wineries on both sides of the river. Holy Rosary School in Warrenton and two Catholic schools in Marthasville serve families who prefer a private option, and the Warrenton branch of the Scenic Regional Library is the public library listed for the county seat.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I pay Warren County property tax?

At the Collector's office, 101 Mockingbird Lane, Suite 200, Warrenton. You can also pay online, by mail, through the vendor phone line or in the 24 hour drop box. The office number is 636-456-3330.

What is the Warren County property tax deadline?

Mail it with a December 31 postmark. Bills go out the first week of November, and earlier delinquent years are cleared before the current one.

When will Warren County reassess homes again?

In 2027. Values reset in odd-numbered years, and in 2026 only new construction or demolition changes a parcel's figure.

Can I make a partial payment on a Warren County bill?

No. The Collector says it cannot take incorrect or partial payments. One check can still cover several bills.

How do I dispute a Warren County valuation?

Ask the Assessor for an informal hearing first, then a Board of Equalization appointment. Bring a sale price or appraisal, because the size of the tax bill is not evidence.

Which Buffalo offices handle Dallas County property tax?

Two courthouse offices share the job. The Assessor sets values, and Collector Amy Faulkner mails statements and takes payment. The Collector works from the Dallas County Administration Building, 102 S Cedar Street, Buffalo, MO 65622, with PO Box 529 for mail. Call (417) 345-7836 between 8:00 and 12:00 or 1:00 and 4:00 on weekdays other than holidays.

The Assessor answers at (417) 345-8774, PO Box 263. Per the Collector's site, the Assessor is the contact for the assessed value of real or personal property, a name or address change, vehicles listed in error and the legal description. The Collector is the contact for a statement that never arrived or for questions about how collection works.

The Missouri Association of Counties also lists the County Clerk at (417) 345-2632, the Recorder, Stacy Satterfield, at (417) 345-2242, and the Treasurer at (417) 345-2020.

When do Dallas County statements arrive and when do they go delinquent?

The county mails real estate and personal property statements in November. Each is payable on receipt and goes delinquent once December 31 passes. Anyone without a statement by the end of November should phone the Collector straight away.

  • Mailed checks need a USPS postmark dated no later than December 31.
  • Later postmarks come back unprocessed unless the penalty and interest are enclosed.
  • Back years must be cleared before the office will take the current year.
  • Send the bottom stub of the statement with a mailed payment, and a single check can pay several bills.

Walk-in, mail and website payments are all accepted at dallascountymocollector.com, with cash, personal check, money order, cashier's check or a debit or credit card. Card use adds a convenience fee. The Collector adds that the office bears no responsibility if you pay tax on someone else's property or overlook one you own, so read the legal description on each statement.

How is a Dallas County house valued for tax?

Missouri splits real estate into classes. The Cole and Dent County assessor pages describe residential property at 19% of market value, agricultural land at 12% of production value and other property at 32%. Dallas County covers 541 square miles of land and had roughly 31.6 residents per square mile in 2020.

Figures come from Census QuickFacts for Dallas County.

A home at the $190,300 median would carry an assessed value near $36,157 at the 19% residential rate, and the levies of the school, fire and other districts apply to that figure. The Assessor can tell you which levies fit your parcel.

What are my options if I think a Dallas County assessment is too high?

Phone the Assessor first and ask how the number was built. If that fails, RSMo 137.275 lets an owner go to the county board of equalization in person, through an attorney or agent, or by letter, filed by the second Monday in July. The County Clerk's office, (417) 345-2632, can tell you about hearing dates.

RSMo 138.060 tells the board to decide such appeals in a summary way, with no presumption favoring the assessor. Where a property's assessed valuation climbed 15% or more over the prior assessment, and the climb is not from new construction or improvements, the Dallas County assessor carries the burden of proving the value. Keep your increase notice handy.

Next comes the State Tax Commission, reachable under RSMo 138.430 within the chapter's time limit or 30 days after the local board's final action, whichever falls later. The Commission fixes assessments it finds unlawful, unfair, improper, arbitrary or capricious. Claims that property is exempt or sits in the wrong taxing location go to circuit court within 30 days.

How does the Dallas County delinquent land sale work?

Each year the Collector offers delinquent parcels at auction on the fourth Monday of August. The 2026 notice scheduled it for August 24, 2026, 10:00 a.m., at the Dallas County Annex Building in Buffalo, and that day is behind us. The 2027 sale will land on the fourth Monday of August 2027 under RSMo 140.150. Taxes, penalty, interest and costs may be paid up to the moment a parcel is sold.

  • Bidders have to live in Missouri or name an agent who does.
  • The notice cautions that parcels may hold hazardous waste, liens or condemned buildings.
  • Owners get one year after the sale to redeem.
  • Money bid above the tax amount earns no interest.

Before parcels are advertised, the Collector must mail the recorded owner a first class notice, plus a certified one when the assessed value tops $1,000. Not receiving a notice does not erase the tax. Owners who are behind should ask the Assessor to confirm the mailing address on file.

What else does the Dallas County Collector handle for new owners?

The Collector also collects utility taxes, merchant and auctioneer license fees and duplicate receipt fees, and issues tax exempt waivers when they apply. Each year she runs the delinquent sale.

People moving to Dallas County from another state have 30 days to get Missouri plates and a Missouri driver's license. For plates the Collector's site lists the title or registration, proof of insurance, a Missouri inspection certificate and either a validated tax receipt from the Collector or a non-assessment clearance from the Assessor. Newcomers moving from another Missouri county need to ask the Assessor for an assessment sheet before March 1 to avoid a penalty.

What is Dallas County like for a home seller?

Organized in 1842 as Niangua County, the county took George M. Dallas, vice president under James K. Polk, as its namesake in 1844. Buffalo is the seat and the biggest city, home to 3,290 people in 2020. US 65 reaches Springfield, 28 miles to the south-southwest, and Routes 32 and 73 meet in town. The county sits in the Springfield metro area and borders Camden, Laclede, Webster, Greene, Polk and Hickory counties.

Dallas County R-I operates Mallory Elementary, Buffalo Prairie Middle School, Buffalo High School and the Dallas County Technical Center. Wikipedia also lists Hickory County R-I, with Skyline schools, at Urbana. The county has two cities, Buffalo and Urbana, plus the village of Louisburg and the census-designated place of Bennett Springs. Thirteen building permits were issued in 2025, and the Census Bureau puts poverty at 17.0%.

When your house sells, have the title company request a current statement from the Collector and settle the year's tax at the table. If the transfer comes after the November mailing, let the Collector know where the new bill should go.

Frequently asked questions

When does Dallas County tax become delinquent?

After December 31. Statements are payable on receipt, and a mailed check needs a postmark of that date or earlier. Later payments come back unless penalty and interest are included. Phone (417) 345-7836 if November ends without a statement.

What are the Dallas County Collector's office hours and address?

The office is in the Dallas County Administration Building, 102 S Cedar Street, Buffalo, MO 65622. Hours run weekdays from 8:00 to 12:00 and 1:00 to 4:00. Mail goes to PO Box 529.

Which Dallas County office sets assessed value?

The Assessor, at (417) 345-8774. The Collector bills whatever the Assessor's records show, so questions about value, owner names, vehicles and legal descriptions go to the Assessor.

What date ends the window to appeal to the Dallas County board of equalization?

The second Monday in July under RSMo 137.275. You may appear in person, send an attorney or agent, or write. The County Clerk can explain the hearing schedule.

Has the Dallas County 2026 tax sale already happened?

Yes, it was set for August 24, 2026. The next sale falls on the fourth Monday of August 2027. A parcel owner can pay what is due before the sale and has one year afterward to redeem.

Which two courthouse offices deal with Henry County property tax?

Both sit at 100 West Franklin in Clinton, ZIP 64735. Scott Largent is the assessor, reachable at 660-885-7212. His page keeps early hours, 7:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Monday to Friday, and offers weekend or evening visits by appointment. The county also publishes a GIS mapping link from the same page.

Bills come from a different desk. The state's collector directory lists the Henry County Treasurer as Ex Officio Collector of Revenue, with phone 660-885-7207, fax 660-885-7259 and email collector@henrycountymo.net. Questions about a value belong with the assessor. Questions about a balance belong with the collector.

What does Henry County look like on the ground?

Henry County sits in west-central Missouri and touches Johnson, Pettis, Benton, St. Clair, Bates and Cass counties. Its land area is 697 square miles, and another 35 square miles is water. It began in December 1834 as Rives County and took the name Henry in 1841, honoring Patrick Henry. The county site styles it the Model County of the Prairies.

The county's own history page calls agriculture the economic base and says about 80 percent of the county is forested, hilly ground, much of it beside federal land around the 55,600 acre Harry S. Truman Reservoir. Hunters and anglers are a steady presence. State routes 7, 13, 18 and 52 are the main roads, and Jefferson Lines provides intercity bus service.

Clinton, the seat, is the largest town at an estimated 8,945 people. Windsor follows with 2,847, then Urich (492), Calhoun (455), Deepwater (422) and Montrose (375). Blairstown, Brownington and Tightwad have fewer than 100 residents each.

How did Clinton become the seat of Henry County, and what is the courthouse like?

The county site says the first hunters and trappers came through in 1826 and the first settlers arrived in the fall of 1830. In 1836 the site for the seat was chosen and named for DeWitt Clinton, then a New York governor. The first court session met in a home on May 4, 1835.

The first courthouse dates to 1837 and was condemned in 1884, then taken down in 1887. Voters approved a $50,000 bond in 1891, and the contract for the present courthouse went to D. J. Hyde and Company of Sedalia for $47,221 in February 1892. Its cornerstone was laid on June 24, 1892.

What outdoor features affect how Henry County properties are marketed?

The county calls itself a sportsman's paradise. It lists many species of fish in local waters, hunting for deer, coyote, squirrel, turkey and dove, and migratory waterfowl on the Truman Reservoir. A parcel near the shoreline, or one with timber and creek frontage, will be described differently from a town lot in Clinton or Windsor, and the assessor's classification can differ too, since farm and residential ground carry different assessment rates.

Which school districts and libraries serve Henry County homes?

Buyers of a Henry County house usually ask which district it falls in, and the assessor's parcel record answers that. Districts anchored in the county include:

  • Clinton School District, with an early childhood center, Henry Elementary, Clinton Intermediate, Clinton Middle and Clinton High
  • Henry County R-1 in Windsor
  • Calhoun R-VIII, Montrose R-XIV, Davis R-XII, Leesville R-IX and Shawnee R-III
  • Lakeland R-III, which serves Deepwater and Lowry City and is physically in St. Clair County

Private options include Holy Rosary Catholic School in Clinton, St. Mary's School in Montrose and the Windsor Amish Schools. The Henry County Library and its Lenora Blackmore Branch serve the public.

What do Census figures say about housing in Henry County?

The county holds 9,217 households averaging 2.39 people. The 2020 count was 21,946, with a median age of 44.7 and 22.9 percent of residents aged 65 or older. About 59.6 percent lived in rural areas.

How does Missouri set the taxable value of a Henry County house?

The assessor applies a fixed share of market value: 19 percent for homes, 12 percent for farmland, 32 percent for commercial property, according to RSMo 137.115. Fresh values go on the books in odd-numbered years and hold through the even year that follows.

  • A jump of more than 15 percent on a home, apart from new construction, triggers an on-site inspection.
  • The owner is told in writing and has 30 days or more to request a look inside.
  • A drive-by does not satisfy the statute.

If such a jump is appealed, RSMo 138.060 puts the burden on the assessor to show the value is no higher than market value.

How can a Henry County owner challenge a value?

The first stop is the county Board of Equalization, with a filing cutoff the State Tax Commission gives as the second Monday in July. A ruling against you can go to the Commission, which allows 30 days from the date of the Board's letter. Filing is online, by email to Legal@stc.mo.gov or by post to PO Box 146, Jefferson City, MO 65102-0146.

Property held by a company, trust or estate needs a lawyer to file. Your complaint should carry the tax bill or the Board's letter, and nothing else at first. An agreed value signed with the assessor closes the door on further appeal. Call 660-885-7212 for the local forms.

What dates matter on a Henry County tax calendar?

Missouri taxes whoever holds the property on January 1. A Henry County owner or seller should watch these dates:

  • January 1: assessment date
  • Odd years: new real estate values
  • Second Monday in July: Board of Equalization filing cutoff
  • December 31: bill due, with mailed payments judged by postmark under RSMo 139.100
  • After January 1: penalty added by the collector
  • Fourth Monday in August: sale of delinquent land

Call the collector for this year's mailing date and the penalty figure.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

What if my Henry County house has back taxes when I sell?

Missouri lets the county sell delinquent land on the fourth Monday of August, and RSMo 140.150 lets the owner stop the sale by paying tax, penalty, interest and costs to the collector first. Notice goes by first class mail to the recorded owner, and a letter that never shows up cancels nothing.

Request a payoff from 660-885-7207 before you list, then hand the figure to your title company. If you dispute the value, RSMo 139.031 allows payment under protest: full payment before delinquency, a written statement to the collector, and a circuit court suit within ninety days.

Frequently asked questions

Who prints the Henry County property tax bill?

The Treasurer, acting as Ex Officio Collector of Revenue, at 100 West Franklin in Clinton. The state directory lists 660-885-7207 for that office.

Which percentage applies to a Henry County residence?

Nineteen percent of true value. Farmland is assessed at 12 percent and commercial property at 32 percent, and the local levy then applies to the assessed figure.

Is there a grace period after December 31 in Henry County?

Missouri judges mailed payments by postmark, and the collector adds a penalty once January 1 arrives. Ask the collector's office whether any exception applies to you.

Could Henry County auction my home over unpaid tax?

Yes, the statute allows a sale of delinquent land on the fourth Monday of August. Paying the tax, penalty, interest and costs to the collector before then stops the sale.

How do I reach the Henry County assessor?

Phone 660-885-7212 or stop by 100 West Franklin in Clinton. Weekday hours are 7:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., and appointments outside those hours are available.

Where do Buchanan County property taxes get billed and collected?

Both the Assessor and the Collector work from the Buchanan County courthouse complex at 411 Jules Street in St. Joseph. The Collector is in Room 123 (816-271-1401, fax 816-271-1584), and the Assessor is in Rooms 122 and 222 (816-271-1520). Both offices keep Monday to Friday hours, 8:00 AM to 4:30 PM.

The Collector's page says the office handles about $100 million in tax revenue each year and passes it to 33 taxing districts. It also prepares the statements, issues Merchant and Manufacturer licenses and runs the delinquent tax sale each August. The Assessor, an elected official, maintains a roll of more than 40,000 real parcels and over 110,000 articles of personal property.

What is Buchanan County like for a home seller?

Buchanan County covers 415 square miles along the Missouri River in the northwest corner of the state. Its seat, St. Joseph, held 72,473 people in 2020, far more than Gower, Agency, Dearborn or any other community. The county was organized in 1838 as Roberts County and renamed in 1839 for James Buchanan. Interstate 29, Interstate 229 and U.S. 36, 59, 71 and 169 are the main roads.

Several school systems serve the county: St. Joseph School District, Buchanan County R-IV at De Kalb, East Buchanan County C-1 at Gower, Mid-Buchanan County R-V at Faucett, and the North Platte County R-I district. Missouri Western State University is in St. Joseph. The population has slipped, from 89,201 in 2010 to an estimated 83,540 in 2025.

How do Buchanan County housing numbers compare?

The following for Buchanan County.

  • Housing units in 2025: 38,615
  • Owner-occupied rate, 2020-2024: 66.3 percent
  • Typical owner-occupied home value: $166,300
  • Median gross rent: $902
  • Median household income: $62,158
  • Building permits in 2025: 52

With the 19 percent residential rate that Boone County's Collector publishes for Missouri, a $166,300 home comes to roughly $31,597 of assessed value. Taxing districts then apply their levies per $100 of that figure. The Assessor's page explains that the Assessor finishes the roll by about July 1 and sends it to the County Clerk, that districts set budgets and levies near the end of September, and that the Assessor has no part in setting those levies.

When does Buchanan County want its tax payments?

Statements go out during the first week of November. The Collector asks for payment upon receipt, and December 31 is the line between on time and late. A payment counts only if it arrives by then or carries an official United States Postal Service postmark, since a private postage meter mark is not accepted. State law on mailed payments appears in RSMo 139.100.

If no statement shows up by the end of November, contact the office for a copy. Not getting one does not waive interest or penalties. Anyone who needs a receipt within seven days should pay in person, since a receipt for an online payment is mailed in three to five business days. The office takes cash, check, American Express, Discover, MasterCard and Visa, but not payments by phone, and a lost receipt can be replaced for $1.

What are the Buchanan County property tax steps in order?

Buchanan County property tax steps, from county and State Tax Commission pages
StepTiming
Assessor finishes the rollAbout July 1
Board of Equalization appealBy the second Monday in July
Taxing districts set leviesTypically by end of September
Tax statements mailedFirst week of November
Payment dueDecember 31, or postmarked that day
Delinquent tax saleAugust, on the fourth Monday under state law

What happens if Buchanan County taxes go unpaid?

Delinquent real estate and personal property taxes are applied first. The Collector's page says any back taxes owed must be paid before a payment goes toward the current year, and that a payment schedule printed on the statement applies after December 31.

Land that reaches the back tax book picks up a penalty of 18 percent of the year's delinquency under RSMo 140.100, limited to 2 percent per month if the owner redeems before the sale. RSMo 140.150 allows sale of delinquent land on the fourth Monday in August, requires the Collector to mail a first class notice to the recorded owner, and adds a certified mailing when the assessed value tops $1,000. The owner can pay the tax, penalty and costs at any point before the sale.

What property tax relief exists for Buchanan County seniors?

Two programs show up on the county's website. The Missouri Property Tax Credit can return up to $750 to residents who are 65 or older, 100 percent disabled, or a veteran disabled by service, or who are 60 or older and receive surviving spouse Social Security benefits. Household income, Social Security included, cannot exceed $25,000 for a single filer or $27,000 for a married couple. The Department of Revenue's number is 573-751-3505, and Form MO-PTC is available by calling 800-877-6881.

The Buchanan County Commission also voted in September 2024 to offer the Senior Citizen Homestead Property Tax Credit under RSMo 137.1050. Residents aged 62 or older can freeze the amount owed on a primary residence at its level for the year they qualify, which is the 2024 amount for those eligible then. It limits future increases only and gives no refund. The first application window ran March 1 through June 30, 2025, so ask the courthouse about any later window.

What should a St. Joseph seller know about tax and recording timing?

A sale does not erase the year's bill, so settle who pays what before closing day. Ask the Collector's office for the current balance on the parcel, and remember that back taxes must be cleared before any money counts toward the current year. Questions about a name, mailing address or legal description belong to the Assessor, not the Collector.

The Recorder of Deeds is in Room 103 of the same building at 411 Jules Street, phone 816-271-1437. That office will not record anything after 4:00 PM. Papers handed in later are recorded in the order received starting at 8:00 AM the next business day, which matters when a closing runs late near December 31 or a payoff deadline. The Recorder also says it cannot prepare a deed or answer legal questions, so use a title company or attorney for the paperwork.

How do you appeal a Buchanan County assessment?

Start with the Assessor's office, which can explain how a value was reached. If the answer is unsatisfactory, the Board of Equalization is the next stop, with a filing deadline of the second Monday in July. The State Tax Commission's guidance says a later appeal to the Commission follows the board's decision by 30 days, and RSMo 138.430 sets that right.

An owner who has paid without protest and skipped both appeals cannot challenge that year's assessment, but may appeal the next year. Property held by an LLC, trust, estate or corporation must use an attorney for a State Tax Commission appeal.

Frequently asked questions

What is the due date for Buchanan County property tax?

December 31. Payment must reach the Collector or carry an official USPS postmark by that day, since private postage meter marks do not count.

Where is the Buchanan County Collector located?

At 411 Jules Street, Room 123, in St. Joseph. Hours are 8:00 AM to 4:30 PM Monday through Friday, and the number is 816-271-1401.

Can I pay Buchanan County taxes online?

Yes, through the county's Pay/View Taxes application, which adds a convenience fee that the Collector neither sets nor keeps. Pay in person if you need a receipt in under seven days.

When is the Buchanan County tax sale?

The Collector holds it each August. State law places delinquent land sales on the fourth Monday in August, and the 2026 sale date has passed.

Is there a senior tax freeze in Buchanan County?

Yes. The county adopted the Senior Citizen Homestead Property Tax Credit in September 2024 for residents 62 and older. It caps future increases on a primary residence and is not a refund.

Who sends the tax bill in Cole County, and who sets the value?

The Assessor decides what a parcel is worth for tax purposes. The Collector of Revenue, in Room 100 of the Courthouse Annex at 311 E High Street, Jefferson City 65101, mails the bills and takes the money. The Collector answers at 573-634-9124 on weekdays from 8 in the morning until 4:30 in the afternoon, and a 24 hour drop box waits outside the Annex entrance that faces High Street.

The Assessor's page counts over 33,000 real estate parcels and more than 30,000 personal property accounts in Cole County. Collections run past 94 million dollars a year, divided among the state, several municipalities, rural fire districts, the public library and the school districts. The County Clerk keeps the hearing calendar for the Board of Equalization.

Above the county sits the Missouri State Tax Commission, which supervises assessors and takes appeals after the local board has ruled. Send value questions to the Assessor and bill questions to the Collector.

What are the payment deadlines and late costs on a Cole County bill?

A real estate bill falls due as soon as you receive it and in any case by December 31. For mail, the postmark counts. Bills go out during November, and the Collector says to phone if yours has not shown up by the second week of December, since an unreceived bill still carries the tax and any late fees.

  • Charges for the first year of delinquency can climb as high as 25%.
  • Unpaid tax is a lien that follows the real estate, so whoever buys the property takes on what is owed.
  • If the bill belongs to your lender's escrow account, pass it along to the lender.
  • Sellers who still receive a bill for a house they sold should give the Collector the buyer's name and address.

The online system takes cards with a 2.25% convenience fee and echecks with a $1.75 fee (plan on 5 to 7 days to clear). You can also call 855-568-0066, walk in, or mail a check. Mail bearing a December 31 postmark is on time, and the drop box stays open until midnight that night. At the counter the office takes cash, personal check, cashier's check, bank draft, money order or card, and one check may cover several bills.

How is the Cole County tax amount worked out?

Divide the assessed value by 100, then multiply by the levy. The Collector's worked example takes $9,500 of assessed value at $5.1240 and arrives at $486.78. Assessed value is a fraction of market value, and the fraction depends on how the parcel is classified.

Class of real estateShare of value assessed
Residential19%
Agricultural12%
Commercial32%

Rates from the county's real estate tax page.

Picture a $200,000 home: at 19%, the assessed figure is $38,000, and the levy is charged against each hundred of that. Voters and the taxing districts set the levies, and the Assessor's page links a rate sheet. Ask which taxing districts cover your parcel before you estimate a bill.

How do I challenge a Cole County valuation?

An informal conversation with the Assessor comes first. It is voluntary and available on weekdays during office hours. Show proof of market value: photographs, an inspection report, a recent appraisal or nearby sales. The county reminds owners that the Assessor's role is to keep values in line with the current market.

Formal review happens at the Board of Equalization, and RSMo 137.275 puts the filing deadline on the second Monday in July. Cole County seats its three Commissioners, a non-voting Assessor, two appointees who hold no county office and, for parcels inside Jefferson City, two city appointees. The County Clerk records the proceedings and mails each taxpayer the written decision.

A remaining dispute can go to the State Tax Commission. RSMo 138.430 allows the appeal within the period stated in that chapter or 30 days after the local board finishes, whichever ends later. Cole County describes these sessions as typically held in September and October, before one Administrative Hearing Officer, with an appraisal expected and a lawyer optional.

When does Cole County sell land for unpaid tax?

Parcels delinquent for three years are eligible for the county's certificate sale. It starts at 10 in the morning on the fourth Monday of August at the Cole County Courthouse, a date that RSMo 140.150 applies across Missouri. Paying the tax, penalty, interest and costs to the Collector ahead of the sale stops it for that parcel.

  • The News Tribune in Jefferson City runs the parcel list for three consecutive weeks beforehand.
  • Whoever wins the bid holds a certificate of purchase, and the owner has a year from the sale to redeem.
  • Liens on the property survive the sale and the redemption window.
  • A winning bidder who fails to pay risks a 25% penalty plus a prosecuting attorney fee.

An owner who is behind and weighing a sale can ask the Collector for the current payoff. The Collector's page says no tax is paid to that office at the moment of a sale, so request any payoff figure in writing through your title company.

Who covers the year's tax when a Cole County house changes hands?

Whoever owns the house in the fall pays the November bill, and that is the buyer. The Collector's page says taxes are generally prorated, so the buyer is credited at closing for the days or months the seller held the property. The buyer then pays the entire bill by December 31.

The county sits in central Missouri below the Missouri River and spans 402 square miles. Jefferson City serves as seat and state capital. William Temple Cole gave the county its name when it was organized on November 16, 1820. It borders Boone, Callaway, Osage, Miller and Moniteau counties, and US 50, 54 and 63 plus Routes 17 and 179 cross it.

Census estimates for July 1, 2025 show 77,908 people and 33,956 homes and other housing units. About 67.9% of units are owner-occupied, the 2020 to 2024 median value is $229,600 and household income has a median of $74,876. Rent has a median of $834, workers travel 17.9 minutes on average, and 154 building permits were issued in 2025.

Public school districts reaching into the county are Jefferson City Public Schools, Blair Oaks R-II, Cole County R-I at Russellville, Cole County R-V at Eugene and Jamestown C-1. Incorporated places include Jefferson City, Lohman, Russellville, St. Martins, St. Thomas, Taos, Centertown and Wardsville.

Frequently asked questions

What day does Cole County property tax become late?

After December 31. The bill is payable on receipt, mailed payments are judged by postmark and the courthouse drop box stays open until midnight that night. Charges during the first delinquent year can run up to 25%.

Can I count on the Collector mailing my bill?

Bills are mailed in November. If none has come by the second week of December, phone 573-634-9124. The obligation and late fees stand even when a bill is lost.

Until what date can a Cole County owner appeal to the Board of Equalization?

The second Monday in July, with the filing made through the County Clerk. An informal meeting with the Assessor can come earlier.

Do the buyer or the seller owe the property tax after a mid-year Cole County sale?

The buyer owes the whole bill due in December. Proration between the parties normally gives the buyer a credit at closing, and nothing is paid to the Collector during closing. A seller who still gets the bill should send the Collector the buyer's address.

How many years of unpaid tax lead to a Cole County sale?

Three. After that the parcel can be offered at the August certificate sale, and the owner may still pay what is due before the sale or redeem within a year after it.

What kind of county is Johnson County, Missouri?

Johnson County lies in western Missouri with Warrensburg as its seat and largest city. It spans roughly 829 square miles of land and borders Lafayette, Pettis, Henry, Cass and Jackson counties. Warrensburg anchors a micropolitan area that belongs to the larger Kansas City combined statistical area.

Holden and Knob Noster are the other cities. Centerview, Leeton, Chilhowee and Kingsville are villages, and Whiteman Air Force Base sits beside Knob Noster. The University of Central Missouri is in Warrensburg. Seven public districts serve the county: Warrensburg R-VI, Holden R-III, Knob Noster R-VIII, Johnson County R-VII, Leeton R-X, Kingsville R-I and Chilhowee R-IV.

The Census Bureau's QuickFacts put the 2025 population at 56,670, up 4.9% from the 2020 base. Owners occupy 63.5% of homes and renters hold the rest. The median owner-occupied home is valued at $235,700 and median gross rent is $932.

Which Johnson County offices handle property tax?

The county splits the work in three, as its Assessor page explains. The Assessor sets value and updates ownership on the roll, the taxing districts set rates, and the Collector prepares bills, takes payment and passes the money to the districts.

  • Assessor: Johnson County South Annex, 1310 S Maguire St, Suite B, Warrensburg, MO 64093. Phone 660-747-9822.
  • Collector: 1310 S Maguire St, Suite A, Warrensburg, MO 64093. Phone 660-747-5531.
  • Closure: county administrative offices are closed Thursday and Friday, November 26 and 27, 2026, for Thanksgiving.

The Assessor is not responsible for rates, collection or the distribution of money to schools and fire districts. A question about why a levy rose belongs with the district that levies it.

How does Johnson County turn market value into a tax bill?

The county publishes the formula. Market value is multiplied by an adjustment factor to get assessed value, then divided by 100 and multiplied by each district's rate, and the results are added up.

Johnson County assessment factors
ClassFactor
Residential19%
Commercial32%
Agricultural12%

The county's worked example uses an assessed value of 21,903 and a combined rate of 7.6697 per $100, which gives $1,679.90. Your own rate depends on the school, fire, ambulance and city districts around your parcel.

Real estate is reassessed in odd-numbered years, and 2027 is next. An owner gets a Change in Assessed Value Notice by mail, typically in June, when assessed value rises by $500 or more, and a notice can arrive in an even year too. It carries no tax estimate. Call the Assessor for one.

What can a Johnson County owner do about a value they dispute?

The county lays out three steps. Check the notice for factual errors, then book an informal hearing with the Assessor if you have evidence of a different value or a data mistake, then file a Property Assessment Appeal Form for a Board of Equalization hearing if the informal talk fails. Hearings run by appointment, and the contact details sit on every mailed notice.

The State Tax Commission's guide says the Board of Equalization filing must be made by the second Monday in July, which will be July 12, 2027. Ask the Assessor or County Clerk for the exact form and office, and for any extension the board grants. A Board decision can go on to the Commission within 30 days of the decision letter.

  • You may owe tax while an appeal is open. Unpaid tax after December 31 draws interest and penalties.
  • Signing a value agreement with the Assessor during a Board appeal makes the matter final, and no State Tax Commission appeal follows.
  • An LLC, trust, estate or corporation must use an attorney for a State Tax Commission appeal.

When does Johnson County property tax come due?

Bills are mailed in late October and become delinquent after December 31. The Collector's FAQ says payments must carry a postmark of December 31 or earlier. A payment postmarked after that date is returned unprocessed unless the late fees are included.

You can check what you owe on the county's Search Taxes page by choosing Real Estate and entering a name, physical address or mailing address. The first number shown is the parcel number. Missouri statute 140.100 sets an 18 percent penalty on each year's delinquency for land in the back tax book, so a lapsed bill grows quickly (RSMo 140.100).

Escrowed owners get their updated tax figures through the mortgage company, though the county reminds them that timely payment still rests with the taxpayer.

Is there senior property tax relief in Johnson County?

Yes. On March 17, 2025 the County Commission passed Ordinance 25-01, which created a Senior Real Estate Tax Credit under section 137.1050. Homeowners 62 and older may qualify for a credit on the primary residence, calculated from tax increases after a starting credit year.

  • The 2026 application window ran April 1 to June 30, 2026 and has closed. Ask the Collector when the next one opens.
  • The credit does not apply to agricultural or commercial property, personal property, voter-approved bond levies or the State Blind Pension levy.
  • All taxes on the homestead must be current to qualify.
  • It does not freeze value, and reassessments continue in odd years.

Sellers should note that the credit does not move with the owner. It stays with the applicant, does not pass to a buyer, and a seller who buys elsewhere must file a new application to set a new starting year.

What happens if Johnson County taxes stay unpaid for years?

Real estate with three years of delinquent tax must be offered at the annual tax certificate sale, held on the fourth Monday in August. The 2026 sale was set for August 24 at 10 a.m. at 301 W Market Street in Warrensburg, and that date has passed. Lists run in a local newspaper for three weeks before the sale.

The buyer purchases a tax lien, not ownership. The owner of record, or anyone with a recorded lien or deed of trust on the property, can redeem for one year and afterward until a collector's deed is issued. Redemption costs the bid amount plus 10% annual interest, and 8% on any later years' tax the buyer paid. A buyer who fails to get a collector's deed within 18 months of the sale loses the lien.

Any bid above the opening amount is held as surplus. It goes to the County Treasurer, and an owner or lienholder must file a claim with the county commission within ninety days after redemption ends, or the money goes to the schools.

How do property taxes affect a Johnson County house sale?

A tax bill left unpaid does not by itself end a sale, because the title company can request a payoff and settle it from the proceeds. Ask the Collector at 660-747-5531 for a payoff that includes penalty and interest, and order it before listing if the house is more than one year behind. A house near the three-year line is the situation to resolve first, because it can reach the August sale.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I pay Johnson County real estate tax?

At the Collector's office, 1310 S Maguire St, Suite A in Warrensburg, or through the county's online payment link. The phone number is 660-747-5531. A mailed payment needs a December 31 postmark.

What is the Johnson County residential assessment rate?

Nineteen percent of market value. Commercial property is 32% and agricultural property 12%. Rates per $100 then come from the districts covering your parcel.

When will Johnson County reassess my house again?

In 2027, since Missouri reassesses real estate in odd-numbered years. A notice goes out by mail, typically in June, if the assessed value rises by $500 or more.

Does the Johnson County senior tax credit pass to the buyer?

No. It stays with the applicant. A buyer who is 62 or older would need a new application, and a seller who moves must apply again for the new home.

How long before Johnson County sells a home for unpaid tax?

A parcel with three years of delinquent tax must be offered at the sale on the fourth Monday in August. The owner can redeem during the following year by paying the bid plus 10% annual interest.

What kind of county is Laclede County, Missouri?

Laclede County is a rural Ozarks county in south central Missouri whose courthouse and biggest city share the name Lebanon. The land runs 765 square miles, and a slice of the Mark Twain National Forest sits inside it. Camden, Pulaski, Texas, Wright, Webster and Dallas counties form the boundary.

Missouri organized the county on February 24, 1849, and named it for Pierre Laclede, who founded St. Louis. The 2020 count was 36,039 residents, and the Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate stands at 36,943.

Lebanon is the only large city. Conway, Richland, Phillipsburg, Stoutland and Evergreen are the other incorporated places, and Bennett Springs is a census-designated place. Check whether your house lies inside a city limit or out on a county road before you list.

How is Laclede County run, and which school districts touch it?

Laclede County is a statutory third class county, and its government works from the Laclede County Government Center in Lebanon. The county's website says the first permanent courthouse opened in 1851, a replacement from 1894 burned in 1920, and the 1925 building cost $72,428. Voters approved a law enforcement sales tax in August 1994, and that money paid for the present center.

The same page gives a 2024 assessed valuation of $549,845,759, up from $20,234,001 in 1960. The county's population estimate there is 36,680 for 2023, and it calls the growth rapid.

Five public school districts have campuses here: Lebanon R-III, Laclede County R-I at Conway, Gasconade C-4 at Falcon, Joel E. Barber C-5 and Stoutland R-II. Whichever one serves your address places a levy on your bill, so list the district when you describe the house to a buyer.

What does the Census Bureau report about homes and incomes in Laclede County?

A typical owned home in Laclede County is valued at $168,400 in the Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 figures, and owners live in 68.2% of homes. Household income sits at $53,282 in 2024 dollars, and 14.9% of residents are below the poverty line.

  • 14,558 households, averaging 2.48 people
  • 16,211 housing units in July 2025
  • Gross rent of $809 at the median
  • Owner costs of $1,160 a month with a mortgage and $405 without
  • A commute of 21.4 minutes on average

Owners with no mortgage have no escrow account paying the bill for them, so the statement from the collector is the only prompt to pay. If you inherited a paid-off house, put the due date on your calendar.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Laclede County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Which Laclede County office does what?

The Assessor decides what a parcel is worth, and the Collector of Revenue turns that value into a bill and takes the payment. The collector's site is firm about the split: the office collects from the assessor's records and cannot edit a bill. A wrong acreage, owner name or parcel description goes to the Assessor at (417) 532-7163.

The Collector's office also handles merchant license fees and railroad and utility tax, and it distributes money to schools, road districts, fire protection entities and other local subdivisions. Mortgage companies send escrow payments to the same counter.

The collector's online center lets you look up a bill by owner name, parcel number, street address or account number and see the payment history. Open your parcel before you list, so you know which years are paid.

When do Laclede County bills arrive and what are the ways to pay?

The office starts printing statements in late October, once the County Clerk delivers the tax books, and mails them in November. December 31 is the due date. Real estate and personal property arrive as two separate statements, and one check may cover both.

The counter is open from 8am to 4pm on weekdays and closes for state and federal holidays. Paying after December 31 means following the delinquency schedule printed on your statement, and the office is the place to ask for a penalty figure.

  • Walk in with cash, a personal check, a money order or a cashier's check
  • Mail a check in the return envelope and never include cash
  • Pay by card on the website or by telephone, with a convenience fee added
  • Use the drop box at the Second Street courthouse entrance, which takes payments at any hour

A paid receipt returns by mail after processing. A late payment dropped in the box without its penalty is sent back.

Which dates should Laclede County owners circle?

The table below strings the local and state dates into a single year so you can see where a listing falls.

A year of Laclede County property tax dates

NovemberReal estate and personal property statements go out
April 1 to the last Friday in MayRenewal period for the senior tax credit
Second Monday in JulyLast day to appeal a value to the county board
Fourth Monday in August, 10 a.m.Delinquent tax certificate sale at the courthouse
December 31Bill due
Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Laclede County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Can I spread the bill out or freeze it as a senior in Laclede County?

Yes to the first for most owners, and maybe to the second. The Collector offers a prepay plan of ten equal payments built from last year's tax, with the eleventh payment settling the remainder. Payments come out of a bank account automatically. Delinquent accounts and parcels paid through a lender's escrow cannot join, and the number to call is (417) 532-4301.

The senior credit locks the homestead real estate tax at the first-year amount. You may claim one home only, you must live in it, and you renew each year between April 1 and the last Friday in May. The first year always shows a credit of zero, because nothing is refunded for earlier years. The county's home page says the 2026 applications have closed.

The program is not an exemption, so the tax stays on the home. A seller who is enrolled should ask the collector what happens to the credit when the house changes hands.

What if I think my Laclede County value is too high?

Go to the Assessor first, then to the county board of equalization, then to the State Tax Commission. The board wants your appeal in by the second Monday in July. After its letter arrives, you have 30 days to go to the Commission.

You may dispute a value and still be current on the bill. The Commission's guidance says to send the full payment to the collector, mark it as a protest, and attach your written reasons and the market value you claim. A postmark of December 31 or earlier counts.

An estate, trust, LLC or corporation cannot file the Commission appeal without a lawyer. A person settling a relative's estate before a sale should keep that rule in mind.

What does a Laclede County tax certificate sale mean for the owner?

At the sale a bidder pays your back tax and receives a certificate, not a deed. It takes place on the fourth Monday in August at 10 a.m. at the courthouse, 200 N. Adams in Lebanon, after a newspaper lists the parcels for three weeks. Paying the taxes, penalty, interest and costs any time before the bidding keeps the property off the block.

A winning bidder walks away with a certificate of purchase. To redeem, the owner pays the certificate's base amount plus 10% annual interest, and adds any later tax the buyer paid with the same interest. The collector asks for a day's notice and suggests allowing 20 minutes.

After the year runs out, the holder can seek a collector's deed, but only after certified-mail notices to the owner and to lienholders at least 90 days earlier. Liens survive the sale itself. Bid money over the taxes and costs belongs to the owner of record.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

How do I sell a Laclede County house that has back taxes?

Ask the collector for an exact payoff, give it to the title company, and let the closing pay it out of the price.

  • If you bought the house before October, the statement may have gone to the previous owner, so ask them and the collector.
  • If the August sale is close, pay the balance before that date.
  • Tell the collector about the sale if you use the installment plan or senior credit.
  • Call the Assessor about a wrong value well before July.

Written payoff figures protect you if the amount changes by the closing date.

Frequently asked questions

Is the Laclede County property tax deadline December 31?

Yes. Statements arrive in November and are due December 31. Anything paid later follows the delinquency schedule on the statement.

Which office fixes an error in my Laclede County parcel record?

The Assessor, at (417) 532-7163. The collector cannot change a bill because it must collect from the assessor's records.

Can I pay Laclede County property tax by card?

Yes. Card payments work online or by phone and carry a convenience fee. The office also takes cash, checks and money orders, and there is a courthouse drop box.

When must I appeal a Laclede County value?

The county board of equalization needs your appeal by the second Monday in July. The State Tax Commission allows 30 days from the date of the board's letter.

Is it possible to close on a Laclede County home with back tax owed?

Yes. Get a written payoff from the collector so the title company can pay it from your proceeds. If the August sale is near, clearing the balance first keeps the parcel off the list.

What is Lafayette County, Missouri, like?

Lafayette County is a western Missouri county on the eastern edge of the Kansas City region, and Lexington is the county seat. It covers 639 square miles in total, 628 of them land, and touches Jackson, Ray, Carroll, Saline, Pettis and Johnson counties.

The legislature carved it out of Cooper County on November 16, 1820 and called it Lillard County at first. In 1825 it took the name of the Marquis de La Fayette, who was visiting the United States at that time. German immigrants arrived shortly before and after the Civil War and came to make up a large share of the people in Concordia, Higginsville, Wellington, Napoleon and Lexington.

The census of 2020 found 32,984 residents. The Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 33,531, a gain of 1.6% from the 2020 base.

One piece of local history stands out. After the sheriff was killed in May 1919, Minnie Mae Talbott won the special election to replace him and became the first woman elected sheriff in the United States.

Which towns and school districts sit inside Lafayette County?

Lexington, Higginsville, Odessa, Concordia, Wellington, Waverly and Alma are the best known towns, with Napoleon, Corder, Dover, Mayview and Bates City among the smaller ones, and a piece of Oak Grove at the western edge. Six public school districts reach into the county, and the levy of yours is printed on the bill.

  • Lexington R-V, which runs Lexington High School
  • Lafayette County C-1 in Higginsville
  • Odessa R-VII
  • Concordia R-II
  • Santa Fe R-X in Alma
  • Wellington-Napoleon R-IX

Metropolitan Community College counts these districts in its service area, though the county lies outside its in-district taxing area.

How does the Census Bureau describe housing and work in Lafayette County?

Homes that owners occupy here have a typical value of $216,500 for 2020 to 2024, and 75.7% of households own. Household income reaches $80,612 in 2024 dollars, and 9.7% of residents live below the poverty line.

Lafayette County housing and income, Census QuickFacts

The same data counts 732 employer establishments in 2023 and 2,364 businesses without employees in 2024.

Other QuickFacts entries add color: 20.8% of residents are 65 or older, 22.5% are under 18, 87.0% of households have broadband, 91.6% of adults finished high school and 26.2% hold a bachelor's degree or more. The 2020 census counted 14,065 housing units, 8.5% of them vacant, and 30.7% of residents lived in urban areas.

Who are the Assessor and the Collector in Lafayette County?

Craig Williams is the Assessor, based in the courthouse at 1001 Main Street, Lexington. His office answers at (660) 259-6158 or assessor@lafayettecountymo.gov from 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM on weekdays.

Lori Fiegenbaum has been Collector since March 1, 2003. The Collector of Revenue takes in current and delinquent real and personal tax for the county and for each district that has an approved levy, then pays out the money to schools, the library, fire districts and other entities every month.

The Assessor's site hosts a free GIS map and sells an enhanced version by annual subscription. Personal property declarations can be filed online until May 1 each year.

How and when do I pay a Lafayette County tax statement?

Statements are mailed in early November and fall due on receipt. After December 31 they are delinquent. If nothing has come by Thanksgiving, call the Collector at (660) 259-6171.

A payment mailed on time needs a December 31 postmark or earlier. Later ones come back unprocessed unless the late fees are enclosed. A single check can settle all statements, and the office takes neither partial nor incorrect amounts.

  • The Collector's website
  • The mail, addressed to P.O. Box 365, Lexington, MO 64067
  • A toll-free number with the PIN printed on your statement
  • The office at 1001 Main Street, with cash, a personal check, a card or a money order

The counter opens from 8:30 to 4:30 on weekdays and stays staffed at noon. Closings around Christmas and New Year's appear on the collector's home page. You can also print a tax receipt from the county site.

Does Lafayette County offer property tax relief to seniors?

Yes. The county commissioners adopted Ordinance #25-01 on April 2, 2025 under Senate Bills 190 and 756 and section 137.1050 of the Missouri statutes, and the credit covers a senior's primary residence.

The collector's page reports that the 2026 application period has ended and promises an update when the 2027 period opens. If you applied and qualified last year, you do not file again. A new applicant uses the application form on that page, and a FAQ covers renewals.

Read the FAQ before a sale to see how a change of residence affects the credit.

How do I contest a Lafayette County value?

Talk with the Assessor, then file with the county board of equalization on or before the second Monday in July. A further appeal goes to the State Tax Commission within 30 days after the date on the board's letter.

The Commission also permits payment under protest. You send the whole amount to the collector by December 31, label it as a protest, and enclose a written statement of your reasons and your idea of market value. Someone who bought less than 30 days after the county mailed the statement, or who never heard about an increase, may skip the board and go straight to the Commission.

A corporation, LLC, trust, estate or limited partnership needs an attorney to file.

What does Lafayette County do about delinquent real estate tax?

The Collector runs a delinquent tax sale in August every year. Missouri's tax sale rules fill Chapter 140 of the state statutes, and the bidder at that sale gets a certificate of purchase rather than an immediate deed.

The county's collector pages give the month and nothing more, so ask the office for this year's date, the list of parcels and the amount needed to remove yours. Ask which tax years put a parcel on the list, too.

If you sell while taxes are open, the title company can pay the balance from your proceeds at closing.

What do I gather before selling a Lafayette County house that owes tax?

Collect a current statement and a written payoff from the Collector, and confirm that both the real estate and personal property accounts are clear. The office refuses partial payment, so the payoff must cover the entire statement.

  • Open the Assessor's GIS map and compare the acreage and address with your deed.
  • Ask whether a senior credit applies and what a sale does to it.
  • Print your paid receipt from the county site.
  • Decide with the buyer how the current year will be split.

Bring the figures to the closing so the settlement statement matches the collector's numbers.

Frequently asked questions

What is the last day to pay Lafayette County property tax without penalty?

December 31. The payment must carry a postmark on or before that date.

What phone number reaches the Lafayette County Collector?

Call (660) 259-6171, weekdays from 8:30 to 4:30. The mailing address is P.O. Box 365, Lexington, MO 64067.

Who runs the Lafayette County Assessor's office?

Craig Williams. The office is at 1001 Main Street in Lexington, and the phone is (660) 259-6158.

Will the Lafayette County Collector accept part of a bill?

No. Partial and incorrect payments are refused, although one check may cover all of your statements.

Is there a Lafayette County tax credit for older homeowners?

Yes, under Ordinance #25-01 for a senior's primary residence. The 2026 window has closed, and the county will announce the 2027 window on the collector's page.

Which McDonald County office does what on a tax bill?

Property tax in McDonald County runs through two courthouse offices. The Assessor sets values and takes questions or appeals. The Collector mails the statements, accepts payment and runs the delinquent tax sale.

  • Collector: 408 Harmon Street, Pineville, MO 64856; mail to PO Box 725; phone (417) 223-7408.
  • Assessor: McDonald County Courthouse, 408 Harmon Street, Pineville; mail to PO Box 726; phone (417) 223-4361 for real estate and mapping.
  • Doors open weekdays from 8:00 am until 4:00 pm with no lunch closure, and both offices skip state holidays.

Address changes on a tax bill go through the Assessor, not the Collector. If you are selling and the bill still carries an old mailing address, fix that first.

What is McDonald County like for a seller?

McDonald County fills the far southwestern corner of Missouri. Arkansas lies to the south and Oklahoma to the west, with Newton County above and Barry County beside it. The county covers 539 square miles of land, was organized in 1849 and has its seat at Pineville. The largest city is Noel, with Anderson, Goodman, Jane, Lanagan and Southwest City among the other incorporated communities. Interstate 49 and U.S. 71 carry traffic north and south, and Routes 43, 59, 76 and 90 cover the rest.

Census estimates for July 2025 show 23,992 residents, 3.0 percent above the 2020 base. The county has 9,940 housing units, and roughly two in three households (67.3 percent) live in a home they own. The five-year survey value for those homes is $154,700, median gross rent is $767, and household income runs $52,375. The county issued 18 building permits in 2025.

The McDonald County R-I School District, based in Anderson, serves most of the county, with campuses in Noel, Pineville, Rocky Comfort, Southwest City and Jane. Small areas fall in other districts, so the school district line on your tax bill matters when you compare homes.

How is a McDonald County home valued?

Every taxable parcel and personal property item is valued as of the January 1 assessment date that state statute sets, and the Missouri State Tax Commission oversees each county assessor. Assessed value is a share of market value, and the share depends on the property class.

McDonald County assessment classes with a worked example on $100,000 of market value
Property classAssessment rateAssessed value on $100,000
Residential19%$19,000
Agricultural12%$12,000
Commercial32%$32,000

The levy then comes from each taxing body that covers the parcel: school districts, road districts, cities, fire districts and others such as a junior college. The Assessor's page adds that McDonald County itself receives no property tax levy for operations and relies on sales tax for day to day funding.

Under RSMo 137.115, new assessed values are set on January 1 of each odd-numbered year and carry into the following even year, except new construction. The same section requires a physical inspection before an assessor raises a residential parcel by more than 15 percent, excluding new construction.

What is the payment deadline for McDonald County taxes?

Personal property and real estate statements leave the Collector's office during the opening week of November each year. Each one is payable as soon as it arrives and turns delinquent once December 31 passes. For the 2026 bills, that means the mailing is already out and the deadline is December 31, 2026.

  • All statements can be paid with a single check, and partial payment cannot be accepted.
  • The Collector takes cash, a personal check, a money order or a credit card, whether you pay at the counter, by mail or online.
  • Payments postmarked after December 31 are returned unprocessed unless late fees are included.
  • If no statement arrives by the end of November, call the Collector. A missing bill does not cancel the debt or any penalty and interest.

Missouri law has the collector add a penalty once taxes go unpaid past the delinquency date (RSMo 139.100). Ask the Collector at (417) 223-7408 for the current penalty and interest percentages before you pay late. The same statute treats a mailed payment as paid on its postmark date.

The Collector also holds the delinquent tax sale in August each year, so a parcel with old unpaid bills can move toward auction long before a seller notices.

What is the route to contest a McDonald County value?

Begin with a call to the Assessor at (417) 223-4361 to request an informal hearing on the value, and bring sales of similar nearby homes, repair estimates or photos that support a lower number. Ask the same office for the filing date for the local equalization board.

If the board leaves the value unchanged, RSMo 138.430 lets an owner appeal to the State Tax Commission by the statutory deadline or 30 days after the board acts finally, whichever falls later. When an appeal is filed, the disputed taxes are impounded in a separate fund instead of going to the taxing bodies.

Missouri also lets a taxpayer pay under protest. Under RSMo 139.031, you settle the whole bill ahead of delinquency and hand the collector a written statement of your grounds. A protest that is not followed by a circuit court suit against the collector within ninety days becomes void. An appeal already pending before the State Tax Commission replaces that suit requirement.

What relief programs apply to McDonald County owners?

The Missouri Department of Revenue runs the Property Tax Credit Claim, often called the circuit breaker. It gives certain senior citizens and 100 percent disabled individuals a credit for part of the property tax or rent they paid, up to $1,100 for owners who own and occupy their home and $750 for renters. The amount depends on taxes paid and total household income, taxable and nontaxable. Questions go to PropertyTaxCredit@dor.mo.gov.

The State Tax Commission also explains a homestead exemption for a former prisoner of war who has a total service-connected disability. The owner must occupy the homestead as a primary residence and give the assessor proof, including a letter from the Department of Veterans Affairs and discharge records or a records center letter showing former prisoner of war status.

Military personnel stationed in the county under orders with a home of record outside Missouri generally do not owe Missouri personal property tax on non-business items, according to the same State Tax Commission FAQ.

What should a McDonald County seller do about unpaid tax?

Treat the tax bill as a closing item. Before listing a McDonald County house, call the Collector for the status of every year on the parcel, then have the closing agent divide the current year's bill between the parties. A parcel with delinquent years can reach the August sale, so clear older balances first.

  • Check the owner name and mailing address on file at the Assessor's office.
  • Request a payoff figure from the Collector for every parcel you are selling, including land and any manufactured home.
  • Keep your settlement statement, because it shows how the year's tax was split.
  • If the assessed value looks high, raise it with the Assessor before the board deadline rather than after closing.

Frequently asked questions

What date makes a McDonald County tax bill late?

Anything unpaid after December 31. Bills go out the first week of November, and a payment postmarked in January comes back unless late fees ride along.

Can I pay half of my McDonald County bill now and half later?

No. The Collector states that partial payment cannot be accepted, though all statements can be paid together with one check.

What assessment rate applies to a McDonald County house?

Houses carry a 19 percent rate, farmland 12 percent and commercial parcels 32 percent of market value. A $100,000 home therefore shows $19,000 of assessed value before any levy is applied.

Where do I send an address correction for my tax statement?

The Assessor's office at (417) 223-4361. The Collector's site routes address changes there.

When is the McDonald County delinquent tax sale?

The Collector holds the delinquent tax sale in August. Call the Collector at (417) 223-7408 for the exact date and the parcels listed.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Dunklin County?
