Which offices handle property tax in Dunklin County, Missouri?

Two elected offices in the Kennett courthouse split the work. The assessor decides what a parcel is worth, and the collector mails the bill and takes the money. Both are at 100 Kennett Court Square, Kennett, MO 63857, and both keep weekday hours listed in the table further down.

The collector page lists Judy Thompson as Collector-Treasurer, with Room 203, a mailing address of PO Box 445 and phone 573-888-2180. The assessor is Rena Ingram, at 573-888-1409 or 573-888-4771. Angela Casey is the recorder of deeds, in Room 204, at 573-888-3468.

The collector sends out money for every body that levies tax on Dunklin County property:

  • The ambulance district and the health center
  • The library and the schools
  • The state and the townships
  • The road and bridge fund and the sheltered workshop

City taxes are a separate bill. The collector says they go to the city, and a county check should never be mailed together with a city payment.

What does a seller need to know about Dunklin County itself?

Dunklin County sits in the Bootheel, the far southeastern corner of Missouri, and Kennett is the seat of government and the biggest town. The county was cut from Stoddard County in 1845 and named for Governor Daniel Dunklin. The state's lowest point is here, where the St. Francis River leaves Missouri for Arkansas in Buffalo Township, and the county lies south of 36 degrees 30 minutes north, which puts most of it in the Sun Belt by one research definition.

Besides Kennett, the incorporated places are Arbyrd, Campbell, Cardwell, Clarkton, Holcomb, Hornersville, Malden and Senath, plus the town of Rives. Census-designated places include Frisbee, Hollywood and White Oak. Buyers in a Dunklin County town pay both a county and a city tax bill, so ask each office what is owed.

The Census Bureau's QuickFacts for Dunklin County give a feel for the housing market:

  • 26,855 residents in the July 2025 estimate, down 5.1 percent from the April 2020 base of 28,292
  • 13,520 housing units, with 62.3 percent of homes occupied by their owners
  • $97,600 median owner-occupied value for 2020 to 2024
  • $648 median gross rent and $47,849 median household income
  • Only 30 permits for new building in 2025

A median home value under $100,000 means a tax bill is often a few hundred dollars, so a small delinquency can still be a large share of a seller's equity. Pull the statement early.

How does the Dunklin County assessor set the value of a house?

Missouri law has the assessor list all taxable real property each year, with new values set as of January 1 of each odd-numbered year. Those values carry into the even-numbered year, except for new construction. Under RSMo 137.115, a home is assessed at 19 percent of true value, farmland at 12 percent and commercial property at 32 percent, so a $100,000 house carries $19,000 of assessed value before the levy is applied.

If the assessor wants to raise a residential parcel by more than 15 percent, apart from new building, a physical inspection has to happen first. The owner can ask for an interior look and has at least 30 days to make that request. A drive-by does not count.

An owner who changes how a property is used, for example from farm to residential, may apply to the assessor for reclassification. The assessor's page for Dunklin County says the office aims for equitable and accurate appraisals, and it also hosts a personal property filing link online.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Dunklin County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How do I appeal a Dunklin County assessment?

Start with the notice. When an assessor raises a value, RSMo 137.180 requires word to the record owner, mailed to the last known address, and in a reassessment year the notice is due by June 15. Call the assessor's office at the numbers above if the new value looks off, and bring sale prices of similar houses.

The formal route is the county Board of Equalization, which hears appeals from the assessor's value under RSMo 138.060 and starts with no presumption that the assessor is right. In a county outside the charter group, the assessor carries the burden of proof only where the value rose 15 percent or more and the cause was not new building. The State Tax Commission says a Board appeal must be filed by the second Monday in July. For 2027 that falls on July 12. Ask the Dunklin County Clerk where the form goes.

If the Board's decision stands, the next step is the State Tax Commission, which takes a complaint by September 30 or within 30 days after the Board's final action, whichever is later. Appeals for property owned by an LLC, corporation, trust, estate or limited partnership must be filed by an attorney. Attach the tax bill or the Board decision letter, and hold other evidence until the Commission asks for it.

When are Dunklin County property taxes due, and what does a late bill cost?

The State Tax Commission puts the due date at December 31 each year. Mailed payments count as paid on the postmark date under RSMo 139.100, so a December 31 postmark is on time. After January 1 the collector adds a penalty, and RSMo 140.100 sets it at 18 percent of each year's delinquency, with a cap of 2 percent per month on land redeemed before the sale.

The Dunklin County collector has house rules worth knowing before anyone drives to Kennett:

  • Send the statement back with the payment, or the check is returned and an in-person payer pays to print a duplicate
  • Partial payments and part-cash, part-check payments are refused
  • Cash, credit and debit cards, personal checks with an address, phone and driver license number, bank checks and money orders are accepted
  • Older delinquent taxes must be paid before current taxes are taken
  • No tax information is given by phone. Visit Room 203, fax the office (a $3 fee applies per parcel) or write

A homeowner disputing the value can still pay under protest. Pay the full bill before the delinquency date, write a statement of the reasons with the claimed value, and file suit against the collector within 90 days under RSMo 139.031. A refund claim for tax paid by mistake must be filed within three years.

What happens at the Dunklin County delinquent tax sale?

The collector runs the sale on the fourth Monday of August, which is the date written into RSMo 140.150. The collector's page says real estate with taxes two years old is offered each August. The 2026 sale has passed, and the collector posted a notice in October 2026 about properties left after a third offering, with deeds issued immediately on purchase.

The statute lets the owner pay taxes, penalty, interest and costs at any time before the sale. Notice goes first by regular mail to the owner of record. A certified second notice follows when the assessed value is over $1,000. Not receiving the notice does not erase the tax.

An owner of a Dunklin County house with old tax years should treat the August calendar as a hard stop. Settling the balance before that Monday keeps the house out of the offering, and after the sale the owner's choices narrow.

Where do I find each Dunklin County office, and what hours do they keep?

All three offices share one courthouse square. The table below pulls the details from each county page.

Dunklin County offices for a property tax and sale file

AssessorRena Ingram100 Kennett Court Sq, 573-888-1409Mon to Fri, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.
Recorder of DeedsAngela CaseyRoom 204, 573-888-3468Mon to Fri, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., closed 12 to 1

Source: Dunklin County website office pages.

What should I do about taxes when selling a Dunklin County house?

Ask the collector for a current statement, and pay any old year first, since current taxes are not accepted ahead of delinquent ones. Give the title company the parcel number and the collector's phone, so the payoff matches the office's records. The sales contract sets how the current year's bill is divided between buyer and seller, so have the title company read that clause.

The recorder's fee schedule changed on August 27, 2026. A one-page document now costs $26, and each added page up to 20 pages costs $3 more, so a three-page deed is $32. Plats and surveys have their own rates. The recorder says Missouri counties accept electronic filing through a shared portal, so ask the office if a title company will file that way.

When liens, tenants or repairs pile up on a Kennett-area house, a written cash offer is one way out, and the tax payoff is taken from the price at closing.

Frequently asked questions

Who sends the property tax bill in Dunklin County?

The Dunklin County Collector-Treasurer, Judy Thompson, sends it from Room 203 of the Kennett courthouse. The assessor, Rena Ingram, only sets the value. City taxes are paid to the city, so check that bill separately.

What is the Dunklin County property tax deadline?

December 31. The State Tax Commission gives that date, and a mailed payment is on time if postmarked by then. Penalty starts the next day under RSMo 140.100 at 18 percent of the year's delinquency.

Can I pay part of my Dunklin County bill?

No. The collector accepts only the full amount due and does not take partial or part-cash, part-check payments. Pay the oldest delinquent year first, because current taxes are not taken until delinquent ones are cleared.

When does Dunklin County sell tax-delinquent houses?

On the fourth Monday of August each year, under RSMo 140.150. The collector offers real estate with taxes two years old. You can pay the taxes, penalty and costs any time before the sale.

How do I contest my Dunklin County home value?

Call the assessor first, then file with the Board of Equalization by the second Monday in July. If the Board does not change the value, file with the State Tax Commission by September 30 or a month after the Board decision, whichever is later.

Which office bills and collects Pike County property tax?

The Pike County Collector of Revenue, Tara J. Eskew, bills and collects tax on land, houses, vehicles and boats from the courthouse in Bowling Green. The office sits at 115 West Main, Bowling Green, MO 63334, and the number is 573-324-3281. The counter opens at 8 in the morning on weekdays and closes at half past four, shutting for lunch between noon and 1 except in tax season.

The collector says it handles more than $20 million a year and passes the money to schools, roads, cities, fire districts, levees and drainage districts every month. It collects what the assessor's records show and cannot change a value, a legal description or a mailing address. Those fixes go to the Pike County Assessor at 573-324-3261. See the collector's general tax page for the current wording.

How does Pike County look in the Census numbers?

Pike County sits on Missouri's eastern edge, with the Mississippi River as its border and Bowling Green as the county seat. The county was organized on December 14, 1818, and it covers about 670 square miles of land. Its cities are Bowling Green, Clarksville, Curryville, Frankford and Louisiana, and its public school districts include Bowling Green R-I, Louisiana R-II and Pike County R-III at Clarksville.

The Census Bureau's QuickFacts page shows a county that is rural and settled mostly by owners. It also shows how modest the housing market is next to the Kansas City side of the state.

  • 17,955 residents in the July 2025 estimate, about 26 per square mile as of 2020.
  • 7,682 housing units, and owners occupy 73.3 percent of the homes that have residents.
  • A typical owned home is worth $146,000, and typical gross rent is $778 a month.
  • Median household income is $54,989, and residents past 65 make up 21.1 percent of the county.
  • Only 20 building permits were issued during 2025.

A low median value means that a single delinquent year can be a large share of what a house is worth, so the timing of the bill matters more here than the rate itself. Source: Census QuickFacts.

When are Pike County tax bills mailed and due?

Pike statements are mailed on November 1. If yours has not arrived by mid-November, call the collector, because a bill that never shows up still carries the tax and the late charges. Payment is on time when it is postmarked by December 31, and anything postmarked later is returned unprocessed unless interest and penalty are included.

The office accepts no partial payments and no pro-rated amounts. If a parcel has more than one unpaid year, the oldest year is paid first, a rule the collector cites as RSMo 140.110. One check can cover several bills as long as you send every statement with it.

How can I pay a Pike County property tax bill?

You can pay at the courthouse, by mail, by phone or online. Cash is taken in person only. Checks, money orders, cashier's checks and certified checks are accepted, and so are credit and debit cards with a convenience fee. A mailed payment counts as paid on its postmark date, and the receipt comes back by mail.

  • E-check: a flat 80 cents.
  • Visa, Mastercard and Discover: 2.35 percent of the total, minimum $1.00.
  • American Express: 2.95 percent of the total, minimum $1.00.
  • Automatic installments: bank draft under the free Pre-Pay program, described below.

How does Pike County assess a home, and when can I appeal?

Values are set on January 1 annually. The residential share is 19 percent of market value, farmland counts 12 percent of production value and all other real estate counts 32 percent. The office says real estate is reviewed every two years and that state law requires values to fall within 5 percent of market value.

The Pike County Assessor's calendar lists the dates that matter for a dispute:

Pike County assessment calendar from the county assessor's site
DateEvent
January 1Assessment date
March 1Personal property list due
June 15Notice of increased value mailed
July 1Totals go to the County Clerk
Third Monday in JulyBoard of Equalization hearings begin
September 30State-level appeal due

The assessor's page says staff will review a parcel and explain how the value was reached. If your taxes are escrowed, tell your lender as soon as a notice arrives so the monthly payment can be adjusted. Source: Pike County Assessor.

Can I dispute a Pike County bill without missing the payment deadline?

Yes. The State Tax Commission says the December 31 tax deadline applies whether or not an appeal is pending, though you may appeal without having paid. To pay under protest, send the full bill to the collector by December 31, write "paid under protest" on the check, and file a written statement of your grounds, including the fair market value you claim.

A dispute already before the county board has to wait for the board's decision letter, and the next filing is due thirty days after the date on that letter. A property held in a trust, LLC, corporation or estate must be appealed through an attorney. See the State Tax Commission guide.

What happens to a Pike County parcel with unpaid tax?

Real estate with a third year of delinquent tax must be offered at the August sale under RSMo 140.160. The auction is held at 10 a.m. on the south side of the courthouse, on August's fourth Monday. Listings run in a local paper for three consecutive weeks, and the last notice appears no later than 15 days ahead of the sale.

  • Bidding opens at the amount of all taxes, interest and charges.
  • The buyer pays at once and holds a Certificate of Purchase.
  • The owner keeps possession during the one-year redemption period (RSMo 140.310).
  • Money paid above the opening bid goes to the County Treasurer, and the owner of record can claim it. After three years it goes to the schools (RSMo 140.230).

The collector says a very high percentage of owners pay after the advertisement and before the sale. The office does not give legal advice, so a seller facing a listing should speak with a Missouri attorney.

Which Pike County programs can lower the cost?

Three programs are worth a call. The collector's Pre-Pay plan draws monthly amounts from a bank account at no charge, with the first installments based on the prior year's totals and the balance collected on November 15. It requires a yearly bill of at least $100 for real estate and $100 for personal property, and a voided check is required to enroll.

The Senior Tax Freeze for 2027 takes applications from March 15 to June 30, 2027. The applicant must hold the deed to a primary residence in Pike County, be 62 by January 1 of the application year, be a Missouri resident and have no delinquent taxes. The state also runs the Property Tax Credit claim, which gives qualifying seniors and 100 percent disabled individuals up to $1,100 as owners, based on income and tax paid (Missouri Department of Revenue).

What does a seller in Pike County need to settle first?

Plan to settle every open year before the sale, since the collector will not accept the current bill until older years are paid. The Pike office does not pro-rate a bill, so the split between buyer and seller is something the closing agent works out in the contract.

If you owe more than one year, call the collector in Bowling Green for exact payoff figures with interest. Get the legal description from the assessor and the mailing address on file before you list, because the collector cannot fix either one.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

What is the Pike County property tax deadline?

The deadline is December 31, judged by postmark. Pike County statements are mailed on November 1, and a payment postmarked after December 31 is returned unless interest and penalty are included.

Can I pay half of my Pike County bill now and half later?

No. The Pike County Collector accepts no partial payments, and payments for the wrong amount are returned. The free Pre-Pay installment plan is the way to spread the cost through the year.

How do I get a Pike County value corrected?

Call the Pike County Assessor at 573-324-3261 before the county board opens its July hearings. If that fails, the State Tax Commission appeal is due by September 30 or thirty days after the board mails its letter.

When is the Pike County tax sale?

The auction runs at 10 a.m. on August's fourth Monday, on the south side of the courthouse. Only parcels with a third year of delinquent tax must be offered, and an owner can pay before the sale to remove the parcel.

Who qualifies for the Pike County Senior Tax Freeze?

An applicant must hold the deed to a primary Pike County residence, be 62 by January 1 of the year applying, live in Missouri and owe no delinquent tax. Applications for 2027 run from March 15 to June 30, 2027.

Which offices handle property tax in Bates County, Missouri?

Three desks in the Bates County offices in Butler cover most property tax questions, and each has a room on West Dakota Street. The Collector/Treasurer, Kacie Robey, is in Room 2 at 103 West Dakota, Butler, MO 64730. The Assessor, Carl Bettels, is in Room 4, and the County Clerk, Jami Page, is in Room 1. Courthouse offices keep 8:30 am to 4:30 pm hours on weekdays and close from noon to 1 pm.

The Collector answers at 660-679-3341 or through the courthouse line at 660-386-7776, option 3. The Assessor is reached at option 4 on the courthouse line, and the Recorder of Deeds, Danyelle Baker, in Room 3 handles the deed side of a sale. The Collector also acts as county Treasurer, so one office both collects and distributes the money to schools, townships and the health center.

What is Bates County like for a home seller?

Bates County is a rural part of west central Missouri, close to the Kansas line and part of the Kansas City metropolitan area. It covers 851 square miles, of which 837 are land, and it was organized in 1841 and named for Frederick Bates, the state's second governor. Butler is the county seat and largest city, and Adrian, Drexel, Rich Hill, Amsterdam, Amoret, Hume and Rockville are among the other towns.

The 2020 census counted 16,042 residents, with an estimate of 16,512 for 2025. All of that population is classed as rural. The county had 7,189 housing units, 11.1% of them vacant, and 74.3% of occupied homes were owner occupied. Interstate 49, US 71 and Routes 18 and 52 are the main roads.

School districts reaching into the county include Butler R-V, Adrian R-III, Rich Hill R-IV, Drexel R-IV, Hume R-VIII, Miami R-I, Ballard R-II and Archie R-V. Which district sits on your parcel affects the levy lines on the bill, so look at the statement itself.

When does a Bates County tax bill turn delinquent?

Missouri law sets the line at the start of the new year. Under RSMo 139.100, once a taxpayer misses the deadline, the collector must add a penalty after the first of January. Mail is treated as paid on its postmark date, and a certified or registered mailing counts on the date of certification. If the postmark is missing or unreadable, the collector uses judgment and documents the call.

For 2026 bills, that makes December 31, 2026 the practical cutoff, with the new penalty arriving on January 1, 2027. The county has a 24-hour drop box on the east side of the Administration Building.

What are the ways to pay in Bates County?

The Collector's website lists payments in person, by mail, online and through the drop box. Card fees are passed to the payer and none of that fee goes to Bates County, which the site ties to RSMo 139.055.

  • In person at Room 2, 103 West Dakota, Butler.
  • By mail to the Collector's office, with a postmark on or before the deadline.
  • Online through the Collector's website, where debit cards cost $4.00 and credit cards cost 2.45%.
  • In the 24-hour drop box on the east side of the Administration Building.

The Collector adds that a paid receipt shown on a phone screen works at the DMV or Department of Revenue office.

How does the Bates County tax sale work?

The Collector holds a delinquent real estate tax certificate sale on the fourth Monday of every August. For the 2026 sale, the eligible properties were published on July 22, 2026, and full payment had to arrive in the office before 4:30 PM on Friday, August 21, 2026 to stop the auction. Both dates have passed, so any 2026 sale outcome is a matter of record at the Collector's office.

Payment on a sale-eligible parcel must be made by cash, money order, card or cashier's check. Web and phone payments were not allowed for those parcels.

If a buyer wins at a tax auction, RSMo 140.405 gives the owner a right to redeem. The buyer must send notice by first class and certified mail at least ninety days before the date they can take the deed, and an owner who wants to sell or add liens must redeem first. Anyone considering a sale of a delinquent parcel should talk to the Collector about the redemption amount first.

How do I appeal a Bates County assessment?

The first step is to ask the Assessor's office, Room 4, to review your value. If the answer is unsatisfactory, the next step is the local Board of Equalization. Ask the County Clerk's office in Room 1 when the board meets and how to book a hearing.

After that, Missouri law gives you a right to appeal to the State Tax Commission. RSMo 138.430 sets that window at the deadline stated in the chapter or thirty days after the board's final action, whichever is later. The Commission says the filing is due on or before September 30 of the assessment year or within thirty days of the board's decision, whichever is later, and the board's decision letter must be uploaded with the complaint.

Owners should note a rule for estates: property held by an LLC, trust, association or estate must be represented by an attorney at the Commission, while a home owned by a person or persons need not be. The Commission's phone number is 573-751-1715.

What if I disagree with a bill and still need to pay?

Missouri allows payment under protest. Under RSMo 139.031, you pay the full bill before the delinquency date and file a written statement with the Collector listing your grounds and the value you claim. The Collector sends the undisputed share to the taxing districts and holds the disputed share in a separate fund.

A taxpayer who protests must start a circuit court action against the Collector within ninety days of filing the protest, unless a timely assessment appeal is already pending. That pending appeal, filed with the State Tax Commission or the court, takes the place of a separate suit.

Refunds of erroneous tax are also possible. A written application must be filed within three years of the payment.

What should a Bates County seller do about taxes before closing?

Ask for a payoff figure from the Collector's office before the contract date, and check the Collector's records for earlier years. Then give that number to the title company.

  • Confirm all current and delinquent real estate bills on the parcel.
  • Find out whether the parcel appears on a tax sale list.
  • Ask the Assessor about any pending change of value.
  • Confirm the Recorder in Room 3 will record the deed and release of any old deed of trust.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I pay property taxes in Bates County, Missouri?

Pay the Bates County Collector in Room 2 at 103 West Dakota, Butler, by mail, online, or in the east side drop box of the Administration Building. Phone 660-679-3341. Card payments carry a fee passed to the payer.

When does a Bates County property tax bill become delinquent?

After December 31. Missouri law adds a penalty after January 1, and mailed payments count on their postmark date. Mail well before the cutoff so the postmark falls inside the window.

When is the Bates County tax sale?

The fourth Monday of August every year. For 2026, owners had to pay in full in the office by 4:30 PM on Friday, August 21, 2026 to prevent the auction, so that date has passed.

How do I appeal my Bates County property value?

Start with the Assessor in Room 4, then use the Board of Equalization through the County Clerk. A further appeal goes to the Missouri State Tax Commission by September 30 or thirty days after the board's decision, whichever is later.

Can I pay my taxes under protest in Bates County?

Yes. Pay the whole bill before it turns delinquent and give the Collector a written statement of your grounds. A court action to recover the protested amount must follow within ninety days unless an assessment appeal is already pending.

Where do I take Dent County property tax questions?

The Dent County courthouse, 400 N. Main Street, Salem, MO 65560, houses most of the offices that touch your tax bill. The Assessor, Alisa Brookshire, is at 573-729-6010 or dentcountyassessor@gmail.com. The Collector of Revenue, Shannon VanKirk, is at 573-729-3911. Weekday hours for both run from 8:00 in the morning to 4:30 in the afternoon, with major holidays off. The County Clerk, Angie Curley, at 573-729-4144, schedules Board of Equalization appointments. The Recorder of Deeds, Cindy Ard, is at 112 E. Fifth Street, Suite 2, phone 573-729-2198.

The Assessor puts a value on taxable property. The Collector bills it, receives payment, hands the money to the taxing districts and also handles escrow payments sent in by mortgage holders. Statements can be viewed and paid at dentcountycollector.com. The Assessor's GIS map lets you pull up a parcel by street address, owner or parcel number, and a yearly subscription is available if you need property data or maps regularly.

Vehicle owners should know that new plates require proof that the previous year's personal property tax was paid, shown by a paid receipt or a waiver from the Assessor. The Collector also takes county merchant license fees and sends the paid personal property list to the License Bureau each month.

When does Dent County mail and collect real estate tax?

Bills for real estate and personal property leave the Collector's office by November 8 and are due by the end of December. A penalty begins on January 1. The Collector distributes the money to 22 political subdivisions with certified levies, a group that includes schools, roads and fire districts, and also collects tax on state assessed utilities such as railroads, pipelines and electric lines.

  • Paying before the new year avoids the penalty, and the Collector can give you the late schedule.
  • Where a lender escrows your tax, check that the lender actually received the bill.
  • Personal property runs on its own clock: owners list it with the Assessor from January 1 to March 1, and lateness can cost up to $105.00 under RSMo 137.280.
  • Newcomers from another Missouri county bring their last paid personal property receipt to open a Dent County account, and anyone new to the state must open one too.

If you sell a house, ask the Collector how to report the new owner's name and mailing address, or have the title company do it, so the next bill goes to the right person.

How is a house in Dent County assessed?

Values are set as of January 1, the assessment date in statute, across more than 11,000 parcels. Real estate has three subclasses: residential at 19% of market value, agricultural at 12% of production value and everything else at 32% of true value in money. Odd-numbered years bring a full reassessment, while new construction and additions join the rolls annually.

Dent County indicatorFigure

A $167,500 house, the county median, would be assessed near $31,825 at 19%. The bill is that figure divided by 100 and multiplied by the combined levy of the districts serving the parcel, which the Collector or Assessor can look up for you.

How do I appeal a Dent County valuation?

Begin by asking the Assessor how the value was reached. The State Tax Commission oversees assessors, and Dent County's page says its field representatives visit monthly and spot-review properties each year. If you remain unconvinced, take the case to the Board of Equalization, where RSMo 137.275 sets the filing cutoff at the second Monday in July.

The County Clerk books those hearings. RSMo 138.060 has the board settle appeals summarily and says the assessor's valuation carries no presumption of being right. When assessed valuation jumped at least 15% over the prior assessment and the jump is not from new construction or improvements, the assessor must prove the value is no higher than true market value. Bring last cycle's notice, photos and any appraisal or sales evidence.

RSMo 138.430 gives owners the State Tax Commission as the next stop, with a clock of 30 days after the board's final action or the chapter's own deadline, whichever comes later. The statute gives the right to appeal to the Commission from the local board's decision, so the board hearing comes first.

What happens to Dent County land when tax goes unpaid?

Delinquent land goes to auction on one statewide date, the fourth Monday in August (RSMo 140.150). Before the hammer falls, the owner can settle with the Dent County Collector by paying the tax plus penalty, interest and costs. Call 573-729-3911 for the current list and amounts.

  • The Collector mails a first class notice to the publicly recorded owner before the list is published.
  • A second notice goes by certified mail only when the assessed valuation is over $1,000.
  • If the certified notice comes back unsigned, the Collector sends a notice by first class mail to both the owner of record and the occupant.
  • An owner who never received a notice still owes the tax.

Under RSMo 140.405, whoever buys at a tax sale must warn owners and lienholders of their right to redeem at least ninety days before taking a deed. If you hold an inherited or vacant house, call the Collector early to learn what is owed.

What is Dent County like for someone selling a house?

Dent County dates from February 10, 1851, when it was named for the early settler Lewis Dent. It covers 755 square miles, with part of the Mark Twain National Forest and the Ozark National Scenic Riverways inside its borders. Salem, the county seat, counted 4,608 residents in 2020, and its Victorian courthouse of 1870 is on the National Register of Historic Places. Bunker is the county's other city. Neighbors are Phelps, Crawford, Iron, Reynolds, Shannon and Texas counties.

The 2020 census found 14,421 people, down from 15,657 ten years earlier, and the 2025 estimate is 14,584. The county history credits mining and timber, with the old Sligo iron furnace and the lead mines about 30 miles east, and names US Foodservice as the largest employer today. Workers average a 21.0 minute commute and 14.4% of residents are in poverty.

The school districts named for the county are Salem R-80, Dent-Phelps R-III, Green Forest R-II, North Wood R-IV and Oak Hill R-I. Salem also has a Southwest Baptist University annex and a public library. The Census Bureau counted three building permits in the county for 2025. Ask a local title company about recent sales near you.

Frequently asked questions

Which day is Dent County's last day to pay without penalty?

The end of December. Bills go out by November 8 and the penalty begins January 1. Phone 573-729-3911 if yours is missing.

Can Dent County taxes be paid on the web?

Yes, through dentcountycollector.com, the portal the Collector's page names for viewing and paying statements. The office at 400 N. Main Street in Salem also takes payment on weekdays during business hours.

How is residential property assessed in Dent County?

At 19% of market value. Farm ground is assessed at 12% of production value and all other property at 32% of true value in money. Full reassessment comes in odd-numbered years, with new construction added every year.

What is the cutoff for a Dent County appeal to the local board?

By the second Monday in July under RSMo 137.275. Reach the County Clerk at 573-729-4144 about hearing dates.

When is the personal property list due in Dent County?

March 1. Property held on January 1 is listed with the Assessor between January 1 and March 1, and a late list can draw a penalty of up to $105.00. Newcomers must set up an account.

Moniteau County, MO Property Tax Guide: Offices, Appeals and Selling With Tax Due

Cash Home Buyers in Missouri
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Moniteau County, MO Property Tax Guide: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Moniteau County, MO Property Tax Guide sale
  • Turn the Moniteau County, MO Property Tax Guide offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling in Moniteau County? Get a Cash Offer

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Moniteau County?

What kind of county is Moniteau, and who lives in its houses?

Moniteau is a rural central Missouri county of about 15,400 people, with California as its seat and largest city, and Jefferson City's metropolitan area includes it. The county was organized in 1845 and named for Moniteau Creek. Of its 419 square miles, 415 are land, and it touches Cooper, Boone, Cole, Miller and Morgan counties. U.S. 50 crosses it, along with state Routes 5, 87 and 179.

Census QuickFacts for the 2020 to 2024 period describe 5,729 households averaging 2.45 people, with roughly four in five homes occupied by the people who own them. Homeowners put the median value of their houses at $181,900, while the median rent is only $735. Workers commute 26.5 minutes on average. Just 6 building permits were issued during 2025.

Besides California, you will find Clarksburg, Jamestown, Lupus and Tipton, plus the communities of Fortuna and Latham. Six school districts serve the county: Clarksburg C-2, High Point R-III, Jamestown C-1, Moniteau County R-I, Moniteau County R-V and Tipton R-VI. The 2020 census counted every resident as rural.

Which Moniteau County offices deal with your tax bill?

Everything runs through the courthouse at 200 E. Main Street in California, and two rooms matter most. Check the numbers below before you call, since each office keeps the same weekday schedule, 8:00 to 4:30, closed on holidays.

  • Assessor, Room 105. Reach it at 573-796-4637 or assessor@moniteaucountymo.gov. According to its own site, this office determines the worth of every piece of taxable real and personal property in the county.
  • Collector, Room 101. Call 573-796-4521. The collector prints the tax statements, sends the money to schools and other taxing districts each month, issues merchant licenses and holds the August sale of delinquent land. Staff stay on through the noon hour.
  • Recorder, Room 102. Moniteau's circuit clerk doubles as the recorder, at 573-796-2071 per the Missouri Association of Counties.

When a statement arrives, read the address, the listed vehicles and the legal description. Taxpayers can settle up at the counter, by phone, through the mail or on the collector's website, using cash, a personal check, an e-check, a money order or a credit card.

How does Moniteau County value a house for tax purposes?

Real estate gets a fresh valuation every other year. Section 137.115 says new assessed values are determined as of January 1 of an odd-numbered year and then carry through the next even-numbered year, apart from new construction.

Missouri taxes only a slice of market value. Under the same law, subclass 1 real property is assessed at 19 percent, subclass 2 at 12 percent and subclass 3 at 32 percent, while personal property is assessed at 33 and one third percent, with lower rates for livestock, farm machinery, poultry and a few other items. Because the subclass determines the percentage, ask the assessor how your parcel is classified. A manufactured home used as a dwelling gets the residential percentage.

If the assessor wants to raise a subclass 1 value by more than fifteen percent, excluding new construction, an on-site physical inspection must come first. A drive-by does not count. The owner may request that the inspection include the interior, and has no less than thirty days after written notice to ask.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Moniteau County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What does the Moniteau County property tax calendar look like?

The cycle begins on January 1, which is the date property is valued, and ends with a December 31 payment cutoff. Personal property lists go to the assessor, and the assessor's instructions say late fees begin if they come back after March 1. Anyone who lived in the county on January 1 should list cars, boats and equipment, and a mobile home owned on someone else's land belongs on the list too. Household goods, inventories, clothing and items of personal use are exempt.

Key dates for a Moniteau County parcel, drawn from county offices and state law
WhenEventWhere it comes from
January 1Values fixed for the yearSection 137.115
March 1Personal property list must be in, or late fees accrueCounty assessor
Second Monday of JulyLast day to file with the local equalization boardState Tax Commission
Early NovemberBills go out by mailCounty collector
After December 31Unpaid bills are delinquentCounty collector
Fourth Monday of AugustDate delinquent land can be soldSection 140.150

If November ends without a bill in your mailbox, the collector wants a call right away. A missing bill does not erase the tax, the penalty or the interest. Couples who are divorcing should know the collector cannot split a statement afterward.

Can you contest a Moniteau County valuation, and how?

Yes, in three steps. Talk to the assessor first, then take the dispute to the county equalization board, and finally to the State Tax Commission. The commission's guidance sets the board deadline at the second Monday of July. Once the board mails its decision letter, the next appeal is due thirty days from that letter's date, a rule that section 138.430 backs with its "whichever date later occurs" wording.

Some owners can skip the board. The commission accepts a direct filing in two situations:

  • The assessor never told the current owner about a new or higher value at least thirty days ahead of the board deadline.
  • A new owner closed on a purchase less than thirty days after the county mailed the tax statement.

Property titled to a corporation, LLC, limited partnership, trust or estate must be appealed through an attorney.

Disputing a value does not pause the due date. To avoid interest, send the full amount to the collector by December 31, write "paid under protest" on the check, and attach a written statement of your reasons and the value you think is fair. Pay without protest and without an appeal, and that year's assessment is closed to challenge, though next year's remains open.

Which Missouri programs lower the bill for Moniteau homeowners?

The Property Tax Credit Claim is the one most people ask about. The Department of Revenue describes it as a credit for certain seniors and 100 percent disabled individuals, worth up to $1,100 for homeowners who live in the house and up to $750 for renters. How much you receive depends on what you paid in tax or rent and on total household income, taxable and not.

Former prisoners of war with a total service-connected disability have a constitutional exemption on the homestead they own and occupy. To claim it, the State Tax Commission says to give the assessor proof of residence, a federal letter confirming the disability and either a DD 214 or an archives or VA letter establishing POW status.

Service members who are away from home on military orders owe no interest on late payment, according to the commission's FAQ, although the collection fee may still apply. For any program, confirm the current rules with the assessor or collector before you plan around it.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Moniteau County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What should a seller do about the tax bill before closing in Moniteau County?

Ask the collector what the parcel owes today, penalty and interest included, before any contract is signed. Under section 140.150, land with unpaid tax is subject to the August sale, set for the fourth Monday, yet the owner may clear the taxes, penalty, interest and costs at the collector's office up until the sale happens. The collector must first mail notice to the recorded owner, and a certified second notice follows when assessed value tops $1,000.

Ask whoever handles your closing to settle the balance with the collector's office so nothing is left behind on the parcel. Our Missouri property tax guide explains how appeals work statewide, and the Missouri homestead page covers exemptions. The collector's website carries the current levy sheet for anyone estimating a bill.

Frequently asked questions

Which office sends property tax statements in Moniteau County?

The county collector in Room 101 at the California courthouse prints and mails them each November. The assessor, down the hall in Room 105, supplies the values behind them.

What day do unpaid Moniteau County taxes turn delinquent?

Anything still owing after December 31 is delinquent. The collector then offers the land at the August sale, and the owner may still pay before the sale.

By when must I contest a value in Moniteau County?

The county board's filing deadline is the second Monday of July. After the board's letter, you get thirty days to continue to the State Tax Commission.

What share of my house's worth is taxed in Moniteau County?

Missouri assesses subclass 1 real property at 19 percent of true value, subclass 2 at 12 percent and subclass 3 at 32 percent. Your assessor can name the class for your parcel.

Is there a credit for older homeowners in Moniteau County?

Seniors and 100 percent disabled individuals may file Missouri's Property Tax Credit Claim, which pays up to $1,100 to homeowners who occupy their house. Income and the tax actually paid set the amount.

Which Pettis County offices handle property tax?

Two courthouse offices split the work, and a third records the deed. The assessor values the property. The collector sends the bill and takes the payment. Both are at 415 S Ohio in Sedalia, MO 65301, and both answer through the county switchboard at 660-826-5000.

  • Assessor Christopher Woolery, Suite 218, extension 920, fax 660-829-2492, wooleryc@pettiscomo.com
  • Collector Marsha Boeschen, second floor, Suite 216, extension 921, fax 660-826-6254, pettiscollector@pettiscomo.com, open 8:00 am to 5:00 pm on weekdays except holidays
  • Recorder of Deeds, Suite 106, extension 922

The assessor's page is blunt about who does what: the assessor does not set tax rates or taxing district budgets. Schools, cities, fire districts and other districts set their own rates, and the collector gathers whatever amount is assigned to each owner.

How does Pettis County value a house, and how often?

Real estate here is revalued in odd numbered years. Whatever the assessor sets as of that January 1 stays on the books through the following even year, and only new construction or demolition moves it in between. The assessor uses sales of comparable properties, the condition and physical attributes of the home, and any building or teardown activity.

Fixed percentages turn market value into assessed value:

  • Homes and other residential land: 19 percent
  • Farmland: 12 percent
  • Commercial parcels: 32 percent

For a home with a market value of $166,300, the Census median for the county, a 19 percent assessment gives an assessed value of about $31,600. Each district's levy is applied to every $100 of that figure to produce the bill. The statute behind the percentages is RSMo 137.115, which also bars the assessor from raising a residential parcel by more than 15 percent without a physical inspection, unless the increase comes from new construction.

How do I appeal a Pettis County property assessment?

The assessor's page lays out three stages. First comes a sit-down at the assessor's office to learn how your number was built and what records sit behind it; the page says many disputes end right there.

  1. Call the assessor soon after the valuation notice reaches you and ask for a meeting.
  2. If that fails, the county clerk supplies forms and deadlines for the Board of Equalization, which hears the assessor and then you.
  3. Still unhappy? The State Tax Commission takes appeals until September 30 or thirty days after the board's last action, whichever comes later.

Two state rules lean toward the owner. A value increase has to be reported to the record owner, with the statute setting June 15 as the mailing date (RSMo 137.180). Before the board, nobody presumes the assessor is correct, and a parcel whose assessed value jumped 15 percent or more, new construction aside, puts the proof on the assessor (RSMo 138.060). The commission route is set out in RSMo 138.430.

When and how do I pay Pettis County property tax?

On the collector's page, December 31 is the date that counts, and money not received by then draws penalties and fees. Because card and phone payments clear slowly, the page tells people to pay well ahead of midnight on the last day.

Choices listed by the collector:

  • Devnet wEdge website with Discover, American Express, MasterCard or Visa; the charge is the larger of $1.55 or 2.45 percent
  • The same website by e-check, free of charge but slow to clear, around ten days
  • Phone line 877-690-3729: enter code 3526, then the account or parcel number
  • The Suite 216 counter in person; the office itself takes no payments by phone

The county pockets none of the card fee. Receipts by mail take roughly a week to ten days, so a vehicle owner who needs proof of payment for a Department of Revenue license renewal late in the month is told to pay in the office.

What does Pettis County say about personal property and new residents?

Personal property such as vehicles, livestock, farm machinery and business equipment is taxed in the county where the owner lived on January 1. The assessor mails forms in January, and a declaration filed by March 1 avoids late assessment penalties. Vehicles and most equipment are assessed at 33 and one third percent of value, while farm equipment and livestock are assessed at 12 percent and a vehicle with historic plates at 5 percent.

A person who moves into Pettis County from another state brings registration papers or titles to the assessor's office to set up an account. Those who were not Missouri residents on January 1 are exempt for that first year and can get a statement of no tax due. People moving within Missouri need proper tax papers from the county where they lived on the prior January 1.

Is there a senior tax credit in Pettis County?

Yes. Pettis County adopted the Senate Bill 190 program, which gives an eligible senior a credit on the real estate tax bill of a primary residence. The county's FAQ sets the main conditions:

  • The applicant is a Pettis County resident who turned 62 before January 1 of the first credit year
  • The applicant owns or has a recorded interest in the home and is liable for its real estate taxes
  • The home is the primary residence, lived in 183 days or more a year, and is assessed as residential
  • Rental portions, bed and breakfast space and short term rental areas do not qualify

The credit equals the difference between the tax owed and what the home owed in the base year, and it is a credit on the statement, not a refund. It does not reach back before the base year. Applications and every renewal must be signed before a notary or collector staff. The 2026 window ran from March 2 through May 29, which has passed, so ask the collector in Suite 216 when the next one opens. Skipping a renewal ends the program and forces a new base year.

How should I handle taxes when selling a Pettis County house?

Call the collector at 660-826-5000 ext 921 before you list and ask for the balance on your account, including any earlier year. The collector looks accounts up by account number or by the name on the tax statement, so have the bill in hand. Ask the title company to show that balance as a line on the settlement statement.

Online and phone payments post slowly, so a payoff made in the last days before closing is better made at the courthouse counter in Suite 216. If your mailing address has changed, tell the assessor's office in Suite 218 so notices reach you.

What is Pettis County like for property owners?

Sedalia anchors a county of roughly 682 square miles in west central Missouri. Small towns such as Green Ridge, Houstonia, Hughesville, Ionia, La Monte, Smithton and Windsor dot the rest. Property bills here include levies for whichever school district covers the parcel, among them Sedalia 200, Pettis County R-V, Green Ridge R-VIII, La Monte R-IV and Smithton.

Population estimate, July 202544,254

Frequently asked questions

What is the last day to pay Pettis County real estate tax?

December 31. The collector's page says any payment not received by that date is subject to late penalties and fees, so allow time for online and phone payments to process.

What assessment rates apply to Pettis County property?

Residential property is assessed at 19 percent of market value, agricultural at 12 percent and commercial at 32 percent.

Where does a Pettis County valuation dispute go?

Meet with the assessor first, then go to the county Board of Equalization through the county clerk, and last to the State Tax Commission. The commission deadline is the later of September 30 or 30 days after the board's final action.

Does paying Pettis County taxes online cost extra?

Card payments carry a fee of at least $1.55 or 2.45 percent, which the county does not keep. E-checks have no fee but need about ten days to clear.

Does Pettis County offer tax relief to seniors?

Pettis County runs the Senate Bill 190 credit for residents 62 and older on a primary residence. The 2026 application period ended May 29, so ask the collector about the next window.

Which offices handle property tax in Benton County, Missouri?

Benton County splits the work among the Assessor, the Clerk and the Collector, all based in Warsaw. The table lists who to call for each job.

Benton County, MO property tax offices
OfficeOfficialContact
AssessorJim HansenP.O. Box 40, Warsaw; real estate 660-438-5323, personal property 660-438-5473
County ClerkSusan PorterfieldP.O. Box 1238, Warsaw; 660-438-7326
CollectorDavid BrodersenP.O. Box 428, Warsaw; 660-438-7721

Source: Benton County, MO official website.

The Collector prepares and mails the bills, collects for the county and for the cities of Warsaw, Lincoln, Cole Camp and Ionia, and gives out duplicate paid receipts. The Clerk schedules Board of Equalization appointments and certifies values and rates for every political subdivision.

What is Benton County like for a home seller?

Benton County sits in west central Missouri and covers 753 square miles, of which 704 are land and 48 are water. Organized on January 3, 1835 and named for Senator Thomas Hart Benton, it has Warsaw as its seat and largest city. Cole Camp, Lincoln and Ionia are the other communities with their own tax bills through the Collector, and U.S. Route 65 and Routes 7, 83, 82 and 52 carry traffic through it.

The county is older and quieter than many of its neighbors. The 2020 census counted 19,394 residents, with a median age of 53.8 and 30.7% of residents 65 or older. The 2025 estimate is 20,536. The county has 13,551 housing units, and 37.1% of them were vacant at the 2020 count, while 80.4% of occupied homes were owner occupied.

Public school districts are Warsaw R-IX, Cole Camp R-I and Lincoln R-II, plus the Lutheran School Association in Cole Camp. Neighbors by county line are Pettis, Morgan, Camden, Hickory, St. Clair and Henry.

How is property valued in Benton County?

Missouri law has the Assessor value all taxable real and personal property as of January 1. In Benton County, the office values more than 32,000 parcels and manages over 12,000 personal property accounts. Real property is reassessed in every odd numbered year, and in even numbered years the staff looks for new construction or lost improvements, so 2026 was a review year and the next full reassessment lands in 2027.

Field staff carry ID badges and drive marked county vehicles. State statute lets them inspect each property from the outside, but it does not allow entry into a structure. Owners provide the rest by questionnaire or on site.

The State Tax Commission requires the Assessor to stay within 10% of market value for real estate, and the state can withhold funding from an office that falls out of tolerance. The taxing districts, not the Assessor, set the levies that turn value into a bill.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Benton County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How can I challenge a Benton County value?

The Assessor's page lists a sequence of steps worth following in order.

  • Request your Property Record Card and look for errors in size, condition or description.
  • Tell the Assessor about issues that affect value and that the office may not know about.
  • Bring an appraisal by a Missouri certified appraiser if you have one.
  • If the value stands, ask the County Clerk for a Board of Equalization appointment.
  • After the board rules, appeal to the Missouri State Tax Commission.

RSMo 138.430 lets an owner appeal from the local board to the Commission within the time set in the chapter or thirty days after the board's final action, whichever is later. The Commission states the deadline as September 30 of the assessment year or thirty days after the board's decision, whichever is later, and asks for the board's decision letter at filing. Property owned by an LLC, trust, association or estate must have an attorney there.

When are Benton County tax bills due?

The Collector's site says statements should arrive by Thanksgiving, and owners who have not received one by then should call. All statements are due on receipt and become delinquent after December 31. To avoid late fees, mail must be postmarked no later than December 31, and a payment postmarked after that date is returned unless the late fees come with it.

In office, you can pay by cash, personal check or credit card. A drop box on the north side of the courthouse takes payments through midnight on December 31 with no penalty. All of your statements can go in one check, but the office does not accept incorrect or partial payments.

Missouri's mail rule is in RSMo 139.100, which treats a mailed payment as paid on its postmark date. For 2026 bills, December 31, 2026 is the date to protect.

Does Benton County prorate taxes for a sale?

The Collector's own explanation is that the tax obligation is set on January 1. By state law, even an owner who moves out the next day is taxable for the year, and the law makes no provision for prorating the bill. The current owner is responsible for paying every dollar due on the property.

In practice, a Benton County sale therefore settles the split by contract. The title company usually collects the seller's share from the proceeds and either pays the county or credits the buyer. Ask the Collector at 660-438-7721 what the parcel owes, including earlier years, before you sign.

The Collector has no authority to change a statement without the Assessor's help, so a value mistake has to go to the Assessor before payment.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Benton County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What happens at the Benton County tax sale?

The Collector conducts the annual tax sale on the fourth Monday in August for real estate that has two years of delinquent tax. The auction is held in front of the courthouse in Warsaw, and the county's tax sale site carries the list of parcels.

A sale does not end an owner's rights at once. RSMo 140.405 requires the buyer to send first class and certified mail notice of the right to redeem at least ninety days before the buyer can take the deed, and an owner who wants to transfer or encumber the property must redeem first.

If you want to sell a delinquent parcel, bring the whole payoff to the Collector and the title company before the sale date, since a redeemed parcel can close like any other.

Can I pay a Benton County bill under protest?

Yes. RSMo 139.031 lets a taxpayer pay the full bill before the delinquency date and file a written statement of the grounds, including the value they claim. The Collector distributes the undisputed part and holds the disputed part separately.

A circuit court action against the Collector must start within ninety days of the protest, unless a timely assessment appeal is already pending with the State Tax Commission or a court. The same statute lets a taxpayer ask for a refund or credit of tax paid by mistake within three years of the payment.

Personal property has its own timeline. Taxpayers must list personal property owned on January 1 with the Assessor by March 1 to avoid penalties.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I pay property tax in Benton County, Missouri?

Pay the Benton County Collector in Warsaw, by mail to P.O. Box 428, in the office, or in the drop box on the north side of the courthouse. Call 660-438-7721 for the current payoff on your parcel.

When do Benton County property taxes become delinquent?

After December 31. Statements are due on receipt, and a payment postmarked after December 31 is returned unless late fees are included. The drop box accepts payments through midnight on December 31.

Does Benton County reassess property every year?

Real property is reassessed in odd numbered years, and the Assessor checks for new construction and lost improvements in even numbered years. The next full reassessment is 2027.

When is the Benton County tax sale?

The fourth Monday in August each year. It covers real estate with two years of delinquent tax and takes place at the Benton County Courthouse in Warsaw.

Is Benton County property tax prorated when I sell?

No, state law does not prorate the bill, and the owner on January 1 stays responsible for the year. The sale contract decides how buyer and seller split it, and the title company handles the payment at closing.

What kind of county is Cedar County, Missouri?

Cedar County lies in the southwest part of Missouri, with Stockton as the seat of government and El Dorado Springs as the biggest town. It was founded on February 14, 1845 and takes its name from Cedar Creek, a tributary of the Sac River. Of its 499 square miles, 474 are land and about 24 are water, much of it Stockton Lake. Its neighbors are St. Clair County to the north, Polk to the east, Dade to the south, Barton to the southwest and Vernon to the west.

Two public school districts serve the county, El Dorado Springs R-II and Stockton R-I. The Census Bureau counts no residents in urban areas, which means a house here usually sits in a small town or on rural land.

Who runs property tax in Cedar County?

Two elected offices split the work. The Assessor values property and the Collector of Revenue sends and collects the bills. Neither sets the tax rate, which comes from the school, fire, ambulance and other taxing districts that appear on each statement.

  • Collector of Revenue: Lisa Nelson, 113 South Street, PO Box 280, Stockton, MO 65785, 417.276.6700 ext. 224, fax 417.276.4658, on the main floor of the courthouse in Room 1.
  • Assessor: main courthouse line 417-276-6700, with ext. 258 or 259 listed for personal property questions.
  • Online payments and bill search run through the Collector's page on cedarcountymo.gov.

The Assessor's site, cedar.missouriassessors.com, has the parcel search, the real estate and personal property FAQs and the newsletters.

When are Cedar County property tax bills due?

The Collector mails statements for land, buildings and personal property in November. Payment is due by December 31, and for mailed payments the postmark decides the month. Anything postmarked after December 31 must include penalty and interest, and the delinquent payment chart on the statement shows the added amount. If no bill has arrived by December 1, call the Collector, because a missing bill does not cancel the obligation.

  • Online payments carry a 2.4 percent card convenience fee, or a $1.95 fee for an e-check.
  • Mailed receipts take 7 to 10 days. Online receipts can be printed once the payment posts.
  • A prepay plan splits last year's amount into nine equal installments, with a September 30 cut-off to start. The November statement then shows the balance left.
  • Personal property is valued on January 1, and the full year's tax is owed even after the owner has moved away.

Real estate tax liability stays attached to the parcel itself.

How does the Cedar County Assessor set home values?

The Assessor's FAQ says real property is reassessed in every odd-numbered year, and in even years the office values new construction. Values reflect the property's condition on January 1. A building torn down after that date is still taxed for the full year. Since 2027 is an odd year, owners should expect a reassessment cycle then.

Field reviewers look at the outside of buildings and enter a home only if the owner asks. The Assessor's office cites RSMo 137.130 for its right to inspect when it lacks information. A separate notice on the Assessor's site explains that the State Tax Commission told Cedar County in 2024 it was out of compliance and ordered a 14.99 percent increase on improved residential and commercial property for 2025, except new construction. The Assessor's example turned an assessed value of $19,300 into $22,193.07. Change in Value notices went out in June 2025.

Personal property sheets are due before March 1, with late penalties from $15 up to $105 depending on assessed value. The Assessor offers e-filing with the account number and ePIN printed on the sheet.

What is the process to dispute a Cedar County assessment?

Start by calling the Assessor to talk through the value. If you still disagree, the next stops are the county board that hears valuation appeals and then the State Tax Commission. Ask the Cedar County Clerk or Assessor for the board's current forms and hearing dates.

StepTiming
Informal review with the AssessorAfter the Change in Value notice arrives
Hearing request to the county boardMust be lodged by the second Monday of July
Appeal to the State Tax CommissionWithin the statutory window or a month after the board decides, whichever comes later

One rule can help an owner whose value jumped. RSMo 138.060 says the board starts with no presumption that the Assessor's number is right. It also puts the burden of proof on the Assessor when a property's assessed valuation rose at least 15 percent from the last assessment, unless the rise came from new construction or improvements.

What tax relief can Cedar County owners ask about?

Cedar County adopted the Senate Bill 190 senior tax freeze, and the Collector's page says senior tax credit applications are taken from March 15 to May 15, 2027. The Assessor's office says seniors and people who are 100 percent disabled can also pick up a 948 form, a credit based on real estate taxes paid in the year.

Disabled veterans should read the Assessor's April 2026 notice. It says 2025 House Bill 921 did not pass, despite what some websites say, and that a similar 2026 bill still needed approval by both houses and the Governor. The office promises to apply any new exemption as soon as the law allows. Ask the Assessor before assuming an exemption applies to your parcel.

What happens if Cedar County taxes go unpaid?

The Collector runs a delinquent land tax sale on the fourth Monday of August every year, and the office issues certificates of purchase and handles redemptions. Unpaid land can end up in that sale, so a seller with back taxes should clear them or tell the title company early.

For a sale in this county, the practical steps are short.

  • Ask the Collector for the current balance on the parcel, including any penalty and interest.
  • Give the title company the Collector's contact details so the payoff appears on the settlement statement.
  • Tell the Collector and the Assessor the buyer's name and mailing address once the deed is recorded so the next bill reaches the right person.

Because the tax liability stays with the land, a buyer inherits an unpaid balance unless it is settled at closing.

How is the Cedar County population changing?

These are Census Bureau QuickFacts figures for Cedar County.

  • Population estimate for July 1, 2025: 14,888, against 14,188 at the 2020 census.
  • Land area 474.47 square miles, about 29.9 people per square mile.
  • Housing units in 2025: 6,985, with a 74.1 percent owner-occupancy rate.
  • Owner-occupied homes had a middle value of $168,100 in the 2020 to 2024 survey.
  • Median gross rent: $767.
  • Median household income: $48,181, with 16.5 percent of people in poverty.
  • Building permits in 2025: 8.
  • People aged 65 and over: 24.1 percent of the population.

Frequently asked questions

When are Cedar County, MO property taxes due?

December 31 each year. The Collector mails statements in November, and the postmark on a mailed payment decides whether it is on time. After December 31, penalty and interest apply. If no bill has come by December 1, call 417.276.6700 ext. 224 in Stockton.

Which office answers questions about my Cedar County value?

The Cedar County Assessor, Leah Morton, at 417-276-6700. Personal property questions go to ext. 258 or 259. The Assessor's website has the real estate FAQ, the parcel search and the latest newsletter. The Collector, a separate office, cannot change a value on a statement.

How do I pay Cedar County property tax online?

Use the Pay/Search link on the Collector's page at cedarcountymo.gov. Cards carry a 2.4 percent convenience fee and e-checks a $1.95 fee. Search by last name then first name with no comma. Receipts for online payments can be printed from the site once the payment is applied.

Is there a way to challenge my Cedar County property value?

Yes. Talk to the Assessor first, then lodge a hearing request with the county board no later than the second Monday of July, as RSMo 137.275 requires. A further appeal to the State Tax Commission is open within the statutory window or a month after the board decides, whichever comes later.

What if Cedar County land has delinquent taxes when I sell?

Pay the balance at or before closing, usually through the title company, because the lien follows the land. The Collector holds a delinquent land tax sale on the fourth Monday of August. Get the exact payoff, with penalty and interest, from the Collector in Stockton while the sale is still being scheduled.

What is Lawrence County, Missouri, and where does it sit?

Lawrence County fills 613 square miles of the southwest Missouri Ozarks, with Mount Vernon as the county seat. 612 of those miles as land, and the Ozark Cavefish National Wildlife Refuge lies inside the line. Dade, Greene, Christian, Stone, Barry, Newton and Jasper counties are its neighbors.

Missouri organized Lawrence County in 1845 and named it for naval officer James Lawrence, the man behind the cry "Don't give up the ship!" The county's website names these communities: Aurora, Freistatt, Halltown, Hoberg, LaRussell, Marionville, Miller, Mt. Vernon, Pierce City, Stotts City and Verona. Part of Monett also lies within the county.

The 2020 census found 38,001 residents, and the July 2025 estimate reaches 39,401, which is 3.7% above the April 2020 base.

Where are the Lawrence County offices and what are the sales tax rates?

Lawrence County is a Class 3 county governed by a three-member commission. Most offices are in Mt. Vernon: the historic courthouse at 1 E. Courthouse Square, the Justice Center at 240 N. Main St., the Law Enforcement Center at 1525 Missouri Dr. and the Health Department at 1549 Missouri Dr.

County Clerk Tammy Riebe handles general inquiries at 1 E. Courthouse Square, Suite 101, phone 417-466-2638.

The county's levies page also posts third quarter 2025 sales tax totals from the state revenue department: 6.725% in the unincorporated county, 9.225% in Aurora, Mt. Vernon, Marionville and Verona, 9.475% in Miller, and 9.850% in Pierce City. The half-cent tax that voters approved in 2025 for the expanded Mt. Vernon Ambulance District is not in those figures.

How do the latest Census numbers describe Lawrence County homes?

Owner-occupied homes in Lawrence County carry a typical value of $175,100 for 2020 to 2024, and 73.9% of households own. Household income comes to $61,215, and 12.6% of residents live in poverty.

  • 16,526 housing units in July 2025
  • A gross rent of $800

About 8.3% of residents age five and older speak another language at home, and 9.0% identify as Hispanic or Latino. The county had 689 employer establishments and 6,385 jobs in 2023, with employment down 0.2% from the year before.

The 2020 census recorded a median age of 40.0, with 25.2% of residents under 18 and 19.0% aged 65 or older. It counted 16,219 housing units, 10.0% of them vacant, and 28.5% of residents lived in urban areas while 71.5% lived in rural areas. Among occupied homes, 71.6% were owner-occupied.

Which Lawrence County offices handle my bill?

Doug Bowerman, the Assessor, sits in the basement of the Historic Lawrence County Courthouse in Mt. Vernon. The mailing address is P.O. Box 188, Mt. Vernon, MO 65712, the phone is (417) 466-2831, and the office is open from 8:00 to 4:00 on weekdays.

Kelli McVey, elected Collector of Revenue in 1998, works on the first floor of the courthouse at #1 Courthouse Square. The office banks the month's collections with the county treasury, which sends them on to schools, libraries, ambulance and fire districts and special road districts.

In August the collector also runs the delinquent real estate auction. The office issues merchant and auctioneer licenses as well and handles the escrow payments that mortgage holders send in for owners.

What levies does Lawrence County print for every property?

Source: the county levies page, which also offers a link to pay taxes online.

What is the Lawrence County payment routine?

Statements are mailed in November and should be in your hands by the second week. Each one is due on receipt and delinquent once December 31 passes. Call 417-466-2410 if nothing arrives by Thanksgiving.

Not receiving a statement never erases the debt or the penalty and interest that follow. Mail postmarked after December 31 is returned unprocessed unless it includes both. The collector also asks you to check the mailing address, the vehicles and the legal description on every statement.

  • Visit the courthouse office on weekdays between 8:00 and 3:55
  • Mail to P.O. Box 29, Mt. Vernon, MO 65712
  • Use the collector's website or its phone payment line
  • Offer cash, a personal check, a money order or a credit card

The office closes for state holidays but works through the lunch hour. A single check may cover all of your statements, and part payments are refused. The card company keeps its own processing cost.

What can I do if the Lawrence County assessor's value looks wrong?

Call the Assessor at (417) 466-2831 and ask for a review. If you still disagree, file with the county board of equalization before the second Monday in July. The State Tax Commission is the next stop, and it takes appeals up to 30 days after the date of the board's letter.

A dispute does not require an early payment. The Commission says you may appeal before paying, or you may pay the whole bill by December 31 as a protest, with a written explanation and your own estimate of market value.

An attorney must file for an LLC, estate, trust, corporation or limited partnership. A buyer who closed less than 30 days after the county mailed the statement can appeal directly to the Commission.

What happens at the Lawrence County delinquent tax auction?

Each August the collector offers delinquent real estate at auction. The county's pages give only the month, so call 417-466-2410 for the date, the list of parcels and the sum that would pull yours off it.

Chapter 140 of the Revised Statutes governs these sales in Missouri. The winning bidder gets a certificate, and the owner then has a redemption period to repay the amount with interest. Ask the collector for the figure on your parcel and the length of the window.

A seller can avoid the whole process. If a closing happens first, the title company pays the collector out of your proceeds.

What should a Lawrence County seller line up before listing?

Ask the Collector for a written payoff, then ask the Assessor to confirm acreage, address and the owner of record. A wrong parcel description is cheaper to fix before a buyer's title search finds it.

  • Compare the vehicles and legal description on the statement with your own records.
  • Save the paid receipt for every year you can.
  • Agree with the buyer on how the current year splits.
  • Confirm the August auction date if any earlier year is open.

Ask the Assessor or the Collector whether any relief program applies to your parcel before closing.

Is December 31 the Lawrence County tax deadline?

Yes. Statements arrive in November, and a payment postmarked after December 31 comes back unless penalty and interest are included.

What is the Lawrence County Collector's address?

The office is on the first floor of the Lawrence County Courthouse, #1 Courthouse Square, Mt. Vernon. Mail goes to P.O. Box 29, and the phone is 417-466-2410.

Who is the Lawrence County Assessor?

Doug Bowerman. The office is in the courthouse basement, and the phone is (417) 466-2831.

How long do I have to file a Lawrence County value appeal?

Until the second Monday in July for the county board. The State Tax Commission then allows 30 days from the board's letter.

Does the Lawrence County Collector hold a delinquent tax auction?

Yes, every August. Call 417-466-2410 for the date and the parcel list.

Who do I call in Galena about my tax bill?

Two county offices share the work. The Assessor builds the list of taxable property, and the Collector of Revenue bills and gathers the money. Both are in Galena.

  • Collector of Revenue: 108 E. 4th Street, P.O. Box 256, Galena, MO 65656; 417-357-6124; the courthouse is open weekdays from eight to four and closes for state and federal holidays.
  • Assessor: 106 E. 5th Street, P.O. Box 135, Galena, MO 65656; real estate line (417) 357-6145; personal property line (417) 357-6141; same weekday hours.

The Assessor's page lays out the calendar. Assessment books normally close around July 1 and go to the County Clerk, who sends the figures on to each taxing district. The districts then set their rates, typically by September 1. The Assessor has no say in those rates.

The Assessor's office also keeps the tax maps, adjusting property lines whenever the Recorder of Deeds forwards a warranty deed, per the Assessor's description of its mapping duties. On the Collector's side, the staff directory names separate deputies for real estate, personal property, merchant licensing and the SB190 tax freeze, so ask for the real estate desk when you call about a house, and keep the parcel number handy.

What is the due date for the 2026 bill?

The Collector's announcement says statements for 2026 went into the mail on Friday, November 13, and online payment has been open since November 6. Payment is due by December 31, and a bill still open on January 1 is delinquent.

Anything sent by post must carry a U.S. Post Office postmark dated December 31 or earlier. The Collector's home page adds several practical notes:

  • Card numbers are no longer taken verbally over the phone. Pay at the office or call the number printed on your statement.
  • Debit and credit card payments carry a fee of 2.4%, with a $1.95 floor.
  • A drop box at the north entrance of the Historic Courthouse is emptied daily.
  • A paid receipt can be printed, or shown on a phone, at the license bureau.

Read your statement for errors, including the mailing address. To change an address, call 417-357-6124.

Is the senior tax freeze open right now?

No. The Collector's home page says the application process for the Senior Citizen Property Tax Credit Freeze is closed. The staff list includes a lead for the SB190 tax freeze, who is the person to ask about the next window.

A second benefit comes from the state: the Missouri Property Tax Credit Claim, filed with the Department of Revenue, refunds part of the tax or rent paid for some seniors, disabled owners and renters. Phone the Collector's office at 417-357-6124 to find out whether you fit either program before the next filing season.
